study.html:
• Prolong & deepen, ↓ toxicity, {{hemostasis|إرقاء}}.
  • Adrenaline max: healthy 0.2 mg; cardiac 0.04 mg (~2 cartridges 1:100,000).
  • {{Felypressin|فيليبريسين}} = alternative; avoid in pregnancy.

Maxilla = V2, mandible = V3 of the {{trigeminal nerve|مثلث التوائم}}.

  • PSA → maxillary molars (except MB root of 1st molar = MSA).
  • Greater palatine / Nasopalatine → palate.
  • IAN, lingual, long buccal, mental/incisive → mandible.

IANB (Halstead)

  • Landmarks: {{coronoid notch|الثلمة المنقارية}}, pterygomandibular raphe; 6–10 mm above occlusal plane; barrel over contralateral premolars; ~20–25 mm to bone.

Alternatives

  • Gow-Gates (neck of condyle, whole V3); Akinosi closed-mouth (for {{trismus|الضزز}}); infiltration; intraligamentary.
• Failure (commonest), hematoma (PSA), trismus, transient facial palsy (LA in {{parotid|النكفية}} during IANB), paresthesia (4% solutions), needle breakage, self-trauma.

• Vasovagal {{syncope|إغماء}} — most common emergency.
  • LAST: circumoral numbness/metallic taste/tinnitus → seizures → CNS depression → CVS collapse.
  • Methemoglobinemia — prilocaine.

Adrenaline cautions: uncontrolled HTN, hyperthyroidism, {{pheochromocytoma|ورم القواتم}}, TCA/MAOI, non-selective β-blockers.

flashcards.q: Transient facial palsy in IANB cause?
flashcards.a: LA in the parotid gland (CN VII).

Why does an inflamed/abscessed area resist LA?
PSA block fails to anaesthetise which root?
Esters cause allergy because of which metabolite?
The preservative in some cartridges that can cause allergy is:
Which property determines POTENCY of an LA?
Intravascular injection is reduced by:
Repeated infiltration fails to anaesthetise an acutely abscessed lower molar before extraction. The BEST explanation and action are:
o: The cartridge is faulty — change brand
Low tissue pH in infection raises the ionised fraction (less base crosses the nerve) — use a regional block in healthy tissue away from the infection
Inject more solution directly into the abscess
quiz.e: Acidic inflamed tissue shifts the equilibrium toward the ionised form, so less lipid-soluble base crosses the nerve membrane; a block placed in non-inflamed tissue is more effective.
w: A — the failure is physiological, not a faulty cartridge
C — more solution in the abscess maintains the low-pH problem and risks spreading infection
D — operating without anaesthesia is unacceptable
quiz.ty: LA fails in infection due to low pH (↑ ionised form) → block in healthy tissue away from the abscess.

quiz.q: A 20 kg child needs treatment with 2% lidocaine with adrenaline (max ~7 mg/kg). The approximate maximum number of 1.8 mL cartridges is:
quiz.e: Max ≈ 7 mg/kg × 20 kg = 140 mg; each 2% cartridge has ~36 mg, so ~3-4 cartridges is the ceiling — weight-based dosing is essential in children.
w: A — one cartridge (36 mg) is well below the 140 mg ceiling
C — ~10 cartridges (360 mg) greatly exceeds the limit and risks toxicity
D — there is always a weight-based maximum
quiz.ty: Calculate LA max by weight: 2% lidocaine = 36 mg/cartridge; child dosing is weight-critical.

quiz.q: Minutes after a dental injection a patient becomes pale, sweaty and light-headed, with a slow pulse, then briefly loses consciousness, recovering quickly when laid flat. The diagnosis and management are:
o: Vasovagal syncope — lay flat, raise the legs, reassure
Local anaesthetic toxicity — give lipid emulsion
quiz.e: Pallor, sweating, bradycardia and a brief faint that recovers on lying flat are classic vasovagal syncope, the commonest office emergency; treatment is positioning.
w: A — anaphylaxis causes tachycardia, urticaria, wheeze and hypotension, not bradycardia with quick recovery
C — LA toxicity presents with CNS excitation/cardiac signs, not a simple faint
D — an MI would not resolve simply by lying the patient flat
quiz.ty: Vasovagal syncope (pale, sweaty, bradycardic faint) = commonest office emergency → lay flat, legs up.

quiz.q: After a large dose of prilocaine a patient becomes centrally cyanosed but the cyanosis does NOT improve with high-flow oxygen and SpO2 reads low. The MOST likely cause is:
quiz.e: High-dose prilocaine can oxidise haemoglobin to methaemoglobin, causing cyanosis that does not respond to oxygen (treated with methylene blue).
w: A — an asthma attack causes wheeze and usually responds partly to oxygen/bronchodilators
C — anxiety does not cause true central cyanosis
D — syncope causes pallor and a faint, not fixed cyanosis
quiz.ty: Cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen after prilocaine = methaemoglobinaemia (treat with methylene blue).

pearls: Limit adrenaline to about 0.04 mg in significant cardiac disease (roughly two cartridges of 1:100,000).
Vasovagal syncope is the commonest office emergency — lay the patient flat and raise the legs.
High-dose prilocaine (or benzocaine) can cause methaemoglobinaemia — central cyanosis that does not improve with oxygen.
A transient facial palsy after an IAN block means the solution reached the facial nerve in the parotid — reassure the patient; it resolves.
For a patient who cannot open the mouth (trismus), the closed-mouth Vazirani-Akinosi technique is the block of choice.
mistakes: Exceeding the maximum dose by not calculating mg/cartridge against body weight.
Giving a standard adrenaline-containing dose freely in significant cardiac disease.
Mistaking a vasovagal faint for an allergic reaction and giving adrenaline unnecessarily.
Missing methaemoglobinaemia (cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen) after high-dose prilocaine.
Using an IAN block in a bleeding-disorder patient without cover (deep bleed risk).
Forgetting that the PSA block risks a haematoma (pterygoid plexus).
Performing a standard IANB in a trismic patient instead of the Akinosi technique.
Choosing a long-acting cardiotoxic agent (bupivacaine) where it is not needed.
Attributing a transient facial palsy after an IANB to a stroke rather than parotid LA spread.
Forgetting felypressin is avoided in pregnancy.
Treating LA toxicity (LAST) without considering intravenous lipid emulsion in severe cases.
Giving repeated palatal injections without recognising they are the most painful and using technique to reduce discomfort.
facts: Esters: procaine, cocaine, tetracaine, benzocaine (metabolised by plasma pseudocholinesterase → PABA → allergy).
Amides: lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, articaine, bupivacaine (hepatic metabolism; rare allergy).
Lidocaine 2% with adrenaline 1:80,000 (UK) or 1:100,000.
Articaine 4% + 1:100,000; has a thiophene ring + an ester link (also broken down in plasma).
Mepivacaine: 3% plain or 2% with levonordefrin (useful when adrenaline is to be limited).
Prilocaine: 4% plain or 3% with felypressin; high doses → methaemoglobinaemia.
Bupivacaine 0.5% = longest acting (high protein binding) but the most cardiotoxic.
Cocaine is the only local anaesthetic that is itself a vasoconstrictor.
Topical agents: benzocaine 20% (ester), lidocaine; EMLA = lidocaine + prilocaine.
Adrenaline 1:100,000 = 10 µg/mL; 1:80,000 = 12.5 µg/mL; cartridge = 1.8 mL.
Maximum adrenaline: healthy ~0.2 mg; cardiac ≤0.04 mg.
Felypressin is avoided in pregnancy (oxytocin-like action).
Maxillary teeth: PSA (molars, except MB root of 1st molar = MSA), MSA, ASA; palate = greater palatine + nasopalatine.
Mandible: inferior alveolar, lingual, long buccal, mental/incisive nerves.
IANB (Halstead) landmarks: coronoid notch, pterygomandibular raphe; 6–10 mm above the occlusal plane; ~20–25 mm to the lingula; aspirate.
Gow-Gates block: targets the neck of the condyle (whole V3); landmarks intertragic notch & corner of mouth.
Vazirani-Akinosi block: closed-mouth technique — the choice in trismus.
Maxillary infiltration is effective because the bone is thin/porous; the mandible needs blocks (dense bone).
Other techniques: supraperiosteal infiltration, intraligamentary (PDL), intraosseous, mental/incisive, palatal.
Most common local complication = failure of anaesthesia (technique, inflammation, accessory supply).
Haematoma is classically associated with the PSA block (pterygoid venous plexus).
Trismus after a block = medial pterygoid trauma or haematoma.
Transient facial palsy in an IANB = LA in the parotid gland (CN VII).
Paraesthesia is linked to higher-concentration (4%) solutions (articaine/prilocaine).
Vasovagal syncope is the most common dental-office emergency.
LA systemic toxicity (LAST): circumoral numbness/metallic taste/tinnitus → CNS excitation (seizure) → CNS depression → CVS collapse.
Methaemoglobinaemia (prilocaine) = cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen → treat with methylene blue.
Allergy is almost exclusively to esters or to preservatives (e.g., methylparaben/metabisulfite).
Always aspirate before depositing to avoid an intravascular injection.
Adrenaline cautions: uncontrolled hypertension, hyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, TCA/MAOI, non-selective β-blockers, cocaine users.
mnemonics: Max adrenaline: Healthy 0.2 mg / Cardiac 0.04 mg.
Toxicity sequence: circumoral numbness/metallic taste/tinnitus → CNS excitation (seizure) → CNS depression → CVS collapse.

study.html:
History & examination

  • Medical history: bleeding tendency/anticoagulants, cardiac disease, diabetes, steroids, bisphosphonates, radiotherapy, allergy, pregnancy.
  • Local exam: degree of access & mouth opening, tooth mobility, crown integrity (caries undermines forceps grip), position/crowding, periodontal status.

Radiographic evaluation (read BEFORE you start)

  • Roots: number, length, curvature, divergence, dilaceration, bulbous/hypercementosed apices, fused vs separate.
  • Surrounding bone: density, sclerosis, ankylosis (loss of PDL space), pathology (cyst/tumour).
  • Relations: to the IAN canal (darkening/notching/diversion of the canal → CBCT/coronectomy) and to the antral floor.

Parts: handle – joint – blades (beaks). The beaks are shaped to adapt to the root surface beneath the gingiva and to engage the furcation of multi-rooted teeth.

ToothForceps design clue
Upper anteriors/premolarsStraight or slightly curved, beaks meet (single root)
Upper molarsRight & left; a buccal beak with a point engages the buccal furcation, a smooth palatal beak
Upper 3rd molar / rootsBayonet design for access
Lower anteriors/premolarsBeaks at ~90° to handle, meet (single root)
Lower molarsTwo pointed beaks engage mesial & distal furcations; cowhorn beaks squeeze the furcation to elevate

Elevators luxate teeth/roots, expand bone, and remove roots & interradicular septa.

Three working principles

  • Lever (first-class) — most used; wedge — drives between root and socket wall; wheel-and-axle — rotates a blade engaged in a purchase point.

Types

  • Straight (Coupland's, gouges 1-2-3) — luxation/wedging.
  • Warwick James (straight + left/right) and Cryer's (left/right, triangular) — removing roots and interradicular bone.
  • Luxators / periotomes — sever the PDL with minimal bone loss (atraumatic/immediate-implant cases).
⭐: An elevator must have a defined point of application and be supported by sound bone — never push against a tooth you intend to keep.

study.h: A6. Extraction Technique by Tooth Group
study.html:
ToothPrimary movement
Upper central/lateral incisor, canineRotation (+ slight labial) — conical roots
Upper premolarsBuccopalatal ONLY (1st premolar often bifid → no rotation)
Upper molarsBuccal then palatal; deliver buccally (3 divergent roots)
Lower incisorsLabiolingual (flat thin roots)
Lower canine/premolarsRotation + buccal (premolars conical)
Lower molarsBuccolingual; figure-of-eight; cowhorn into furcation

General rule: apical pressure (to displace the centre of rotation apically and dilate the crest) → expansion → delivery along the path of least resistance.

study.h: A7. Removal of Roots & Retained Apices
study.html:
• First try a closed approach: narrow-bladed (root) forceps, or an elevator/luxator with a purchase point; for a multi-rooted tooth, remove the interradicular septum then elevate each root.
  • If closed methods fail: open (surgical) approach — flap, conservative buccal bone removal, create a purchase point, elevate; or the open apical window for a high root.
  • A small, deep, non-infected apex close to the IAN/antrum may be left under review when removal risks more harm than the fragment.

Indications: failed forceps, retained/fractured roots, ankylosis/hypercementosis, grossly carious crown, impaction, thick dense bone, dilacerated/divergent roots.

Steps

  1. Flap: full-thickness mucoperiosteal, broad base, on sound bone; relieving incision avoiding the mental nerve & not over the defect.
  2. Bone removal: a buccal gutter with an irrigated bur (avoid overheating → necrosis).
  3. Tooth division: section crown/roots to deliver along separate paths of least resistance.
  4. Debride & smooth: remove follicle/granulation, file sharp edges, irrigate copiously.
  5. Closure: tension-free sutures; achieve haemostasis.

• Fracture of: crown, root, alveolar bone, maxillary tuberosity, or the mandible (deep impaction / atrophic or pathological bone).
  • Displacement of a root into the maxillary antrum, the IAN canal, the infratemporal fossa (upper 8), or the sublingual/submandibular space (lower 8 lingual plate).
  • Oro-antral communication (upper molars/premolars).
  • Nerve injury: inferior alveolar, lingual, mental, (rarely) nasopalatine.
  • Soft-tissue injury (slipped elevator), damage to the adjacent tooth, fractured/dropped instrument, swallowed or aspirated tooth/fragment, TMJ dislocation, haemorrhage.
⭐ Aspiration vs ingestion: a coughing/choking, dyspnoeic patient → suspect aspiration (airway emergency, urgent chest imaging/bronchoscopy); a comfortable patient who swallowed it → usually passes, confirm radiographically.

• Pain, swelling (oedema), trismus — expected; peak ~48-72 h.
  • Haemorrhage: primary, reactionary (within hours), secondary (days, infective).
  • Dry socket (alveolar osteitis) — see A11.
  • Infection of the socket/space; delayed healing; osteomyelitis (esp. mandible, immunocompromised).
  • MRONJ (antiresorptives) and osteoradionecrosis (irradiated bone) — poor/non-healing exposed bone.
  • Chronic nerve dysaesthesia; sharp bony spicules/sequestra needing removal.

study.h: A11. Dry Socket (Alveolar Osteitis) — in depth
study.html:
Pathophysiology: premature breakdown of the blood clot by fibrinolysis (plasmin), exposing bone; it is a localised osteitis, NOT a true infection.

Risk factors

Mandibular molars (esp. 3rd), smoking, oral contraceptives/oestrogen, traumatic or surgical extraction, females, poor oral hygiene, previous dry socket, excess vasoconstrictor.

Prevention & management

  • Prevention: atraumatic technique, chlorhexidine rinse, avoid smoking, careful in high-risk patients.
  • Presentation: severe throbbing pain at day 3-5, empty socket with exposed bone, bad taste/odour, no pus, no swelling.
  • Management: gentle irrigation (warm saline/chlorhexidine) + an obtundent sedative dressing (e.g., ZOE/Alvogyl) changed every few days + analgesia. Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is true spreading infection.

study.h: A12. Oro-antral Communication & Fistula — in depth
study.html:
• OAC = fresh socket-to-antrum opening; OAF = an epithelialised chronic tract.
  • Diagnosis: bubbling of blood/air at the socket, air/fluid into the nose, Valsalva (nose-holding) test, a 'hollow' note on suction; confirm size & antral health on imaging.

Management by size

SizeManagement
< 2 mmEncourage a clot; figure-of-eight suture; sinus precautions
2-6 mmFigure-of-eight suture ± resorbable dressing; antibiotics; decongestant; precautions
> 6 mm / fistulaBuccal advancement (Rehrmann) flap, palatal rotation flap, or buccal fat pad; excise an established OAF tract first

Sinus precautions: no nose-blowing, no straws, no smoking, sneeze with the mouth open. A displaced root in the antrum is retrieved via Caldwell-Luc/endoscopy.

Classification

  • Primary — at the time of extraction.
  • Reactionary/intermediate — within a few hours, as the vasoconstrictor wears off or a vessel re-opens.
  • Secondary — after several days, due to infection eroding a vessel.

Causes

Local: torn soft tissue, fractured bone, granulation tissue, a persistent vessel. Systemic: anticoagulants/antiplatelets, liver disease, haemophilia/vWD, thrombocytopenia.

Management ladder

  1. Reassure, position, suction to find the source; firm pressure on a gauze 10-20 min.
  2. LA with vasoconstrictor; suture the socket; place a haemostatic (oxidized cellulose/Surgicel, gelatin sponge, collagen).
  3. Tranexamic acid mouthwash/pack; diathermy of a discrete vessel.
  4. Persistent/severe or known bleeding disorder → bloods (FBC, coagulation), correct the cause, refer.

Sequence: blood clot (haemostasis) → granulation tissue (days 1-7, fibroblasts/angiogenesis) → woven (immature) bone (weeks 2-6) → lamellar bone & remodelling (months). Epithelium covers the socket by ~1-2 weeks.

  • Radiographic bone fill is well advanced by ~6-8 weeks; full remodelling and ridge resorption continue for months.
  • Impaired by: smoking, infection, diabetes, steroids, irradiation, bisphosphonates, foreign body, poor blood supply.

study.h: A15. Extraction in the At-risk Patient
study.html:
• Anticoagulated (warfarin INR <~3.5-4 / DOAC per protocol / aspirin): proceed atraumatically with local haemostasis — do not stop the drug routinely.
  • Bleeding disorder (haemophilia/vWD): liaise with haematology; factor cover/DDAVP + tranexamic acid; avoid IAN blocks.
  • Bisphosphonate/antiresorptive: MRONJ risk — exhaust alternatives, atraumatic technique, consider specialist referral.
  • Irradiated jaw: ORN risk — ideally extract before radiotherapy; atraumatic technique, consider hyperbaric O₂.
  • Uncontrolled diabetes / immunosuppression: infection & healing risk — optimise control, consider antibiotic cover.

• Bite on a gauze pack for 30-60 min; do not rinse for 24 h (protect the clot).
  • Avoid smoking, sucking, hot drinks and strenuous activity for 24-48 h.
  • Analgesia (paracetamol ± NSAID if not contraindicated); soft diet; gentle warm saline rinses after 24 h.
  • Return if: bleeding not controlled by pressure, increasing pain/swelling after day 3, fever, or numbness that persists.

flashcards.a: Within hours as vasoconstrictor wears off.
Broad base; not over a bony defect.

quiz.q: Reactionary (intermediate) haemorrhage typically occurs:
o: Within a few hours as vasoconstrictor wears off

quiz.q: Secondary haemorrhage after extraction is usually due to:
A useful local antifibrinolytic agent for socket bleeding is:
Healing of an extraction socket begins with:
Post-extraction instructions include all EXCEPT:
quiz.e: No rinsing for 24 h to protect the clot.

quiz.q: A local contraindication to extraction is:
o: Acute pericoronitis/spreading infection with no drainage plan

quiz.q: Extraction in a previously irradiated jaw risks:
A patient on warfarin (INR 2.5) needing a simple extraction should:
o: Proceed with local haemostasis without stopping

quiz.q: The lower incisors are usually extracted with:
Upper canines often need extra effort because of their:
o: Long, robust root and dense buccal bone
quiz.e: Long single root; risk of buccal plate fracture.

quiz.q: The cowhorn forceps work by:
o: Engaging the bifurcation and squeezing to elevate the molar
quiz.e: Beaks engage furcation of lower molars.

quiz.q: To avoid inferior alveolar nerve injury when removing a deep lower molar root you should:
o: Avoid blind apical instrumentation; consider surgical/open approach
quiz.e: Controlled, often surgical removal; image the canal.

quiz.q: An oroantral communication is confirmed by:
A 1-2 mm oroantral communication is best managed by:
o: Encouraging a clot and primary closure of gingiva
quiz.e: Small OAC may heal with a clot + suture.

quiz.q: Definitive closure of a large (>6 mm) OAC commonly uses a:
After creating an OAC you should advise the patient to avoid:
o: Nose-blowing, sucking through a straw, and smoking

quiz.q: Excess apical force on a lower 3rd molar root risks pushing it into the:
The principal aim during socket debridement is to remove:
o: Granulation tissue, debris and sharp edges

quiz.q: Trismus after a lower molar extraction is most often due to:
A patient on IV bisphosphonates needing an extraction is at risk of:
quiz.e: Avoid extraction where possible; conservative care.

quiz.q: The correct sequence of socket healing is:
Which suture is resorbable and suitable for intra-oral closure?
The 'dry socket' classically presents with:
o: Severe throbbing pain 3-5 days later, empty socket, foul odour, NO pus

quiz.q: A retained root tip that is small, deep, and non-infected near the IAN canal may be:
o: Always removed surgically at any cost
Left under review if removal risks nerve damage
quiz.e: Risk-benefit: leaving may be safer than nerve injury.

quiz.q: Mandibular fracture during extraction is most likely with:
o: A deeply impacted lower 3rd molar in an atrophic/large-cyst mandible

quiz.q: The best immediate action for a post-extraction bleed at home is to:
o: Bite firmly on a gauze/clean cloth pad for 20-30 min

quiz.q: Which factor most increases extraction difficulty?

During extraction of an upper first molar the palatal root suddenly disappears and is no longer visible in the socket. The patient reports a 'salty' taste and there is bubbling at the socket. The MOST appropriate next step is:
o: Continue digging through the socket apex with a fine elevator
Stop, take a radiograph, and plan retrieval (Caldwell-Luc/endoscopic) if it is in the antrum
Irrigate vigorously through the socket into the nose
quiz.e: Bubbling + salty taste indicate an oro-antral communication with the root likely displaced into the maxillary antrum — confirm radiographically and retrieve via an antral approach.
w: A — blind apical instrumentation pushes the root further into the sinus/tissues and enlarges the defect
C — antibiotics alone leave a foreign body in the sinus → chronic sinusitis
D — forcing irrigation through an OAC drives infection into the sinus and worsens the communication
quiz.ty: A vanished maxillary molar root is in the antrum or infratemporal fossa until imaging proves otherwise — never poke blindly.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old on warfarin (INR 2.6 today) needs a single lower premolar extracted. The BEST management is:
o: Postpone and ask the GP to stop warfarin for 5 days
Proceed atraumatically with sutures + oxidized cellulose ± tranexamic acid
quiz.e: For a simple extraction with INR in therapeutic range (<~3.5-4), continue the anticoagulant and control bleeding with local measures.
w: A — stopping warfarin risks thromboembolism/stroke, a far greater harm than a manageable socket bleed
C — heparin bridging is unnecessary and increases bleeding for minor oral surgery
D — INR 1.5 is sub-therapeutic; deliberately under-anticoagulating exposes the patient to clot risk
quiz.ty: Don't stop anticoagulation for simple extractions — local haemostasis controls the bleeding.

quiz.q: Four days after a traumatic lower third molar extraction, a 24-year-old smoker on the oral contraceptive pill has severe throbbing pain, an empty socket with exposed bone and a foul odour, but no swelling or pus. The diagnosis and best treatment are:
o: Alveolar osteitis (dry socket) → irrigation + sedative dressing + analgesia
quiz.e: Classic dry socket: severe pain at day 3-5, empty malodorous socket, no pus/swelling, with the typical risk factors (mandibular molar, smoking, OCP, trauma).
w: A — osteomyelitis is rare, follows weeks, and shows systemic/radiographic changes, not an empty socket at day 4
C — there is no radiographic/clinical evidence of a retained root; the socket is empty
D — an abscess produces pus, swelling and trismus, which are absent here
quiz.ty: Dry socket has NO pus and does NOT need antibiotics — it needs a sedative dressing and analgesia.

quiz.q: While extracting a lone-standing upper second molar, you feel a large segment move with the tooth and the buccal sulcus balloons. This most likely indicates:
quiz.e: A lone upper molar with a large antrum and dense bone is prone to tuberosity fracture; a mobile segment moving with the tooth is the hallmark.
w: B — the IAN is mandibular and irrelevant to an upper molar
C — TMJ dislocation presents as an open lock/inability to close, not a mobile maxillary segment
D — the zygomatic arch is not engaged by intra-oral extraction forces here
quiz.ty: If the tuberosity moves with the tooth, STOP — dissect it free or stabilise and reassess to avoid a large OAC.

quiz.q: A patient receiving IV zoledronic acid for metastatic disease has a non-restorable lower molar. The MOST important consideration is:
o: High risk of MRONJ — exhaust conservative options and involve the oncology team before any extraction
Give prophylactic antibiotics and extract immediately
Place an immediate implant in the socket
quiz.e: IV antiresorptives carry a high risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw; extraction is avoided where possible and managed cautiously with multidisciplinary input.
w: A — false reassurance; IV bisphosphonates are the highest-risk MRONJ group
C — antibiotics do not abolish MRONJ risk; the decision is whether to extract at all
D — implant surgery in a high-MRONJ-risk patient is contraindicated
quiz.ty: IV bisphosphonates = high MRONJ risk → avoid extractions where possible; never place an implant.

quiz.q: After surgically removing a deeply impacted lower third molar whose roots overlapped the inferior alveolar canal, the patient has numbness of the lower lip and chin. The MOST likely nerve injury and prognosis are:
o: Inferior alveolar nerve neurapraxia — usually recovers over weeks-months
Mental nerve transection — no recovery expected
quiz.e: Lower lip/chin numbness localises to the inferior alveolar nerve; most surgical injuries are neurapraxia and recover, though close roots raise the risk.
w: A — the lingual nerve supplies the tongue/floor of mouth, not the lip/chin
C — the facial nerve is motor to facial muscles, not sensory to the lip
D — assuming the worst (transection) is unjustified; document and review, as most recover
quiz.ty: Lip/chin numbness = IAN; most are neurapraxia (recover). Persistence >6 months suggests a worse grade.

quiz.q: Three hours after an uneventful extraction under lidocaine with adrenaline, the patient returns with fresh bleeding from the socket. The MOST likely cause is:
o: Reactionary haemorrhage as the vasoconstrictor wears off
quiz.e: Reactionary (intermediate) bleeding occurs within hours as the adrenaline-induced vasoconstriction resolves; treat with pressure ± suture/haemostatic.
w: A — a primary clotting disorder usually bleeds from the outset and across multiple sites, not isolated at 3 hours
C — secondary haemorrhage is infective and appears days later
D — major arterial injury is rare and would present with brisk pulsatile bleeding intra-operatively
quiz.ty: Bleeding a few hours later = reactionary (vasoconstrictor worn off); days later = secondary (infective).

quiz.q: A maxillary molar extraction leaves a 3 mm oro-antral communication confirmed on the Valsalva test, with healthy surrounding tissue. The BEST management is:
o: Leave it completely alone with no review
Encourage a clot, place a figure-of-eight suture, give sinus precautions and antibiotics
Immediately raise a large buccal advancement flap
Pack the socket open to drain the sinus
quiz.e: A 2-6 mm OAC is managed by supporting a clot, a figure-of-eight suture, sinus precautions and antibiotics; most heal.
w: A — even small OACs need review and precautions to prevent a chronic fistula
C — a large advancement flap is reserved for defects >6 mm and reduces sulcus depth unnecessarily here
D — packing it open invites a persistent oro-antral fistula
quiz.ty: OAC by size: <2 mm clot, 2-6 mm suture + precautions, >6 mm flap.

quiz.q: A tooth gives a dull (non-resonant) percussion note, shows no periodontal ligament space on the radiograph, and will not luxate at all with an elevator. The BEST course is:
o: Apply progressively greater forceps force until it moves
Recognise ankylosis and switch to a surgical/sectioning approach
quiz.e: Loss of PDL space + a dull note + no luxation indicate ankylosis (bone fused to root); force will fracture bone/tooth, so a planned surgical, sectioning approach is correct.
w: A — escalating force on an ankylosed tooth fractures the alveolus or mandible
C — antibiotics do nothing for ankylosis and only delay definitive removal
D — orthodontic extrusion of an ankylosed tooth fails because it cannot move
quiz.ty: Ankylosis (no PDL space, dull note, no luxation) → plan surgical removal from the start, never brute force.

quiz.q: During an upper molar extraction a small fragment is lost; the patient immediately coughs violently, becomes distressed and is short of breath. The priority action is:
o: Reassure and discharge — it was swallowed
Treat as possible AIRWAY ASPIRATION: support breathing, urgent chest imaging ± bronchoscopy
Give antibiotics and review in a week
quiz.e: Coughing, choking and dyspnoea after losing a fragment suggest aspiration into the airway — a potential emergency needing urgent assessment and removal.
w: A — a swallowed object causes no respiratory distress; the symptoms here point to the airway
C — antibiotics do not address a foreign body in the bronchial tree
D — continuing surgery while the airway is threatened is dangerous
quiz.ty: Coughing/choking/dyspnoea after a lost fragment = aspiration until proven otherwise → urgent chest imaging.

quiz.q: Five days after an extraction a patient returns with bleeding, a foul-smelling socket, pus and low-grade fever. This bleeding is BEST classified and managed as:
o: Secondary (infective) haemorrhage — treat the infection (drainage/antibiotics) + local measures
A clotting factor deficiency — give factor VIII
quiz.e: Bleeding several days later with pus, odour and fever is secondary haemorrhage from infection eroding a vessel; management targets the infection plus local haemostasis.
w: A — reactionary bleeding occurs within hours and has no infective features
C — primary haemorrhage is at the time of extraction, not day 5
D — there is no history suggesting haemophilia; the picture is clearly infective
quiz.ty: Bleeding + pus + days later = secondary (infective) haemorrhage → treat the infection, not just the bleed.

quiz.q: A patient with severe haemophilia A needs a lower molar extracted. Which of the following is the MOST important to AVOID without prior factor cover?
quiz.e: An IAN block risks deep bleeding into the pterygomandibular space (potential airway compromise) in a haemophiliac; it should be avoided unless adequate factor cover is given.
w: A — superficial infiltration is far lower risk than a deep block
C — topical anaesthetic carries no bleeding risk
D — suturing is part of haemostasis, not a hazard
quiz.ty: In haemophilia, avoid IAN blocks (deep bleed risk); use infiltration/intraligamentary with factor cover + tranexamic acid.

quiz.q: While removing a deeply impacted lower third molar in an elderly patient with an atrophic mandible, you hear a crack and the patient cannot bring the teeth together normally afterwards. The MOST likely complication is:
quiz.e: A crack with a sudden change in occlusion during forceful removal in a thin/atrophic or pathological mandible indicates a mandibular fracture.
w: A — TMJ dislocation gives an open lock (cannot close at all), not the described malocclusion from a fractured body
C — dry socket causes pain days later, not an immediate occlusal change
D — a lingual nerve injury causes tongue numbness, not malocclusion
quiz.ty: A crack + new malocclusion during a difficult lower 8 in an atrophic mandible = iatrogenic mandibular fracture.

quiz.q: An upper third molar root is lost superiorly and posteriorly and cannot be seen in the socket or the antrum. It has most likely been displaced into the:
quiz.e: Loss of an upper 8 root in a postero-superior direction displaces it into the infratemporal fossa; retrieval is planned with imaging.
w: A — the submandibular space is related to LOWER molars
C — the IAN canal is mandibular, not relevant to an upper 8
D — the orbital floor is not a route for a displaced upper third molar root
quiz.ty: Upper 8 root lost postero-superiorly → infratemporal fossa; lower 8 root lost lingually → submandibular/sublingual space.

quiz.q: Local anaesthesia repeatedly fails to numb an acutely abscessed lower molar before extraction. The BEST explanation and action are:
o: The drug is faulty — change brands
Low tissue pH in infection reduces the active base — use a regional block away from the infected area
Give more of the same infiltration into the abscess
quiz.e: Acidic inflamed tissue increases the ionised fraction so less base crosses the nerve membrane; a block placed in healthy tissue away from the infection is more effective.
w: A — failure is due to local tissue conditions, not the cartridge
C — injecting more into the abscess maintains the low-pH problem and risks spreading infection
D — operating without anaesthesia is unethical and impractical
quiz.ty: LA fails in infection because low pH ↑ the ionised form → block away from the infected/acidic area.

quiz.q: Cowhorn (Ashe) forceps achieve extraction by engaging and squeezing the bifurcation. They are designed primarily for the:
quiz.e: Cowhorn beaks engage the buccal and lingual furcation of a two-rooted lower molar and, when squeezed, wedge against the septum to elevate the tooth.
w: A — an upper incisor is single-rooted and conical (rotation), not suited to furcation beaks
C — the canine is single-rooted
D — a lower incisor is single, flat-rooted
quiz.ty: Cowhorn forceps = lower molars (engage the furcation to elevate).

quiz.q: Three days after a routine lower molar extraction a patient has limited mouth opening and a tender, swollen cheek but the socket looks healthy with a clot. The MOST likely cause of the trismus is:
o: Inflammation/oedema (± haematoma) of the masticatory muscles
quiz.e: Post-operative trismus a few days after a lower molar extraction is usually transient muscular inflammation/oedema or a small haematoma, and resolves with time, heat and gentle exercises.
w: A — a fractured mandible gives malocclusion/mobility, not isolated trismus with a healthy socket
C — ankylosis develops over months/years, not in 3 days
D — dry socket causes severe socket pain with an EMPTY socket, but here the socket has a clot
quiz.ty: Early post-extraction trismus is usually muscular (oedema/haematoma) and self-limiting; exclude infection/fracture if it worsens.

quiz.q: A patient with chronic liver disease has prolonged oozing after a single extraction despite a suture. The MOST likely underlying reason is:
quiz.e: The diseased liver synthesises fewer coagulation factors (and may cause thrombocytopenia), so haemostasis is impaired; manage with local measures and correct the cause.
w: A — vitamin K is typically reduced/ineffective in liver disease, not in excess
C — polycythaemia would not cause bleeding
D — a high platelet count promotes clotting, not bleeding
quiz.ty: Liver disease → reduced clotting-factor synthesis (± low platelets) → bleeding tendency; use local haemostasis and correct the cause.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old smoker on the combined oral contraceptive pill is having a lower third molar removed. The single most useful piece of counselling to reduce her main risk is:
o: Take prophylactic antibiotics for a week
Avoid smoking and follow clot-protection instructions to reduce dry-socket risk
quiz.e: She has multiple dry-socket risk factors (mandibular molar, smoking, OCP); the key prevention is avoiding smoking and protecting the clot, not antibiotics.
w: A — antibiotics do not prevent dry socket (it is not an infection)
C — vigorous rinsing dislodges the clot and increases dry-socket risk
D — stopping the pill permanently for one extraction is inappropriate advice
quiz.ty: Dry-socket prevention = stop smoking + protect the clot (not antibiotics).

quiz.q: A small, deep, vital-looking apical fragment lies in direct contact with the inferior alveolar canal after an otherwise clean extraction, with no infection. The MOST appropriate decision is often to:
o: Remove it at all costs with aggressive bone removal
Leave it under radiographic review when retrieval risks more harm (nerve injury) than the fragment
Push it into the canal to free the socket
quiz.e: A small, non-infected apex against the IAN may be left and reviewed, because chasing it risks permanent nerve injury that outweighs the harm of the retained fragment.
w: A — aggressive removal next to the canal risks IAN injury, the very thing to avoid
C — deliberately displacing it into the canal is harmful and never appropriate
D — there is no infection to justify antibiotics, and they do not remove the fragment
quiz.ty: A small, non-infected apex on the IAN may be safer LEFT and reviewed than chased — weigh the nerve against the fragment.

quiz.q: During an upper canine extraction the patient opens very wide and suddenly cannot close the mouth; there is a pre-auricular hollow. The diagnosis and immediate management are:
o: TMJ dislocation — reduce by downward then backward pressure on the posterior teeth (Hippocratic)
quiz.e: Sudden inability to close after wide opening with a pre-auricular hollow is an anterior TMJ dislocation; reduce by the Hippocratic method.
w: A — a fracture gives malocclusion/mobility, not an open lock from wide opening
C — dry socket is a late painful complication, unrelated to jaw locking
D — an abscess presents with swelling/pus/fever, not a sudden open lock
quiz.ty: Open lock + can't close + pre-auricular hollow during wide opening = TMJ dislocation → Hippocratic reduction (down then back).

quiz.q: A lower first molar has widely divergent mesial and distal roots that resist delivery as one unit. The MOST efficient atraumatic strategy is to:
o: Apply stronger buccolingual force until it comes out whole
Section the tooth between the roots and deliver each root separately
Remove all the buccal bone first
quiz.e: Sectioning between divergent roots converts one difficult extraction into two simple single-rooted removals along separate paths, sparing bone and force.
w: A — escalating force on divergent roots fractures roots or bone
C — extensive buccal bone removal is more destructive than simply sectioning the tooth
D — referral is unnecessary for a manageable problem with a clear technique
quiz.ty: Divergent multi-rooted teeth: SECTION and deliver each root separately rather than fracturing with force.

quiz.q: A chronic oro-antral fistula (present for several weeks, epithelialised, with sinusitis symptoms) is referred to you. Definitive management requires:
o: Excision of the epithelialised tract PLUS a flap closure (and treating the sinusitis)
quiz.e: An established OAF will not heal by suture alone; the epithelial tract must be excised and the defect closed with a flap, alongside managing the sinus disease.
w: A — a suture closes a small fresh OAC, not an epithelialised chronic fistula
C — precautions help a fresh small OAC, not an established fistula
D — antibiotics may settle infection but cannot close an epithelialised tract
quiz.ty: Fresh small OAC may close with a suture/clot; an established OAF needs excision of the tract + flap closure.

quiz.q: After an atraumatic extraction in a patient on apixaban for atrial fibrillation (taken as prescribed), the BEST routine plan is to:
o: Proceed with local haemostasis (suture + oxidized cellulose ± tranexamic acid); follow the patient's anticoagulation protocol for dose timing
quiz.e: For most simple extractions, DOAC-treated patients are managed with local haemostasis and protocol-based dose timing, not by stopping the drug, because stroke risk outweighs the manageable bleed.
w: A — prolonged cessation exposes an AF patient to stroke risk
C — heparin bridging is for specific high-thrombotic situations, not routine simple extractions
D — vitamin K does not reverse DOACs (it reverses warfarin)
quiz.ty: DOAC + simple extraction: local haemostasis + protocol dose timing — don't bridge, don't reverse with vitamin K.

pearls: When elevating, the force should be controlled and incremental; sudden uncontrolled force is how roots are launched into the antrum or the lingual space.
A finger of the non-operating hand on the alveolus is your most important instrument — it senses expansion and protects the patient if the tooth gives way.
For the lower third molar, the lingual plate is thin: keep instruments away from the lingual tissues to protect the lingual nerve.
If a tooth is ankylosed (no PDL space, dull percussion note, no movement on luxation) plan a surgical/sectioning approach from the start — do not keep applying force.
Before extracting a lone upper molar, warn the patient about the antrum and have an OAC plan ready.
In bleeding-risk patients, a well-placed suture + an oxidized-cellulose dressing + tranexamic acid controls almost all socket bleeding without stopping anticoagulation.
Document nerve function (lip/tongue sensation) when roots are close to the canal — both for the patient and medico-legally.
Pain that improves then worsens around day 3-5 with an empty socket is a dry socket; pain with swelling, pus and fever is an infection — they are managed differently.
A retained vital root tip deep against the IAN may be safer left and reviewed than chased — weigh the nerve against the fragment.
Sectioning a multi-rooted tooth converts one difficult extraction into two easy ones — divide early rather than fracturing bone.
Copious irrigation during bone removal prevents thermal necrosis, the hidden cause of delayed healing after surgical extraction.
After multiple adjacent extractions, palpate and smooth bony spicules and perform conservative alveoloplasty for a denture-ready ridge.
Always account for the whole tooth/instrument after extraction — a missing fragment is in the patient (socket, tissues, antrum, airway, or GI tract) until proven otherwise.
In the irradiated jaw, prevention beats cure: extract doubtful teeth before radiotherapy and avoid surgery in irradiated bone afterwards.
Reassurance and correct positioning stop most 'continued bleeding' calls — much is a small ooze magnified by anxiety and repeated rinsing.
Choose the LEAST traumatic technique that will work — every extra bit of bone removed and force applied adds to post-op morbidity.
mistakes: Rotating an upper first premolar or a multi-rooted tooth → root fracture.
Continuing to apply force to an ankylosed tooth instead of switching to a surgical approach.
Removing too little bone in a surgical extraction so you fracture the rest of it with force.
Removing too MUCH bone / overheating it without irrigation → necrosis and delayed healing.
Leaving granulation tissue or a retained follicle in the socket → persistent pain/infection.
Closing a surgical flap under tension → dehiscence and breakdown.
Prescribing antibiotics for every socket pain instead of diagnosing dry socket vs infection.
Discharging a patient who is coughing after losing a fragment — that may be aspiration, an airway emergency.
Treating reactionary bleeding as a coagulopathy and over-investigating instead of suturing/packing.
Forgetting sinus precautions after creating an OAC, so a simple communication becomes a chronic fistula.
Using an adjacent restored tooth as an elevator fulcrum and fracturing it.
Operating on an anticoagulated patient without any local haemostatic plan — or, worse, stopping their anticoagulant.
Failing to warn high-risk (smoker/OCP, mandibular molar) patients about dry socket and prevention.
Not checking that the extracted tooth is complete, missing a retained apex.
facts: Irradiated bone → osteoradionecrosis: extract needed teeth BEFORE radiotherapy.
Post-op: bite gauze 30-60 min, no rinsing 24 h, no smoking/sucking/hot fluids, warm saline after 24 h.
Two routes of extraction: intra-alveolar (closed/forceps) and trans-alveolar (open/surgical).
Forceps grip the ROOT beneath the gingiva, not the crown.
Upper molar forceps: right & left, with a buccal beak 'point' for the buccal furcation; lower molar forceps have two pointed beaks.
Cowhorn forceps engage the lower-molar furcation and are squeezed to elevate the tooth.
Elevator working principles: lever, wedge, wheel-and-axle.
Elevators: straight (Coupland's), Warwick James, Cryer's; luxators/periotomes sever the PDL atraumatically.
Maxilla = thin porous bone (expands, favours infiltration); mandible = dense cortical (resists, needs blocks/surgery for molars).
Buccal plate is usually the thinnest wall (path of least resistance).
Upper incisors & lower premolars (single conical roots) are extracted by rotation.
Upper first premolar roots are often bifid/thin → buccopalatal expansion only (no rotation).
Surgical extraction indications: failed forceps, retained/fractured roots, ankylosis, hypercementosis, impaction, dense bone, dilacerated roots.
Surgical flap = full-thickness mucoperiosteal, broad base, on sound bone, not over a bony defect.
Bone removal uses an irrigated bur (avoid >47°C overheating → necrosis).
Sectioning a multi-rooted tooth converts one difficult extraction into simpler single-rooted ones.
Ankylosis: no PDL space, dull percussion note, no luxation → plan a surgical approach.
Radiographic pre-op check: root number/curvature, hypercementosis, relation to the IAN canal & antrum, ankylosis.
Aspiration (coughing/choking/dyspnoea) is an airway emergency; ingestion (asymptomatic) usually passes.
Sinus precautions after an OAC: no nose-blowing, straws, or smoking; sneeze with the mouth open.
Debride the socket (granulation/follicle), smooth sharp bone, irrigate, close without tension.
Reactionary haemorrhage = within hours (vasoconstrictor off); secondary = days (infective).
Post-op: bite gauze 30–60 min; no rinsing for 24 h; warm saline rinses after 24 h.
A small, deep, non-infected apex near the IAN may be left under review (nerve > fragment).
Mandible fracture during extraction is a risk in atrophic/pathological bone with force.
Support the alveolus with the non-operating hand during every extraction.
Most extraction difficulty comes from root morphology, hypercementosis, ankylosis and dense bone.
Primary haemorrhage = at the time of extraction; control with pressure → sutures → haemostatics → tranexamic acid.
mnemonics: Causes of failed LA before extraction 'ALPHA': Anatomy variation, Low pH (infection), Poor technique, High anxiety, Accessory innervation.
Haemorrhage timing: Primary (now) – Reactionary (hours, adrenaline off) – Secondary (days, sepsis).
Roots displaced: Upper molar → Antrum / Infratemporal fossa; Lower molar → IAN canal / Submandibular space.
Nerve injury severity 'N-A-N' worsening: Neurapraxia → Axonotmesis → Neurotmesis.
Surgical extraction steps 'F-B-D-D-C': Flap, Bone removal, Divide tooth, Debride, Closure.
Post-op instructions 'No-RSH for 24h': No Rinsing, Smoking, Hot fluids; bite gauze first.
Healing order 'Clot-Gran-Woven-Lamellar' (CGWL).

study.h: 16. Tooth in the Fracture Line & Complications
study.html:
• A tooth in the fracture line: retain if it is functional, not grossly mobile, not preventing reduction, and not infected; remove if fractured root, periapical infection, grossly mobile, or impeding reduction.
  • Any fracture communicating with a tooth socket/mouth is compound (open) → antibiotics indicated.
  • Complications: infection, malunion (malocclusion), non-union (mobility/gap, more in atrophic/infected mandible), nerve injury, TMJ ankylosis (esp. condylar/children), growth disturbance.

Primary survey (ATLS) identifies and treats immediate threats in order:

  • A – Airway with cervical-spine control: look for obstruction (blood, teeth, displaced fractures, the tongue); chin lift/jaw thrust, suction, adjuncts, then definitive airway; surgical airway if 'cannot intubate, cannot ventilate'.
  • B – Breathing: oxygen, exclude chest injury.
  • C – Circulation + haemorrhage control: facial bleeding is controlled by pressure/packing and reducing displaced fractures; beware swallowed blood.
  • D – Disability: GCS, pupils (a head injury may co-exist).
  • E – Exposure/environment.

The secondary survey is the systematic head-to-toe (and face) examination once the patient is stabilised: inspect/palpate the facial skeleton, check the occlusion, cranial nerves (esp. infraorbital & inferior alveolar sensation, facial-nerve function, eye movements), and look for CSF leak.

SiteNotes
CondyleMost common; intracapsular vs subcondylar; deviation toward the side on opening; bilateral → anterior open bite
AngleOften related to an impacted/erupting 3rd molar (weak point)
Body / parasymphysisCanine region is a weak point; sublingual ecchymosis
Ramus / coronoidUncommon (protected by muscle & zygoma)

A blow to the chin (e.g., a fall) classically produces the 'guardsman' fracture: bilateral condyles ± symphysis.

• The pull of the masticatory and suprahyoid muscles either holds a fracture together (favourable) or distracts it (unfavourable), assessed in horizontal and vertical planes.
  • At the angle, the elevators (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) pull the posterior fragment up; the depressors (digastric/suprahyoids) pull the anterior fragment down → an unfavourable pattern that usually needs ORIF.

study.h: B4. Fixation — Closed vs Open, Champy, Load
study.html:
• Closed reduction: intermaxillary (maxillomandibular) fixation (IMF/MMF) using arch bars, eyelet wires, or IMF screws — the teeth/occlusion guide reduction.
  • Open reduction & internal fixation (ORIF): mini-plates/screws; placed along Champy's lines of ideal osteosynthesis where a single plate neutralises tensile forces.
  • Load-sharing (mini-plates, simple fractures) vs load-bearing (a reconstruction plate for comminuted, atrophic or defect/continuity cases that cannot share load).
⭐: Restore the pre-injury occlusion first; the plates then maintain that reduction.

• Most are managed closed: analgesia, soft diet, a short period of IMF/guiding elastics if needed, and early mobilisation + physiotherapy to prevent ankylosis.
  • ORIF indications (selected): displacement into the middle cranial fossa, inability to obtain an occlusion by closed means, lateral extracapsular displacement, a foreign body in the joint, or bilateral condylar fractures with a comminuted midface.
  • Children: high remodelling potential → conservative care and early movement to avoid growth disturbance and ankylosis.

Test maxillary mobility by grasping the anterior maxilla and feeling the level at which movement occurs (palate only = I; nose moves with maxilla = II; whole face = III). See the Diagrams tab.

  • Le Fort I (Guérin): horizontal, above the apices — mobile tooth-bearing maxilla.
  • Le Fort II: pyramidal — through the nasofrontal suture & infraorbital rims.
  • Le Fort III: craniofacial disjunction — high, across the orbits/zygomatic arches; CSF rhinorrhoea.
  • NOE: naso-orbito-ethmoid — telecanthus, flattened nasal bridge, CSF leak.

• The ZMC ('tripod/quadripod') separates at the frontozygomatic suture, infraorbital rim, zygomaticomaxillary buttress and zygomatic arch.
  • Signs: flattened malar prominence, infraorbital paraesthesia, subconjunctival haemorrhage, a palpable step at the infraorbital rim, and trismus from the depressed body/arch impinging on the coronoid.
  • An isolated arch fracture causing trismus is reduced via a Gillies (temporal) approach, deep to the temporalis fascia.

See the Diagrams tab. A sudden rise in intra-orbital pressure fractures the thin floor (± medial wall); orbital fat ± the inferior rectus herniate into the antrum.

  • Signs: enophthalmos, diplopia (worst on upgaze), restricted upgaze with a positive forced-duction test (entrapment), infraorbital paraesthesia, orbital emphysema.
  • Imaging: coronal CT — herniated 'teardrop' into the maxillary sinus.
  • Repair indications: significant enophthalmos, persistent diplopia, a large defect, or entrapment — the paediatric 'white-eye' blowout is a surgical emergency for the eye.

• Dentoalveolar: concussion, subluxation, luxation, avulsion, alveolar-segment fracture. Avulsed permanent tooth — replant ASAP, store in milk/HBSS/saliva, do NOT scrub the root, splint 1–2 weeks (longer for alveolar fractures).
  • Soft tissue: clean, explore for foreign bodies/tooth fragments, conservative debridement (rich facial blood supply), accurate layered closure, tetanus prophylaxis; map and repair facial-nerve and parotid-duct injuries.

study.h: B10. Tooth in the Fracture Line, Complications & Imaging
study.html:
• Tooth in the line: retain if sound, functional and aiding reduction; remove if fractured, periapically infected, grossly mobile or preventing reduction. Any fracture through a socket is compound → antibiotics.
  • Complications: infection, malunion (malocclusion/deformity), non-union (mobility/gap — more in atrophic/infected mandibles), nerve injury, TMJ ankylosis (condylar/children), growth disturbance.
  • Imaging: CT is the gold standard; OPG + PA mandible for the mandible; occipitomental (Waters') for the midface; submentovertex for the arch.

study.h: LF1. Le Fort — concept & lines of weakness
study.html:
René Le Fort showed the midface fractures along three predictable lines of weakness. A point common to all three is fracture of the pterygoid plates — they anchor the maxilla to the skull base, so a true Le Fort separation requires them to give way.

LevelLine runs through
Le Fort I (low transverse / Guérin)Above the apices of the upper teeth: lower nasal septum, lateral antral walls, lower pterygoid plates → frees the tooth-bearing maxilla
Le Fort II (pyramidal)Nasal bones → frontal process of maxilla → lacrimal → infraorbital rim/floor → anterior maxillary wall → pterygoid plates → a central 'pyramid' of nose + maxilla
Le Fort III (high transverse / craniofacial disjunction)Nasofrontal suture → medial & lateral orbital walls → zygomaticofrontal suture → zygomatic arch → pterygoid plates → separates the whole face from the cranial base
⭐ Reality: pure symmetrical Le Fort fractures are uncommon — patterns are often asymmetric or combined (e.g., Le Fort II on one side, III on the other). Diagnose each side separately.

study.h: LF2. The KEY differentiator — the mobility test
study.html:
The single most useful bedside test is to grasp the anterior maxillary teeth/alveolus with one hand and stabilise the face with the other, then gently move the maxilla and feel WHERE the movement occurs:

Stabilising hand on…What movesDiagnosis
Over the nasal bridge & foreheadOnly the maxilla / palate moves; nose & upper face stillLe Fort I
Over the nasal bridge (root of nose)The nose moves WITH the maxilla (movement felt at the nasofrontal region)Le Fort II
At the frontozygomatic suturesThe whole face (incl. both zygomas) moves relative to the craniumLe Fort III
⭐ Rule: the level of the fracture = the highest level at which independent movement is felt. (Move the maxilla, feel where it stops being attached.)

study.h: LF3. Differentiating the three levels — features
study.html:
FeatureLe Fort ILe Fort IILe Fort III
Mobile segmentMaxilla/palate onlyNose + maxilla (pyramid)Whole face
OcclusionDeranged (often anterior open bite / retruded)Deranged + lengthened faceGrossly deranged; 'dish/long face'
Infraorbital (V2) numbnessNoYes (rim/floor involved)Variable
Periorbital signsMinimalBilateral 'raccoon eyes', subconjunctival haemorrhageGross 'panda facies', oedema
CSF rhinorrhoeaRarePossibleCommon
Telecanthus / NOENoPossibleYes
'Cracked-pot' percussion of upper teethMay be presentMay be presentMay be present

study.h: LF4. Differentiate from OTHER midface fractures (high-yield)
study.html:
• Zygomatic complex (ZMC) fracture: cheek flattening + infraorbital paraesthesia + trismus, but the maxilla is NOT mobile and the occlusion is intact → this is the key point separating it from a Le Fort.
  • NOE fracture: telecanthus + flattened nasal bridge (medial canthal disruption) without whole-maxilla mobility.
  • Nasal fracture: isolated nasal deformity/epistaxis; the maxilla is stable.
  • Dentoalveolar fracture: only a segment of teeth/alveolus is mobile, not the whole maxilla.
  • Isolated palatal (split) fracture: mobility between the two halves of the palate.
⭐ The discriminator: ask "Is the maxilla/occlusion mobile, and at what level?" Mobile maxilla → Le Fort; immobile maxilla with cheek/eye signs → think ZMC/NOE/orbital.

• After ATLS, examine: occlusion, midface mobility (the test above), infraorbital sensation, eyes (visual acuity, pupils, eye movements, diplopia), the medial canthi (telecanthus), and for a CSF leak (halo/double-ring sign, glucose-positive fluid).
  • Imaging: CT (axial + coronal + 3D) is definitive and shows the pterygoid-plate involvement; occipitomental (Waters') views are a screening adjunct.
  • Document the airway, cervical spine and any head injury.

• Airway: a maxilla driven postero-inferiorly lengthens the face and can obstruct the nasopharynx — relieve by disimpaction/forward traction and secure the airway.
  • Haemorrhage: from the maxillary artery/pterygoid plexus can be severe.
  • CSF leak/meningitis risk (II & III); ocular injury/blindness (orbital/optic), C-spine and head injury.
  • Management (after stabilisation): reduction and fixation restoring the occlusion (IMF) and the vertical/horizontal buttresses with ORIF (mini/recon plates); manage CSF leak (avoid nasal instrumentation), and liaise with ophthalmology/neurosurgery.

study.h: M1. Muscles that move the mandible (vectors)
study.html:
Displacement of a mandibular fracture is dictated by the muscles attached to each fragment. Know each muscle's origin → insertion and the direction it pulls.

MuscleOrigin → insertionPull / action
MasseterZygomatic arch → lateral ramus/angleElevates; pulls the posterior fragment UP
TemporalisTemporal fossa → coronoid/anterior ramusElevates; posterior fibres retract; pulls coronoid/ramus UP
Medial pterygoidPterygoid fossa → medial angle/ramusElevates; pulls the angle UP & MEDIALLY (sling with masseter)
Lateral pterygoidSphenoid/lateral pterygoid plate → condylar neck & discProtrudes/depresses; pulls the condyle FORWARD & MEDIALLY
Suprahyoids (ant. digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, genioglossus)Mandible → hyoid/tongueDepress/retract; pull the anterior/symphyseal fragment DOWN, BACK & LINGUALLY
⭐ The two opposing groups: elevators (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) pull fragments UP; depressors (suprahyoids/digastric) pull them DOWN. The fracture displaces along the resultant of these vectors.

study.h: M2. Favourable vs Unfavourable — the principle
study.html:
Whether the muscle pull impacts (compresses) the fragments together or distracts (separates) them defines the fracture; it is judged on the direction/obliquity of the fracture line relative to the muscle pull, in TWO planes:

  • Horizontally favourable / unfavourable — assessed on a lateral view: does the line resist the upward (vertical) pull of the elevators?
  • Vertically favourable / unfavourable — assessed on an occlusal/AP view: does the line resist the medial pull of the pterygoid/mylohyoid?
FavourableUnfavourable
Effect of muscle pullCompresses/impacts the fragments togetherDistracts/displaces the fragments apart
StabilityRelatively stableUnstable
Tends to needMay be managed closedUsually ORIF

study.h: M3. Worked example — the mandibular ANGLE fracture
study.html:
This is the classic exam example.

  • The posterior fragment carries the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid → pulled UP (and medially).
  • The anterior fragment carries the suprahyoids → pulled DOWN (and lingually).
  • If the fracture line runs from antero-superior to postero-inferior such that the masseter pull seats the posterior fragment against the anterior one → favourable (the muscles hold it).
  • If the line runs the opposite way so the upward pull lifts the posterior fragment off → unfavourable (the muscles displace it) → needs ORIF.
⭐: 'Unfavourable' means the muscle vector is unfavourable to spontaneous reduction — the muscles work against you.

Fracture siteTypical muscle-driven displacement
CondyleLateral pterygoid pulls the condylar head antero-medially (classic medial override); jaw deviates to the fractured side on opening; bilateral → anterior open bite
AnglePosterior fragment UP (elevators) vs anterior fragment DOWN (suprahyoids)
BodySimilar elevator/depressor split across the line
Symphysis / parasymphysisBilateral suprahyoid/mylohyoid/genioglossus pull → lingual collapse; bilateral fracture → tongue falls back (airway risk)

• It predicts displacement and the need for fixation: favourable patterns may be stable; unfavourable patterns are pulled apart and need ORIF.
  • It explains the clinical signs (open bite, deviation, lingual displacement) from first principles rather than memorisation.
  • It guides airway concern (bilateral anterior fractures) and reduction strategy (overcome the muscle pull, then fix).

flashcards.a: Craniofacial disjunction; may have CSF rhinorrhea.
Through tooth-bearing area / skin → needs antibiotics.

quiz.q: The classic sequence of fracture management is:
In jaw fractures, the best guide to correct reduction is the:
Intermaxillary fixation (IMF) achieves reduction by:
o: Wiring the upper and lower teeth together in the correct occlusion
quiz.e: Closed reduction using the occlusion as a guide.

quiz.q: A favourable fracture is one in which muscle pull:
o: Tends to hold the fragments together

quiz.q: The posterior fragment of an unfavourable mandibular angle fracture is pulled UPWARD by the:
A fracture through a tooth-bearing area is classified as:
A tooth in the fracture line should generally be REMOVED if it is:
o: Grossly mobile, fractured, or periapically infected

quiz.q: An avulsed permanent tooth is best transported in:
When replanting an avulsed tooth you should:
o: Avoid handling/scrubbing the root surface; replant quickly and splint

quiz.q: Soft-tissue facial wounds can often be closed primarily even after some delay because of the:
quiz.e: Good vascularity aids healing; still debride/explore.

quiz.q: A deep cheek laceration must be explored for injury to the:
quiz.e: Map CN VII branches and Stensen's duct.

quiz.q: Non-union of a mandibular fracture is MOST likely in:
Malunion of a jaw fracture presents as:
TMJ ankylosis is a feared late complication particularly after:
Lower-lip and chin numbness after a mandibular fracture indicates injury to the:
The commonest sign that should make you suspect a mandibular fracture clinically is:
Gillies approach reduces a fractured zygomatic arch from:
o: A temporal incision above the hairline (deep to temporalis fascia)
quiz.e: Temporal approach, elevator beneath the arch.

quiz.q: The most common site of midface CSF leak collection sign is:
In Le Fort I the mobile segment is the:
A patient with a suspected basal skull fracture should NOT have:
quiz.e: Risk of intracranial passage; use oral route.

quiz.q: Enophthalmos after orbital trauma is due to:
After reduction, mandibular fractures are typically immobilised (if IMF) for about:
o: 2-6 weeks (commonly ~4-6 weeks; less with rigid ORIF)
quiz.e: Rigid internal fixation reduces/eliminates IMF time.

quiz.q: The 'guardsman' (bilateral) fracture pattern from a chin blow typically involves the:
quiz.e: Fall on the chin → condyles + symphysis.

quiz.q: An unconscious patient after a road accident has a bilateral parasymphyseal mandibular fracture and is making snoring respiratory efforts. The immediate priority is:
o: Secure the airway (the unsupported tongue is falling back) with C-spine control
Take a CT before doing anything
quiz.e: A bilateral anterior mandibular ('bucket-handle') fracture removes tongue support; with reduced consciousness the tongue obstructs the airway, so airway management with C-spine control is first.
w: A — definitive fracture fixation never precedes airway control
C — imaging waits until the airway is secured in an obstructing patient
D — suturing lacerations does nothing for a threatened airway
quiz.ty: Bilateral parasymphyseal fracture + reduced GCS = tongue prolapse → airway first (ATLS).

quiz.q: After a blow to the eye a patient has enophthalmos, vertical diplopia worst on looking up, and infraorbital numbness. Coronal CT shows a 'teardrop' in the antrum. The diagnosis is:
o: Orbital floor blowout with inferior rectus entrapment
quiz.e: Enophthalmos, restricted upgaze (entrapped inferior rectus), infraorbital paraesthesia and a herniated 'teardrop' are the classic blowout picture.
w: A — Le Fort I gives a mobile tooth-bearing maxilla, not isolated eye signs
C — an arch fracture causes trismus/flat cheek, not entrapment diplopia
D — a nasal fracture does not restrict eye movement
quiz.ty: Enophthalmos + diplopia on UPGAZE + infraorbital numbness + teardrop = orbital floor blowout.

quiz.q: A patient with a high midface injury has clear, blood-tinged fluid dripping from the nose that forms a double ring on gauze and is glucose-positive. You must AVOID:
o: Passing a nasogastric or nasopharyngeal tube
quiz.e: The halo sign + glucose-positive nasal fluid indicate a CSF leak (anterior cranial fossa/Le Fort III); a naso-tube risks intracranial passage and must be avoided (use the oral route).
w: A — analgesia is appropriate
C — assessing the occlusion is part of the facial exam
D — CT is exactly what is needed to define the injury
quiz.ty: Suspected CSF leak / base-of-skull fracture → never pass anything up the nose.

quiz.q: A patient struck on the cheek has a flattened malar prominence, numbness of the cheek and upper lip, and limited mouth opening. The MOST likely fracture and the nerve responsible for the numbness are:
o: Le Fort I; greater palatine nerve
quiz.e: A flattened malar prominence with infraorbital paraesthesia and trismus (coronoid impingement) is a ZMC fracture; the infraorbital nerve (V2) supplies the cheek/upper lip.
w: A — the IAN is mandibular and supplies the lower lip, not the cheek
C — Le Fort I causes a mobile maxilla, not malar flattening/cheek numbness
D — a nasal fracture does not flatten the cheek or numb the upper lip
quiz.ty: Flat cheek + infraorbital numbness + trismus = ZMC fracture (infraorbital nerve, V2).

quiz.q: On asking a trauma patient to open, the mandible deviates to the right and there is right pre-auricular tenderness. This indicates a fracture of the:
quiz.e: On opening, the mandible deviates TOWARD the side of a condylar fracture because translation is lost on that side; right deviation + right pre-auricular pain = right condylar fracture.
w: A — a left condylar fracture would deviate the jaw to the left
C — a symphyseal fracture does not cause unilateral deviation on opening
D — an angle fracture does not typically cause this deviation pattern
quiz.ty: On opening, the jaw deviates TOWARD the fractured condyle.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old has a unilateral condylar fracture with a normal occlusion and good mouth opening. The BEST management is usually:
o: Closed management: analgesia, soft diet, short observation/IMF if needed, and EARLY mobilisation/physiotherapy
quiz.e: Most condylar fractures, especially in children, are managed closed with early mobilisation to preserve function and avoid ankylosis; children have high remodelling potential.
w: A — open reduction of a paediatric condyle risks growth-centre and facial-nerve injury and is reserved for specific indications
C — condylectomy is not indicated for a simple fracture
D — prolonged IMF in a child promotes ankylosis, the very thing to avoid
quiz.ty: Condylar fractures (especially children) → closed treatment + EARLY mobilisation to avoid ankylosis.

quiz.q: An avulsed upper central incisor is brought in 20 minutes after injury, carried in milk. The BEST immediate management is:
o: Scrub the root clean, then store dry until an appointment
Gently rinse without scrubbing the root, replant immediately, and splint for 1-2 weeks
Discard the tooth and plan an implant
quiz.e: Rapid replantation with a preserved periodontal ligament gives the best outcome: do not scrub the root, replant at once, and apply a flexible splint.
w: A — scrubbing the root and dry storage destroy the PDL cells and doom the replant
C — discarding a replantable tooth in a young patient is premature
D — alcohol is cytotoxic to PDL cells
quiz.ty: Avulsed permanent tooth: don't scrub the root, replant ASAP, store in milk/HBSS/saliva, splint 1-2 weeks.

quiz.q: A mandibular fracture line passes through the socket of a sound, firm second molar that is helping to locate the reduction. The tooth should be:
o: Retained, as it is sound and aids reduction (remove only if fractured, infected or grossly mobile)
Extracted and replaced with a plate screw
quiz.e: A tooth in the fracture line is kept if it is sound, functional and aids reduction; it is removed only when fractured, periapically infected, or grossly mobile/preventing reduction.
w: A — routine removal sacrifices a useful, sound tooth and can destabilise reduction
C — immediate endodontics is not required for a sound tooth
D — extracting a helpful sound tooth to place a screw is unjustified
quiz.ty: Tooth in the fracture line: keep if sound and helpful; remove if fractured/infected/mobile. (And the fracture is compound → antibiotics.)

quiz.q: A patient has marked limitation of mouth opening after a blow to the side of the face, with a flattened cheek but a normal occlusion. A submentovertex view shows an isolated depressed zygomatic arch. The trismus is due to, and reduced by:
o: The depressed arch impinging on the coronoid process; a Gillies (temporal) elevation
quiz.e: An isolated depressed zygomatic arch mechanically blocks the coronoid, causing trismus; it is elevated through a Gillies temporal approach.
w: A — the limitation is mechanical, not simple muscle spasm
C — the occlusion is normal and the imaging shows an arch fracture, not a mandibular fracture
D — there is no open lock; this is mechanical impingement
quiz.ty: Isolated depressed zygomatic arch → coronoid impingement → trismus → Gillies (temporal) reduction.

quiz.q: A young man falls and strikes his chin. He has bilateral pre-auricular pain, an anterior open bite, and tenderness at the symphysis. The MOST likely fracture pattern is:
o: Bilateral condylar fractures ± a symphyseal fracture ('guardsman')
quiz.e: A fall onto the chin transmits force to both condyles (often with a symphyseal fracture) — the 'guardsman' pattern; bilateral condylar fractures produce an anterior open bite.
w: A — Le Fort II is a midface fracture from a different mechanism
C — an arch fracture would not cause bilateral condylar signs/open bite
D — a nasal fracture does not explain the occlusal change
quiz.ty: Fall on the chin → bilateral condyles ± symphysis ('guardsman'); bilateral condylar fractures → anterior open bite.

quiz.q: After midface trauma a patient has widening of the distance between the inner canthi (telecanthus) and a flattened nasal bridge. The fracture involved is:
quiz.e: Telecanthus with a flattened nasal bridge indicates a naso-orbito-ethmoid fracture disrupting the medial canthal attachment.
w: A — Le Fort I gives a mobile tooth-bearing maxilla, not telecanthus
C — an arch fracture causes cheek flattening/trismus
D — a mandibular fracture does not cause telecanthus
quiz.ty: Telecanthus + flattened nasal bridge = NOE fracture (medial canthal disruption).

quiz.q: A patient with peri-orbital trauma cannot elevate the eye and a forced-duction test is positive. This indicates:
o: Mechanical entrapment (e.g., inferior rectus in an orbital floor fracture)
quiz.e: A positive forced-duction test means the globe cannot be passively rotated — mechanical entrapment (typically inferior rectus in a blowout), not a nerve palsy.
w: A — a nerve palsy gives a NEGATIVE forced-duction test (the muscle is weak, not trapped)
C — oedema does not fix the globe on forced duction
D — a retrobulbar haemorrhage causes proptosis/visual loss, not a positive forced-duction from entrapment
quiz.ty: Positive forced-duction test = mechanical entrapment (blowout), not a nerve palsy.

quiz.q: A mandibular fracture runs through the socket of a partially erupted third molar that is carious and mobile. Regarding the tooth and antibiotics:
o: Keep the tooth; no antibiotics needed
Remove the tooth (carious/mobile in the line) and give antibiotics (the fracture is compound)
quiz.e: A carious, mobile tooth in the fracture line is removed, and because the fracture communicates with the mouth (compound/open) antibiotics are indicated.
w: A — a carious mobile tooth in the line is a source of infection, and a socket-communicating fracture is compound
C — a carious mobile tooth should not be retained just because antibiotics are given
D — a compound fracture needs antibiotic cover
quiz.ty: Tooth in the line: remove if carious/mobile/infected; any socket-communicating fracture is compound → antibiotics.

quiz.q: At the mandibular angle, an 'unfavourable' fracture is one in which:
o: Muscle pull holds the fragments together
The elevator muscles distract the posterior fragment upward, displacing the fracture (usually needs ORIF)
quiz.e: An unfavourable fracture is distracted by muscle pull (elevators lift the posterior fragment), so it usually requires open reduction and internal fixation.
w: A — that describes a favourable fracture
C — unfavourable fractures are displaced by muscle action
D — greenstick is a paediatric incomplete fracture, a different concept
quiz.ty: Unfavourable fracture = muscles distract the fragments → usually ORIF; favourable = muscles hold it.

quiz.q: A comminuted, infected mandibular fracture in an atrophic edentulous mandible needs fixation. The MOST appropriate hardware is:
quiz.e: Comminuted/atrophic/defect fractures cannot share load, so a load-bearing reconstruction plate is used to bridge and stabilise the segment.
w: A — a small mini-plate (load-sharing) is inadequate for comminuted/atrophic bone
C — IMF is impractical in an edentulous atrophic mandible and does not stabilise comminution
D — leaving it unfixed risks non-union
quiz.ty: Comminuted/atrophic/defect fractures → load-bearing reconstruction plate (not load-sharing mini-plates).

quiz.q: Mini-plates for a simple mandibular body fracture are best positioned along:
o: Champy's lines of ideal osteosynthesis (to neutralise tensile forces)
quiz.e: Champy described lines along which a single mini-plate neutralises the tensile forces of mastication, allowing load-sharing osteosynthesis.
w: A — random placement does not address the tension band
C — plates are placed on the buccal/outer cortex, not the lingual
D — plating across the mental foramen risks nerve injury
quiz.ty: Mini-plates follow Champy's lines (the tension band) for load-sharing fixation.

quiz.q: During closed reduction of a mandibular fracture, the surgeon's primary guide to a correct reduction is:
o: The shape of the skin scar
quiz.e: Restoring the occlusion is the reference standard for reduction of tooth-bearing jaw fractures.
w: A — skin appearance does not confirm bony/occlusal reduction
C — mucosal colour is irrelevant to reduction
D — swelling is not a reduction guide
quiz.ty: The occlusion is the guide to correct reduction of jaw fractures.

quiz.q: On grasping the anterior maxilla and testing mobility, only the tooth-bearing maxilla (the palate) moves as a unit. This corresponds to a:
quiz.e: Movement limited to the tooth-bearing maxilla indicates a Le Fort I (horizontal) fracture above the apices.
w: B — in Le Fort II the nose moves with the maxilla
C — in Le Fort III the whole face moves
D — a zygomatic fracture is detected at the malar region, not by maxillary mobility
quiz.ty: Only the palate/maxilla mobile = Le Fort I; nose moves too = II; whole face = III.

quiz.q: An avulsed permanent incisor is brought in dry, 2 hours after the injury. Compared with a tooth replanted within minutes in milk, the expected outcome is:
o: A much poorer prognosis (non-viable PDL → likely ankylosis/replacement resorption)
Better prognosis because it is cleaner
No difference if antibiotics are given
quiz.e: Extended dry time kills the periodontal ligament cells, so the prognosis is poor (ankylosis/replacement resorption), unlike rapid replantation in a physiologic medium.
w: A — dry time for 2 hours destroys the PDL; the prognosis is not identical
C — being dry does not help; it is harmful
D — antibiotics do not restore dead PDL cells
quiz.ty: Dry extra-oral time kills the PDL → poor replantation prognosis; speed + milk/HBSS storage matter most.

quiz.q: A deep laceration of the cheek crosses a line from the tragus to the upper lip and there is weakness of the upper lip on smiling plus clear fluid in the wound. You must specifically explore for injury to the:
o: Facial nerve branches and the parotid (Stensen's) duct
quiz.e: A laceration over the parotid/cheek region with facial-muscle weakness and clear (salivary) fluid suggests facial-nerve branch and parotid-duct injury, which must be identified and repaired.
w: A — the lingual nerve/submandibular duct are in the floor of mouth, not the cheek
C — the IAN is intrabony, not in a cheek laceration
D — the hypoglossal is deep in the neck, not the cheek
quiz.ty: Deep cheek laceration + facial weakness + clear fluid → explore the facial nerve & parotid (Stensen's) duct.

quiz.q: Examining a midface-trauma patient, you grasp the upper teeth and move the maxilla while steadying the nasal bridge; only the tooth-bearing maxilla moves, the nose and upper face stay still, and there is no infraorbital numbness or CSF leak. The level is:
quiz.e: Independent movement limited to the tooth-bearing maxilla (with a stable nose/upper face and no V2 numbness/CSF leak) is a Le Fort I (low transverse) fracture.
w: B — in Le Fort II the nose moves WITH the maxilla and there is infraorbital numbness
C — in Le Fort III the whole face moves and CSF rhinorrhoea is common
D — a ZMC fracture leaves the maxilla/occlusion immobile
quiz.ty: Only the maxilla/palate mobile, stable nose, no V2 numbness/CSF = Le Fort I.

quiz.q: A patient has bilateral periorbital ecchymosis, numbness of both cheeks/upper lip, a nasal deformity, and on the mobility test the NOSE moves together with the maxilla. The MOST likely level is:
quiz.e: Movement of the central pyramid (nose moving with the maxilla) plus bilateral infraorbital (V2) paraesthesia and periorbital signs indicates a Le Fort II (pyramidal) fracture.
w: A — in Le Fort I the nose stays still and there is no infraorbital numbness
C — Le Fort III moves the WHOLE face including the zygomas, not just the central pyramid
D — an isolated nasal fracture does not make the maxilla mobile or numb the cheeks
quiz.ty: Nose moves WITH the maxilla + infraorbital (V2) numbness = Le Fort II (pyramidal).

quiz.q: A severely injured patient has gross facial oedema, an elongated 'dish' face, CSF rhinorrhoea, and on examination the entire face (including both zygomas) moves relative to the skull, with movement felt at the frontozygomatic sutures. The level is:
quiz.e: Whole-face mobility with movement at the frontozygomatic sutures, a lengthened face and CSF rhinorrhoea is Le Fort III (craniofacial disjunction).
w: A — Le Fort I moves only the maxilla
B — Le Fort II moves the nose+maxilla pyramid, not the whole face at the FZ sutures
D — an NOE fracture is a localised medial-canthal injury, not whole-face disjunction
quiz.ty: Whole face mobile at the frontozygomatic sutures + long 'dish' face + CSF leak = Le Fort III.
