quiz.q: A patient has a flattened cheek, numbness of the cheek, and trismus, BUT the maxilla is NOT mobile and the occlusion is intact. This is MOST likely:
quiz.e: Cheek flattening + infraorbital paraesthesia + trismus with an IMMOBILE maxilla and intact occlusion points to a zygomatic complex fracture, not a Le Fort — the mobile maxilla is the key Le Fort feature that is absent here.
w: A — Le Fort I produces a mobile maxilla and deranged occlusion
B — Le Fort II produces a mobile nose+maxilla and deranged occlusion
D — Le Fort III produces gross whole-face mobility
quiz.ty: Cheek flattening + V2 numbness + trismus but IMMOBILE maxilla/intact occlusion = ZMC fracture, not Le Fort.

quiz.q: What anatomical feature is fractured in ALL THREE Le Fort levels, reflecting separation of the maxilla from the skull base?
quiz.e: Fracture of the pterygoid plates is common to all three Le Fort patterns because they anchor the maxilla to the skull base.
w: A — the zygomatic arch is involved in Le Fort III, not I/II
C — the frontozygomatic suture is a Le Fort III feature
D — the nasal bones are involved in II and III, not I
quiz.ty: Pterygoid plate fracture is common to ALL Le Fort levels (I, II, III).

quiz.q: During the midface mobility test, the level of the Le Fort fracture is best defined as:
o: The lowest point where the face is tender
The HIGHEST level at which independent movement of the maxilla is felt
The level of the worst laceration
quiz.e: You move the maxilla and feel where it remains attached; the fracture level corresponds to the highest point at which independent movement is detected.
w: A — tenderness is non-specific and does not define the level
C — swelling does not define the fracture level
D — laceration position is unrelated to the bony level
quiz.ty: Le Fort level = the highest level at which the mobile maxilla becomes independently movable.

quiz.q: A midface-injured patient is developing airway difficulty; the face looks lengthened and the maxilla is displaced backward and down. The MOST appropriate immediate manoeuvre (with airway/C-spine care) is:
o: Disimpact and pull the maxilla forward/up to relieve the nasopharyngeal obstruction and secure the airway
quiz.e: A posteroinferiorly displaced maxilla obstructs the nasopharynx; disimpaction and forward/upward traction relieves it, alongside definitive airway control.
w: A — waiting risks airway loss
C — tight nasal packing does not relieve the displaced maxilla and is hazardous if a CSF leak/cranial-base fracture is present
D — IMF is a definitive fixation step, not the emergency airway manoeuvre
quiz.ty: A backward-displaced maxilla obstructs the airway → disimpact and pull it forward/up + secure the airway.

quiz.q: Which investigation is definitive for classifying a Le Fort fracture and confirming pterygoid-plate involvement?
quiz.e: CT with coronal and 3D reconstructions is the definitive investigation, demonstrating the fracture lines and the pterygoid-plate involvement.
w: A — a periapical film cannot assess the midface/skull base
C — vitality testing is irrelevant to fracture classification
D — ultrasound is not used to classify facial-skeleton fractures
quiz.ty: CT (axial+coronal+3D) is definitive for Le Fort classification and pterygoid-plate involvement.

quiz.q: In a displaced mandibular ANGLE fracture, the posterior fragment is pulled upward mainly by which muscle group?
o: The elevators: masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid
quiz.e: The elevators (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) attach to the posterior fragment and pull it upward; the suprahyoids pull the anterior fragment down.
w: A — the suprahyoids pull the ANTERIOR fragment DOWN, not the posterior up
C — the lateral pterygoid mainly displaces the condyle antero-medially, not the angle's posterior fragment up
D — the buccinator is a muscle of facial expression and does not displace the fragment
quiz.ty: Angle fracture: elevators (masseter/temporalis/medial pterygoid) pull the posterior fragment UP; suprahyoids pull the anterior fragment DOWN.

quiz.q: A fractured mandibular condyle is typically displaced antero-medially. The muscle responsible is the:
quiz.e: The lateral pterygoid inserts on the condylar neck/disc and pulls the fractured condylar head forward and medially (the classic medial override).
w: A — the masseter elevates the ramus, it does not pull the condyle antero-medially
B — the medial pterygoid elevates the angle and pulls it medially, not the condyle forward
D — the temporalis elevates/retracts via the coronoid
quiz.ty: The lateral pterygoid displaces a fractured condyle ANTERO-MEDIALLY.

quiz.q: Which statement BEST defines an 'unfavourable' mandibular fracture?
o: A fracture with a poor cosmetic outcome
One in which the muscle pull distracts the fragments apart (usually needing ORIF)
quiz.e: Favourability describes whether the muscle vectors compress (favourable) or distract (unfavourable) the fragments; unfavourable patterns are displaced by muscle pull and usually require open fixation.
w: A — favourability is a biomechanical term, not a cosmetic one
C — comminution is a separate descriptor, not the definition of unfavourable
D — being in a child does not define favourability
quiz.ty: Unfavourable = muscle pull distracts the fragments → usually ORIF; favourable = muscle pull compresses them.

quiz.q: All of the muscles of mastication are innervated by which nerve?
quiz.e: The four muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid) are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).
w: A — VII supplies the muscles of facial expression
C — IX supplies stylopharyngeus and sensation/taste of the posterior tongue
D — XII supplies the tongue muscles
quiz.ty: Muscles of mastication = V3 (mandibular nerve).

quiz.q: In a bilateral parasymphyseal mandibular fracture with reduced consciousness, the airway is threatened because the suprahyoid muscles:
o: Pull the anterior (symphyseal) fragment and tongue down/back, allowing the tongue to fall into the airway
quiz.e: With the anterior mandible separated, the suprahyoid/genioglossus pull loses its forward tongue support, so the tongue falls back and obstructs the airway.
w: A — the suprahyoids depress the mandible; they do not elevate the maxilla
C — protrusion is the lateral pterygoid's action, not the cause here
D — the suprahyoids do not 'open the larynx'
quiz.ty: Bilateral anterior mandibular fracture → suprahyoid pull → tongue prolapse → airway obstruction.

pearls: A child's 'white-eye' blowout can look almost normal yet have a trapped muscle — it is a surgical emergency for the eye.
Suspect a CSF leak with clear/blood-tinged nasal fluid (halo sign, glucose-positive) and avoid passing anything up the nose.
Champy's lines tell you where one mini-plate neutralises tension; comminuted/atrophic bone needs a load-bearing reconstruction plate.
An avulsed permanent tooth is a time-critical emergency: replant within minutes, store in milk/HBSS/saliva, never scrub the root.
Trismus after a zygomatic fracture is usually the depressed body/arch impinging on the coronoid, not muscle spasm.
Reduce a zygomatic arch fracture through a Gillies temporal approach, deep to the temporalis fascia.
A tooth in the fracture line is kept if it is sound and aids reduction, and removed if it is fractured, infected or mobile.
A positive forced-duction test distinguishes mechanical entrapment (blowout) from a neurological cause of impaired eye movement.
Comminuted, atrophic or continuity-defect mandibles need a load-bearing reconstruction plate; simple fractures take load-sharing mini-plates on Champy's lines.
Telecanthus with a flattened nasal bridge is the signature of a naso-orbito-ethmoid (NOE) fracture.
A fall onto the chin classically fractures both condyles (± the symphysis) — the 'guardsman' fracture.
mistakes: Over-debriding facial soft tissue — the rich blood supply allows conservative debridement and primary closure.
Missing facial-nerve or parotid-duct injury in a deep cheek laceration.
Confusing a positive forced-duction test (entrapment) with a cranial nerve palsy (negative test).
Using a small load-sharing mini-plate on a comminuted/atrophic mandible that needs a load-bearing plate.
Missing a parotid-duct/facial-nerve injury in a deep cheek laceration.
Thinking 'unfavourable' means a worse injury — it means the MUSCLE VECTOR is unfavourable to spontaneous reduction.
Assessing favourability in one plane only (must check horizontal AND vertical).
Forgetting the lateral pterygoid pulls the fractured condyle antero-medially (explaining the displacement).
Not anticipating airway compromise from suprahyoid pull in a bilateral anterior mandibular fracture.
Attributing an anterior open bite after a chin blow to dental causes instead of bilateral condylar fractures.
Choosing a load-sharing mini-plate for an unfavourable comminuted pattern that needs a load-bearing plate.
Forgetting that pterygoid-plate fracture is common to all Le Fort levels.
Confusing ZMC (immobile maxilla) with a Le Fort (mobile maxilla).
facts: Avulsed tooth storage: milk / HBSS / saliva; replant fast; don't scrub the root; splint 1-2 wk.
Best imaging for facial fractures: CT (Waters'/occipitomental view for midface).
Complications: malunion, non-union (atrophic/infected), nerve injury, TMJ ankylosis (condyle/children).
Elevators of the mandible: masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid (pull fragments UP).
Depressors (suprahyoids): anterior digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, geniohyoid/genioglossus (pull DOWN/back).
Masseter: zygomatic arch → lateral ramus/angle; elevates.
Temporalis: temporal fossa → coronoid; elevates + posterior fibres retract.
Medial pterygoid: pterygoid fossa → medial angle (sling with masseter); elevates + pulls medially.
Lateral pterygoid: → condylar neck/disc; protrudes/depresses; pulls condyle antero-medially.
Condylar fracture: lateral pterygoid displaces the head ANTERO-MEDIALLY.
Angle fracture: posterior fragment UP (elevators) vs anterior fragment DOWN (suprahyoids).
Favourable fracture = muscle pull compresses fragments; unfavourable = muscle pull distracts them.
Favourability is assessed in TWO planes: horizontal (lateral view) & vertical (AP/occlusal view).
Unfavourable fractures usually need ORIF; favourable may be managed closed.
Bilateral parasymphyseal fracture → suprahyoid pull lets the tongue fall back (airway risk).
Muscles of mastication are all supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).
Jaw deviates TOWARD the side of a condylar fracture on opening (lost translation).
Bilateral condylar fractures → anterior open bite (loss of posterior ramus height).
Compound (open) fracture = communicates with mouth/socket/skin → antibiotics indicated.
Le Fort I = horizontal/Guérin; II = pyramidal (nasal bridge + infraorbital rims); III = craniofacial disjunction.
Pterygoid plate fracture is common to ALL three Le Fort levels.
Midface mobility test: only maxilla moves = I; nose moves with maxilla = II; whole face moves = III.
NOE fracture sign = telecanthus + flattened nasal bridge (medial canthal disruption).
ZMC vs Le Fort: in ZMC the maxilla/occlusion is NOT mobile (key differentiator).
Orbital blowout: positive forced-duction test = mechanical entrapment (not a nerve palsy).
Isolated zygomatic arch fracture → trismus (coronoid impingement) → Gillies temporal reduction.
Best imaging for facial fractures = CT (axial+coronal+3D); Waters'/occipitomental for the midface.
Avoid a nasal tube (NG/nasopharyngeal) in suspected base-of-skull/high-midface fracture.
Mini-plates (load-sharing) for simple fractures along Champy's lines; reconstruction plate (load-bearing) for comminuted/atrophic.
Avulsed tooth: splint 1–2 weeks (longer for an associated alveolar fracture); endodontics usually after replantation.
mnemonics: Blowout = Enophthalmos + Diplopia + restricted Upgaze + teardrop ('EDU-teardrop').
Fracture management 'R-F-I-R': Reduction, Fixation, Immobilisation, Rehabilitation.
CSF leak clues: Halo (double-ring) sign + glucose-positive fluid.
Avulsion storage best-to-worst: HBSS ≈ Milk > Saliva > (avoid) Water/Dry.
Elevators 'MTM' (Masseter, Temporalis, Medial pterygoid) pull UP; Suprahyoids pull DOWN.
Lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle Antero-Medially ('LP = Lateral Pterygoid → Lower & forward/Medial').
Favourability planes: Horizontal (lateral view) + Vertical (AP view).

study.html:
TermMeaning
SterilizationDestroys ALL microbes incl. spores
DisinfectionKills most pathogens, not all spores (on surfaces/instruments)
AntisepsisMicrobial control on living tissue
  • Autoclave (moist heat) 121°C/15 psi/15 min — most reliable; 134°C/3 min flash.
  • Dry heat 160°C/2 h; chemical (glutaraldehyde, ethylene oxide) for heat-sensitive items.
  • Biological (spore) indicator = gold-standard test of efficacy; chemical/Bowie-Dick are adjuncts.
  • Spaulding: critical items (enter tissue) must be sterile; semi-critical high-level disinfected; non-critical low-level.

Phases: Haemostasis → Inflammation (0–3 d) → Proliferation (granulation/angiogenesis/epithelialisation, 3–21 d) → Remodelling/Maturation (up to 1 yr).

  • Collagen: type III early → replaced by type I; tensile strength keeps rising for months (never regains 100%).
  • Primary (apposed/sutured), secondary (granulation fills, more scar/contraction), tertiary/delayed primary (contaminated, closed later).

Factors impairing healing

Ischaemia/smoking, infection, diabetes, steroids/immunosuppression, malnutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), radiotherapy, foreign body, tension, age.

• Stages: vascular spasm → platelet plug (primary) → coagulation cascade/fibrin (secondary) → fibrinolysis.
  • PT/INR → extrinsic pathway (warfarin); aPTT → intrinsic (heparin); bleeding time/platelets → primary haemostasis.

Local haemostatic methods

  • Mechanical: pressure, sutures, bone wax, diathermy/cautery.
  • Materials: oxidized cellulose (Surgicel), gelatin sponge (Gelfoam), collagen, fibrin glue.
  • Pharmacological: tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic), adrenaline (vasoconstriction).

• Incisions along Langer's (skin tension) lines / RSTLs for best scars; avoid major vessels/nerves.
  • Flap rules: broad base (blood supply), full thickness, length:base ratio safe, no sharp angles, margins on sound bone, tension-free closure.

Sutures

TypeExamples
ResorbableCatgut (plain/chromic), Vicryl (polyglactin), PGA, Monocryl
Non-resorbableSilk, nylon, polypropylene (Prolene), PTFE

Silk handles well but is most reactive; monofilament has less infection than braided. Oral mucosa sutures removed in 5–7 days.

• History + examination + special tests (imaging, vitality, aspiration, bloods).
  • Incisional biopsy: large/suspicious lesions — include lesion + margin, avoid necrotic centre.
  • Excisional biopsy: small benign lesions removed whole.
  • FNAC for neck/salivary masses; aspirate first if a vascular lesion is suspected (avoid catastrophic bleeding).

• Wound classes: clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated, dirty — risk of surgical-site infection rises across the classes.
  • Surgical scrub, sterile field, gloves/gown, skin prep (chlorhexidine/povidone-iodine).
  • Prophylactic antibiotic given within 60 min before incision for indicated cases; therapeutic course only if established infection.

• Shock types: hypovolaemic (haemorrhage — commonest in trauma), cardiogenic, distributive (septic/anaphylactic/neurogenic), obstructive.
  • Haemorrhagic shock: tachycardia → falling BP (late); manage with control of bleeding + fluids/blood.
  • ASA physical status classification grades peri-operative risk (I–V).

quiz.q: An autoclave cycle completes and the colour-change strip has turned, but you must confirm true sterilisation efficacy. The definitive check is:
o: The colour strip is sufficient proof
quiz.e: Chemical indicators only confirm a condition was reached; a biological spore test confirms that resistant spores were actually killed, which is the definitive proof of sterilisation.

C — clean-looking instruments can still carry spores

quiz.q: A surgical flap was raised with a narrow base and the incision placed directly over the bony defect. Postoperatively it breaks down. The MOST likely cause is:
o: Compromised blood supply + incision over the defect (poor flap design)

w: A — antibiotics do not cause breakdown
C — appropriate suturing supports, not harms, healing
D — ambient temperature is irrelevant
quiz.ty: Flap survival needs a BROAD BASE and the incision on SOUND BONE, not over the defect.

quiz.q: A patient is on warfarin. The single test that BEST reflects the effect of this drug is:
quiz.e: Warfarin acts on the extrinsic/common pathway, monitored by PT/INR; aPTT monitors heparin (intrinsic pathway).
w: A — aPTT tracks heparin, not warfarin
C — bleeding time reflects platelet/vessel function
D — platelet count is normal in warfarin therapy
quiz.ty: Warfarin → PT/INR (extrinsic). Heparin → aPTT (intrinsic).

quiz.q: A 3 cm indurated ulcer with rolled margins is found on the lateral tongue. The correct biopsy approach is:
o: Excisional biopsy removing the whole lesion immediately
quiz.e: Large or suspicious lesions are sampled by incisional biopsy first to obtain a diagnosis before planning definitive treatment.
w: A — excising an unknown malignancy without planning compromises definitive surgery
C — delaying biopsy of a suspicious indurated ulcer is dangerous
D — cytology is not definitive for an invasive lesion
quiz.ty: Large/suspicious lesion → incisional biopsy first; small benign → excisional.

pearls: Match the test to the drug: warfarin → PT/INR (extrinsic); heparin → aPTT (intrinsic).
Biopsy rule of thumb: incise large/suspicious lesions (sample + margin), excise small benign ones whole, and image a vascular lesion before any tissue is taken.
Control bone bleeding mechanically (bone wax/pressure); control soft-tissue bleeding with pressure, sutures, diathermy or a haemostatic agent.
Prophylactic antibiotics work only if tissue levels are present at incision — give them within ~60 minutes before, not after.
Tensile strength of a wound climbs for months but never reaches 100% — respect the healing curve before loading a repair.
mistakes: Designing a flap with a narrow base or an incision over the defect → necrosis/dehiscence.
Closing a wound under tension → breakdown.
Ordering the wrong coagulation test for the anticoagulant in use (PT vs aPTT).
Excising a large suspicious ulcer instead of taking an incisional biopsy first.
Giving 'prophylactic' antibiotics after the operation, when tissue levels are too late.
Ignoring early tachycardia in haemorrhage and waiting for hypotension.
Overheating bone during osteotomy (no irrigation) → necrosis/delayed healing.
Using a reactive braided suture where infection risk is high.
Forgetting vitamin C / nutrition in a poorly healing wound.
Mislabelling a clean-contaminated wound as clean and under-dosing prophylaxis.
Treating all bleeding as a coagulopathy without first controlling local causes.
Biopsying a suspected vascular lesion without prior imaging.

Rigid fixation with anatomical reduction → primary (direct) bone healing; a mobile gap → secondary healing with callus.

study.html:
• Sequential graduated drilling under copious irrigation, low speed, sharp burs — avoid bone temperature >47°C (causes necrosis & fibrous healing).
  • Primary (mechanical) stability at placement is essential; insertion torque ~30–35 Ncm typical.
  • One-stage (healing abutment exposed) vs two-stage (submerged, second-stage uncovering).

ProtocolTiming
Conventional loadingAfter ~3 mo (mandible) / 4–6 mo (maxilla)
Early loading1 week – 2 months
Immediate loadingWithin 48 h (needs high primary stability)
Immediate placementImplant into a fresh extraction socket

Osseointegration = direct bone-implant contact (no fibrous layer); micromotion >100 µm during healing → fibrous encapsulation/failure.

• GBR (guided bone regeneration): barrier membrane (resorbable collagen / non-resorbable PTFE) ± particulate graft to exclude soft tissue.
  • Block grafts (autogenous, e.g., ramus/chin/iliac) for larger defects; ridge split/expansion for narrow ridges.
  • Socket preservation after extraction to limit resorption.
  • Graft types: autograft (best, osteogenic), allograft, xenograft (Bio-Oss), alloplast.

• Indicated when posterior maxillary residual bone height is insufficient for implant length.
  • Direct (lateral window / Caldwell-Luc-type): lateral antrostomy, elevate Schneiderian membrane, place graft; used when residual height is very low.
  • Indirect (osteotome / Summers): trans-crestal elevation, used when ~5–8 mm height remains.
  • Main complication: Schneiderian membrane perforation; also sinusitis, graft loss.

• Indications: single/multiple tooth replacement, free-end saddles, edentulous arch (implant-retained overdenture/fixed bridge), retention/anchorage.
  • Absolute contraindications: recent MI, uncontrolled systemic disease, IV bisphosphonates / antiresorptives (MRONJ), head & neck radiotherapy (ORN risk), uncontrolled diabetes, active malignancy at site, growing child (incomplete growth).
  • Relative: smoking, bruxism, poor oral hygiene, inadequate bone/space, periodontal disease.

Peri-implant mucositisPeri-implantitis
InflammationSoft tissue onlySoft tissue + bone loss
Reversible?Yes (with hygiene)No (progressive)
SignsBleeding on probing, rednessBOP/suppuration + radiographic bone loss, deepening pockets

Risk factors: poor hygiene, smoking, history of periodontitis, residual cement, overload.

• Early (before integration): surgical trauma/overheating, poor primary stability, infection, contamination, low-density bone.
  • Late (after loading): peri-implantitis, occlusal overload, parafunction, poor hygiene.
  • Mobility of an integrated fixture = failure → removal.

• IAN/mental nerve injury (posterior mandible) → paraesthesia; plan with CBCT, leave a safety margin.
  • Maxillary sinus/nasal floor perforation; bleeding (floor of mouth – sublingual/submental arteries, can be life-threatening in the anterior mandible lingual concavity).
  • Adjacent tooth/root damage, fixture fracture, screw loosening.
⭐: Brånemark discovered osseointegration; the implant's success ultimately depends on bone biology + primary stability + load control, not just the fixture.

quiz.q: An implant placed with fast, non-irrigated drilling fails to integrate and histology shows a fibrous tissue layer at the interface. The MOST likely cause is:
o: Bone overheating (>47°C) causing necrosis and fibrous encapsulation
quiz.e: Heat above ~47°C necroses bone; instead of bone-to-implant contact the interface heals as fibrous tissue, which is implant failure.
w: A — a fibrous interface is the opposite of osseointegration

quiz.ty: Keep bone <47°C with irrigation; overheating → fibrous encapsulation = failure.

quiz.q: A patient wants a posterior maxillary implant but has only 4 mm of bone below the sinus floor. The MOST appropriate procedure is:

quiz.q: An implant that osseointegrated and was restored two years ago is now mobile, with deep pockets and radiographic bone loss. The correct management is:

quiz.e: Mobility of a previously integrated implant means loss of integration (failure) and the implant must be removed; the bone loss/pockets indicate peri-implantitis.
w: A — screw tightening does not address a failed, mobile fixture
C — adding load worsens the situation
D — implant mobility is never normal
quiz.ty: A mobile integrated implant = failure → explant. Mobility is never observed.

quiz.q: While placing an implant in the anterior mandible, brisk bleeding fills the floor of the mouth and it begins to swell rapidly. The MOST likely cause is:
o: Perforation of the lingual plate injuring sublingual/submental vessels
quiz.e: A lingual concavity in the anterior mandible means the drill can perforate the lingual plate and lacerate the sublingual/submental arteries, causing a potentially airway-threatening floor-of-mouth haematoma.
w: A — the maxillary sinus is not in the anterior mandible
C — nerve injury causes numbness, not brisk bleeding/swelling
D — Frey's syndrome is gustatory sweating after parotid surgery, unrelated
quiz.ty: Anterior mandible lingual-plate perforation → sublingual/submental artery bleed → life-threatening floor-of-mouth swelling.

pearls: Before posterior mandibular implants, plan on CBCT and leave a safety margin above the inferior alveolar canal.
In the anterior mandible, perforating the lingual plate can lacerate sublingual/submental vessels and cause life-threatening floor-of-mouth bleeding.
Peri-implant mucositis (soft tissue, reversible) becomes peri-implantitis once there is bone loss — manage hygiene early.
An integrated implant that becomes mobile has failed and must be removed; mobility is never 'watch and wait'.
IV bisphosphonates and head-and-neck radiotherapy are major contraindications — implants in those beds risk osteonecrosis.
mistakes: Forcing primary stability in D4 bone instead of choosing a delayed/longer-healing protocol.
Ignoring the IAN canal on imaging and causing nerve injury (plan with CBCT).
Perforating the lingual plate in the anterior mandible without anticipating major bleeding.
Calling peri-implantitis 'mucositis' and missing progressive bone loss.
Leaving a mobile, integrated implant in situ instead of explanting it.
Placing implants in an IV-bisphosphonate or irradiated patient.
Leaving residual subgingival cement (a peri-implantitis risk).
Loading immediately when primary stability is inadequate.
Placing implants too close together / too near a tooth or the IAN.
Calling an allograft/xenograft 'osteogenic' (only autograft is).
Performing a sinus lift without recognising/repairing a membrane perforation.
facts: Peri-implant mucositis (soft tissue, reversible) vs peri-implantitis (+ bone loss, progressive).
Early failure: heat/poor stability/infection. Late failure: peri-implantitis/overload.
Anterior mandible lingual perforation → sublingual/submental artery bleed (can be life-threatening).
Brånemark coined 'osseointegration' = direct bone-to-implant contact with no fibrous layer.
Implant material: commercially pure titanium (grade 4) or Ti-6Al-4V; passive TiO2 oxide; zirconia = metal-free option.
Components: fixture (endosseous), abutment (transmucosal), prosthetic screw, crown.
Connection types: external hex, internal hex, conical (Morse taper) — affects micro-gap/screw stability.
Surface treatments (SLA, anodised, blasted) increase roughness → faster osseointegration.
Bone overheating threshold = >47°C for ~1 minute → necrosis → fibrous encapsulation.
Micromotion threshold >100 µm during healing → fibrous encapsulation (failure).
Primary stability target torque ≈ 30–35 Ncm.
Bone quality (Lekholm & Zarb) D1 dense cortical → D4 thin cortex/low-density trabecular.
Best primary stability D1/D2; most challenging D4 (posterior maxilla).
Healing: ~3 months mandible, ~4–6 months maxilla.
Loading: conventional (after healing), early (1 wk–2 mo), immediate (<48 h; needs high stability).
Immediate placement = implant into a fresh extraction socket (engage native apical/palatal bone).
Minimum distances: ~1.5–2 mm bone buccal/lingual, ~1.5 mm from a tooth, ~3 mm between implants, ~2 mm above the IAN.
Graft properties: osteogenesis (autograft only), osteoinduction (BMP), osteoconduction (scaffold).
Graft types: autograft (gold standard), allograft (human), xenograft (Bio-Oss), alloplast (HA/β-TCP).
Sinus lift: direct (lateral window) for very low bone; indirect (osteotome/Summers) for ~5–8 mm.
Main sinus-lift complication: Schneiderian membrane perforation.
GBR uses a barrier membrane to exclude faster-growing soft tissue from the bony defect.
Ridge split/expansion for a narrow (knife-edge) ridge; socket preservation limits resorption.
Peri-implant mucositis = soft-tissue inflammation (reversible); peri-implantitis = + bone loss (progressive).
Early failure: overheating/poor stability/infection; late failure: peri-implantitis/overload.
Anterior mandible lingual-plate perforation → sublingual/submental artery bleed (life-threatening).
Absolute contraindications: recent MI, IV bisphosphonates, head/neck radiotherapy, uncontrolled disease.
Relative contraindications: smoking, bruxism, poor hygiene, periodontitis, inadequate bone.
mnemonics: Loading: Conventional (after healing) · Early (1wk-2mo) · Immediate (<48h, needs high stability).
Implant success 'PILS': Primary stability, Irrigation (<47°C), Low micromotion, Sterile/atraumatic.
Contraindications (absolute): IV Bisphosphonates, Radiotherapy, recent MI, Uncontrolled disease.
Sinus lift: low bone → Direct (lateral window); moderate → Indirect (osteotome).

study.html:
A hamartoma, not a true neoplasm — the most common odontogenic tumor overall.

  • Compound: multiple small tooth-like denticles (anterior maxilla).
  • Complex: disorganized conglomerate mass of enamel/dentin (posterior mandible).
  • Often associated with an unerupted/impacted tooth; well-defined radiopacity with radiolucent rim.
  • Treatment: simple enucleation; excellent prognosis.

TumorKey point
CementoblastomaRadiopaque mass fused to a root with radiolucent halo; vital tooth, often painful
Ameloblastic fibromaYoung; epithelium + mesenchyme, no hard tissue; better prognosis than ameloblastoma
Ameloblastic fibro-odontomaTrue mixed tumor that forms enamel/dentin
Squamous odontogenic tumorFrom rests of Malassez; triangular radiolucency between roots
Calcifying odontogenic cyst (Gorlin)Contains ghost cells; may calcify
KCOT / OKCDental lamina origin; highest recurrence; multiple → Gorlin syndrome

Normal bone replaced by fibro-osseous tissue (GNAS mutation). Painless, slow facial swelling in adolescents/young adults; maxilla > mandible.

  • Radiology: "ground-glass" / orange-peel, ill-defined borders blending into normal bone.
  • Monostotic (one bone, commonest) vs polyostotic. McCune–Albright = polyostotic FD + café-au-lait macules + endocrinopathy (precocious puberty).
  • Treatment: observation; conservative contouring once mature for cosmesis/function. Avoid radiotherapy (risk of post-irradiation sarcoma).
⭐ FD vs ossifying fibroma: FD blends into bone (ill-defined); ossifying fibroma is well-defined/encapsulated and shells out. Juvenile ossifying fibroma is aggressive and recurs.

• Reactive fibro-osseous lesion at tooth apices; teeth remain vital.
  • Periapical (anterior mandible), focal, and florid (multiquadrant, in middle-aged Black women).
  • Usually no treatment; avoid unnecessary surgery (poorly vascular → infection risk).

• Central giant cell granuloma (CGCG): anterior mandible, crosses midline; multilocular radiolucency; osteoclast-like multinucleated giant cells in vascular stroma. Can be aggressive in young patients.
  • Peripheral giant cell granuloma (PGCG): soft-tissue gingival/alveolar mass (the "giant cell epulis"); may cup-shaped resorb crestal bone.
  • Brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism: histologically identical to CGCG — always check serum Ca, phosphate, PTH, look for loss of lamina dura.
  • Aneurysmal bone cyst: blood-filled spaces, "blow-out" expansion.
  • Cherubism: bilateral, symmetric, familial (autosomal dominant) childhood jaw expansion; "eyes to heaven"; tends to regress after puberty.

• Older adults; disordered remodeling. Jaw enlargement (maxilla), denture/hat no longer fits, spacing of teeth, hypercementosis.
  • Radiology: "cotton-wool" patches; biochemistry: markedly raised alkaline phosphatase (Ca & phosphate usually normal).
  • Complications: bone pain, fractures, osteosarcoma transformation, extraction bleeding/poor healing.

• Most common primary malignant bone tumor of the jaws; jaw cases ~a decade later than long-bone (3rd–4th decade).
  • Rapid swelling, pain, paresthesia, loosening teeth.
  • Radiology: "sunburst/sunray" spiculation, Codman triangle, and early symmetrical widening of the PDL space (Garrington sign).
  • Treatment: wide/radical surgical resection ± chemotherapy; prognosis depends on complete excision.

TumorClue
ChondrosarcomaCartilage-forming sites (anterior maxilla, condyle); does NOT respond well to radio/chemo
Ewing sarcomaChildren; "onion-skin" periosteal reaction; small round blue cells
Burkitt lymphomaAfrican form in jaws of children; EBV-associated; "starry-sky" histology
Multiple myeloma"Punched-out" radiolucencies; Bence-Jones protein; monoclonal gammopathy
Langerhans cell histiocytosis"Floating teeth" (alveolar destruction); Birbeck granules, CD1a+

• Primary sources: breast (F), lung/prostate (M), kidney, thyroid, colon.
  • Most common jaw site: posterior mandible (residual haematopoietic marrow).
  • "Numb chin" (mental nerve neuropathy) without a dental cause is a red flag for malignancy/metastasis.
  • Often ill-defined, "moth-eaten" radiolucency; may be the first sign of an unknown primary.

• Central haemangioma / AVM: may show as multilocular radiolucency; aspirate/image before any biopsy or extraction — risk of torrential, life-threatening haemorrhage. Look for bruit, pumping tooth.
  • Melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy: pigmented, rapidly growing anterior maxilla mass in infants; neural crest origin; raised urinary VMA.
⭐ Safety: Never biopsy/extract into a suspected vascular jaw lesion without imaging — fatal bleeding can occur.

SignLesion
Soap-bubble / honeycombAmeloblastoma, myxoma, CGCG
Tennis-racket / step-ladderOdontogenic myxoma
Driven snowCEOT (Pindborg)
Snowflake calcificationsAOT
Ground-glassFibrous dysplasia
Cotton-woolPaget's disease
Sunburst + Garrington (PDL widening)Osteosarcoma
Onion-skinEwing sarcoma
Punched-outMultiple myeloma
Floating teethLangerhans cell histiocytosis

SyndromeFeatures
GardnerMultiple osteomas + supernumerary teeth + intestinal polyps (FAP → colon cancer risk)
Gorlin (NBCCS)Multiple OKCs + basal cell carcinomas + rib anomalies + falx calcification
McCune-AlbrightPolyostotic fibrous dysplasia + café-au-lait + endocrinopathy
CherubismBilateral familial giant-cell jaw lesions in childhood

Management principles

  • Biopsy (histopathology) is definitive — but image first if vascular lesion suspected.
  • Benign aggressive (ameloblastoma, myxoma, KCOT): resection/margin or adjuncts due to recurrence.
  • Hamartomas/encapsulated (odontoma, AOT, cementoblastoma): enucleation.
  • Malignant: wide resection ± radio/chemo; manage the neck as indicated.

o: Image first (angiography/CT) — suspect a central haemangioma/AVM
Extract the mobile tooth to decompress it
quiz.e: A pulsatile/pumping tooth, bluish mucosa and a bruit suggest a vascular lesion; biopsy or extraction can cause fatal haemorrhage, so imaging comes first.
w: A — biopsy of a vascular lesion can bleed catastrophically
C — extracting a tooth in an AVM can cause exsanguinating haemorrhage
D — curettage of a vascular lesion is equally dangerous
quiz.ty: Pumping tooth + bruit + bluish swelling = vascular lesion → IMAGE first; never biopsy/extract blindly.

quiz.e: Ground-glass bone blending into normal bone in a young patient is fibrous dysplasia; it is observed/recontoured when mature, and radiotherapy is avoided because of malignant transformation risk.
w: A — ossifying fibroma is well-defined and shells out, unlike this blending lesion
C — Paget's is a disease of older adults with cotton-wool bone
D — this is benign fibrous dysplasia, not osteosarcoma
quiz.ty: Ground-glass, ill-defined, young patient = fibrous dysplasia → observe/recontour; NEVER irradiate.

quiz.q: A 14-year-old female has a painless swelling of the anterior maxilla. A radiograph shows a well-defined unilocular radiolucency around the crown of an unerupted canine, extending past the CEJ, with faint flecks of calcification. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
quiz.e: The 'two-thirds' tumour (anterior maxilla, young female, around an impacted canine, often extending apical to the CEJ with snowflake calcifications) is an AOT, treated by simple enucleation with an excellent prognosis.
w: A — a dentigerous cyst attaches at the CEJ and lacks calcifications; AOT classically extends past the CEJ
C — ameloblastoma is usually a multilocular posterior-mandible lesion in older patients
D — CEOT is typically a posterior-mandible mixed lesion ('driven snow'), not this picture
quiz.ty: Anterior maxilla + young female + impacted canine + snowflake flecks = AOT (enucleation).

quiz.e: A mental-nerve neuropathy ('numb chin') with an ill-defined destructive lesion and no dental cause is a red flag for malignancy or metastasis and needs urgent investigation/biopsy.
w: A — dry socket is an acute post-extraction pain, not a chronic numb chin
C — periodontal disease does not cause lip/chin numbness
D — fluorosis affects enamel, not nerves or bone destruction
quiz.ty: 'Numb chin' + moth-eaten mandibular lesion + no dental cause = think malignancy/metastasis.

quiz.q: A patient has rapid mandibular swelling, pain and paraesthesia; the radiograph shows a 'sunburst' periosteal reaction and symmetrical widening of the periodontal ligament space around a tooth. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
quiz.e: A sunburst reaction with symmetrical PDL widening (Garrington sign) and rapid painful growth indicates osteosarcoma, managed by wide surgical resection ± chemotherapy.
w: A — fibrous dysplasia is a slow, painless, ground-glass lesion
C — an odontoma is a benign radiopaque hamartoma
D — ameloblastoma is slow-growing and does not give a sunburst reaction
quiz.ty: Sunburst + symmetric PDL widening (Garrington) + rapid pain = osteosarcoma.

quiz.q: A pericoronal radiolucency around an impacted lower third molar is enucleated; histology shows an ameloblastic epithelial lining within the cyst wall. This is BEST classified as:
quiz.e: Ameloblastic lining in what looked like a dentigerous cyst is a unicystic ameloblastoma — it must be recognised because it requires closer follow-up/more than simple curettage depending on subtype.
w: A — a true dentigerous cyst has a thin non-ameloblastic reduced enamel epithelium lining
C — a radicular cyst is periapical on a non-vital tooth, not pericoronal
D — an odontoma is a calcified hamartoma, not a cystic lining
quiz.ty: A 'dentigerous cyst' with ameloblastic lining = unicystic ameloblastoma — don't under-treat it.

pearls: Any giant-cell lesion of the jaw mandates serum calcium, phosphate and PTH — a brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism is histologically identical to CGCG.
A 'numb chin' with no dental cause is a red flag for malignancy/metastasis in the mandible.
Never irradiate fibrous dysplasia — it risks post-irradiation sarcoma; recontour conservatively once mature.
Histopathology is the final arbiter — but image a suspected vascular lesion before any tissue is taken.
Odontoma is the commonest odontogenic tumour but is a hamartoma; ameloblastoma is the commonest true neoplasm.
An impacted-tooth pericoronal radiolucency that is larger than a normal follicle, or has ameloblastic lining, may be a unicystic ameloblastoma rather than a dentigerous cyst.
mistakes: Treating a solid/multicystic ameloblastoma by enucleation/curettage (high recurrence) instead of resection with a margin.
Calling every multilocular radiolucency an ameloblastoma without histology (DDx: myxoma, CGCG, OKC).
Irradiating fibrous dysplasia (risk of post-irradiation sarcoma).
Not checking Ca/PO4/PTH for a giant-cell lesion and missing hyperparathyroidism.
Biopsying/extracting into a central haemangioma/AVM without prior imaging.
Mistaking fibrous dysplasia (ill-defined, blends) for ossifying fibroma (well-defined, shells out).
Assuming a pericoronal radiolucency is always a benign dentigerous cyst (could be unicystic ameloblastoma).
Ignoring a numb chin as benign instead of investigating for malignancy/metastasis.
Forgetting that odontoma (the commonest odontogenic tumour) is a hamartoma, not a true neoplasm.
Treating cemento-osseous dysplasia surgically (poorly vascular → infection) when observation is correct.
Confusing compound (denticles) and complex (mass) odontomas.
Overlooking the systemic/syndromic associations (Gorlin, Gardner, McCune-Albright, cherubism).
facts: Jaw metastasis: breast (F), lung/prostate (M); posterior mandible; 'numb chin' red flag.
Syndromes: Gardner (osteomas+polyps), Gorlin (OKCs+BCCs), McCune-Albright (FD+café-au-lait+endocrine), cherubism.
Vascular jaw lesion (central haemangioma/AVM): image before any biopsy/extraction — fatal bleeding risk.
Ameloblastoma peak age = 3rd–5th decade; ~80% in the mandible (molar/ramus).
Unicystic ameloblastoma subtypes: luminal, intraluminal (better prognosis), mural (more aggressive).
Desmoplastic ameloblastoma: often anterior maxilla, mixed radiolucent–radiopaque.
Ameloblastic carcinoma = malignant histology; metastasising ameloblastoma = benign histology but distant (lung) spread.
AOT is benign & encapsulated → enucleation is curative; recurrence is rare.
CEOT (Pindborg) amyloid is Congo-red positive with apple-green birefringence; Liesegang-ring calcifications.
Odontogenic myxoma has NO capsule → infiltrative → recurs.
Compound odontoma = denticles (anterior maxilla); complex odontoma = disorganised mass (posterior mandible).
Cementoblastoma: attached to a VITAL tooth root, often painful, continues to grow.
Calcifying odontogenic cyst (Gorlin): ghost cells; may be associated with an odontoma.
Fibrous dysplasia: GNAS mutation; monostotic is commonest; ALP may be raised; AVOID radiotherapy.
Café-au-lait in fibrous dysplasia = 'coast of Maine' (irregular) vs 'coast of California' (smooth) in NF1.
Ossifying fibroma is encapsulated and 'shells out'; juvenile ossifying fibroma is aggressive/recurs.
Cemento-osseous dysplasia: vital teeth, usually NO treatment; florid type in middle-aged women.
Central giant cell granuloma: anterior mandible, crosses the midline; ALWAYS check Ca/PO4/PTH (brown tumour).
Aneurysmal bone cyst: blood-filled spaces, rapid 'blow-out' expansion.
Cherubism: autosomal dominant, bilateral, childhood; tends to regress after puberty.
Paget's: raised alkaline phosphatase, cotton-wool bone, hypercementosis, dentures stop fitting; osteosarcoma risk.
Osteosarcoma of the jaw occurs ~a decade later than long-bone osteosarcoma (3rd–4th decade).
Ewing sarcoma: 'onion-skin' periosteum, small round blue cells, children.
Burkitt lymphoma (African): jaws of children, EBV-associated, 'starry-sky' histology.
Multiple myeloma: 'punched-out' lesions, Bence-Jones proteinuria, monoclonal gammopathy.
Langerhans cell histiocytosis: 'floating teeth', CD1a+/S100+, Birbeck granules.
Melanotic neuroectodermal tumour of infancy: pigmented anterior-maxilla mass, raised urinary VMA.
Jaw metastasis sources: breast (F), lung/prostate (M), kidney, thyroid, colon; site = posterior mandible.
mnemonics: Most common: Odontoma (overall hamartoma) vs Ameloblastoma (true neoplasm).
Giant-cell lesion work-up 'Check the PTH' (rule out brown tumour).
Ameloblastoma malignancy: Ameloblastic CARCINOMA = bad histology; METASTASISING ameloblastoma = good histology, bad behaviour.
Giant-cell lesion work-up: always 'check the PTH' (exclude brown tumour).
Odontoma: COMpound = COMpartments/denticles (anterior); COMplex = COMbined mass (posterior).

Which structure does NOT pass through the parotid gland?
quiz.e: Lingual nerve is in the floor of mouth.

quiz.q: PSA nerve block spares which root?
Immediately after an inferior alveolar nerve block the patient cannot fully close the eye and the corner of the mouth droops on that side, but recovers in ~90 minutes. The explanation is:
o: Local anaesthetic deposited too far posteriorly, reaching the facial nerve in the parotid gland
quiz.e: If the needle is placed too deep/posterior the LA can enter the parotid and anaesthetise the facial nerve (VII), causing a transient facial palsy that resolves as the LA wears off.
w: A — a stroke would not resolve in 90 minutes with the LA
C — transection is permanent; this recovered
D — trigeminal neuralgia is paroxysmal facial PAIN, not weakness
quiz.ty: Transient facial palsy during an IANB = LA in the parotid (CN VII); reassure, it recovers.

quiz.q: A swelling rapidly appears in the cheek/infratemporal region just after a posterior superior alveolar nerve block. The MOST likely source is the:
quiz.e: The PSA block is near the pterygoid venous plexus; puncturing it causes a haematoma.
w: A — the facial artery is more anterior/superficial and not the classic PSA-block bleeder
C — the internal carotid is deep and not encountered here
D — the antrum is an air space, not a source of haematoma
quiz.ty: Haematoma after a PSA block = pterygoid venous plexus.

quiz.q: After raising a lingual flap to remove a lower third molar, the patient has numbness of the ipsilateral anterior tongue and altered taste. The nerve injured carries general sensation from V3 and taste fibres from:
o: The chorda tympani of the facial nerve (VII)
quiz.e: The lingual nerve gives general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (V3) and carries taste fibres from the chorda tympani (VII); it is vulnerable at the lingual plate of the third molar.
w: A — the glossopharyngeal supplies the POSTERIOR third (taste and sensation)
C — the hypoglossal is purely motor to the tongue
D — the vagus supplies the epiglottic region, not the anterior tongue
quiz.ty: Lingual nerve = anterior 2/3 sensation (V3) + taste via chorda tympani (VII); at risk at the lower 8 lingual plate.

quiz.q: A patient develops gustatory sweating over the cheek when eating, months after a superficial parotidectomy. This is due to aberrant regeneration of the:
quiz.e: Frey's syndrome results from parasympathetic auriculotemporal fibres re-innervating sweat glands, causing gustatory sweating after parotid surgery.
w: A — facial nerve injury causes facial weakness, not sweating
C — great auricular injury causes numbness of the ear lobe
D — the lingual nerve is unrelated to cheek skin sweating
quiz.ty: Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating after parotid surgery) = auriculotemporal nerve misdirection.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient has a 'lucid interval' then rapid deterioration; CT shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) extradural haematoma. The artery typically responsible and its foramen are:
quiz.e: The middle meningeal artery, entering the skull via the foramen spinosum, is the classic source of an extradural (epidural) haematoma.
w: A — the facial artery is extracranial and unrelated
C — the foramen rotundum transmits V2, not the artery causing extradural bleeds
D — the foramen ovale transmits V3
quiz.ty: Extradural haematoma = middle meningeal artery via the foramen spinosum.

quiz.q: On asking a patient to protrude the tongue it deviates to the right. This indicates a lesion of the:
quiz.e: The genioglossus protrudes the tongue; with a right hypoglossal (XII) lesion the right side is weak and the tongue deviates TOWARD the lesion (to the right).
w: B — a left XII lesion deviates the tongue to the left
C — the lingual nerve is sensory; it does not cause deviation
D — the glossopharyngeal supplies the posterior third sensation/taste, not protrusion
quiz.ty: Tongue deviates TOWARD the side of a hypoglossal (XII) lesion.

pearls: A haematoma after a posterior superior alveolar block comes from the pterygoid venous plexus.
Infections and emboli reach the cavernous sinus through the valveless pterygoid plexus and ophthalmic veins — the anatomical basis of cavernous sinus thrombosis.
The middle meningeal artery (through foramen spinosum) is the classic source of an extradural haematoma.
Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels with the lingual nerve via the chorda tympani (VII); general sensation is the lingual nerve (V3).
The internal carotid gives NO branches in the neck — that distinguishes it from the external carotid.
mistakes: Forgetting buccinator is a muscle of facial expression (VII), not mastication.
Forgetting palatoglossus is the only tongue muscle NOT supplied by the hypoglossal (it is vagus).
Mixing Stensen's duct (parotid, opposite upper 2nd molar) and Wharton's duct (submandibular).
Forgetting the facial nerve is the structure most at risk in parotid surgery.
Saying the tongue deviates AWAY from a hypoglossal lesion (it deviates TOWARD it).
Forgetting tensor veli palatini is the only palate muscle supplied by V3 (the rest are vagus).
Saying the maxillary sinus drains into the inferior meatus (it drains into the MIDDLE meatus).
Forgetting the lingual nerve loops UNDER Wharton's duct in the floor of mouth.
Confusing the parasympathetic ganglia: pterygopalatine (VII) vs otic (IX) vs submandibular (VII).
Forgetting the only MEDIAL branch of the ECA is the ascending pharyngeal.
Forgetting the lateral pterygoid PROTRUDES/depresses (the only depressor-direction muscle of mastication).
Mislocating the middle meningeal artery's foramen (spinosum, not ovale).
Forgetting PSA spares the mesiobuccal root of the maxillary 1st molar (supplied by MSA).
facts: TMJ ligaments: lateral (temporomandibular); accessory = stylomandibular & sphenomandibular.
TMJ nerve supply: auriculotemporal + masseteric (both V3).
TMJ disc divides joint: upper (translation) & lower (rotation) compartments.
Anterior triangle: submental, submandibular (digastric), carotid, muscular.
Posterior triangle: occipital + supraclavicular; SCM forms the anterior boundary.
Tip of tongue lymph drains to submental nodes (bilateral).
Lateral tongue lymph drains to submandibular then deep cervical nodes.
Jugulodigastric (tonsillar) node = main node for tonsil & posterior tongue.
1st pharyngeal arch (Meckel): nerve V3; malleus & incus; muscles of mastication.
2nd arch (Reichert): nerve VII; stapes, styloid; muscles of facial expression.
3rd arch: nerve IX; stylopharyngeus; greater horn of hyoid.
4th & 6th arches: nerve X; pharyngeal & laryngeal muscles.
Maxillary, frontal, anterior ethmoid sinuses drain to the MIDDLE meatus.
Posterior ethmoid drains to superior meatus; sphenoid to spheno-ethmoidal recess.
Nasolacrimal duct drains to the inferior meatus.
Mandibular foramen leads to inferior alveolar nerve/vessels; guarded by the lingula.
Mental foramen usually lies between the mandibular premolar apices.
PSA supplies maxillary molars except the mesiobuccal root of the 1st molar (MSA).
Inferior alveolar nerve terminal branches: mental (lip/chin) + incisive.
Lingual nerve carries chorda tympani and lies near the lower 3rd molar.
Buccinator is a muscle of facial expression (CN VII), NOT mastication.
Sphenomandibular ligament = remnant of Meckel's cartilage; IANB landmark.
Stensen's duct pierces the buccinator muscle.
Common carotid bifurcates at ~C3-C4 (upper thyroid cartilage) into ICA & ECA.
ICA gives NO branches in the neck (distinguishes it from ECA).
Vagus (X) supplies all pharyngeal/palate muscles except stylopharyngeus (IX) & tensor veli palatini (V3).
Carotid sheath: common/internal carotid, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve.
Facial nerve = structure most at risk in parotid surgery.
Frey's syndrome: auriculotemporal misdirection to gustatory sweating after parotid surgery.
Lingual nerve loops UNDER (below) Wharton's duct in the floor of mouth.
Mylohyoid forms the floor of the mouth; nerve to mylohyoid (V3).
Greater palatine foramen lies near the maxillary 3rd molar.
Pterygopalatine ganglion = parasympathetic relay for lacrimal & nasal/palatal glands (VII).
Otic ganglion = parasympathetic relay for the parotid (IX).
Recurrent laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus (X).
Tensor veli palatini is the only palate muscle supplied by V3.
Stylopharyngeus is the only muscle supplied by glossopharyngeal (IX).
Muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve (VII); orbicularis oculi, oris, buccinator, etc.
Facial artery branches: ascending palatine, tonsillar, glandular, submental, inferior & superior labial, lateral nasal, angular.
The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic & deep facial veins (the facial 'danger area').
The 'danger triangle' of the face drains toward the cavernous sinus → risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis.
Retromandibular vein = superficial temporal + maxillary veins; splits into anterior & posterior divisions.
The pterygoid venous plexus connects with the cavernous sinus (route of spread).
Maxillary artery 3 parts: mandibular (incl. middle meningeal & inferior alveolar), pterygoid, pterygopalatine (incl. PSA, infraorbital, sphenopalatine, greater palatine).
Lingual artery branches: suprahyoid, dorsal lingual, sublingual, deep lingual.
Carotid sheath contents: common/internal carotid, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve.
Mandibular foramen → inferior alveolar nerve & vessels; guarded by the lingula (IANB landmark).
mnemonics: Tongue: motor = Hypoglossal (all but palatoglossus); ant.2/3 taste = chorda tympani (VII), sensation = lingual (V3); post.1/3 = glossopharyngeal (IX).
Tongue deviates TOWARD a hypoglossal (XII) lesion.
Only the ascending pharyngeal is a MEDIAL branch of the ECA.
Maxillary sinus drains into the MIDDLE meatus.
Tensor veli palatini = the only palate muscle from V3 (the rest = vagus).
