study.html:
• Canine space (from maxillary canine): swelling of the upper lip/nasolabial fold, loss of nasolabial groove; risk of spread to the eye.
  • Buccal space (premolars/molars): cheek swelling.
  • Infratemporal space (upper 3rd molar / PSA): deep, may track to cavernous sinus via pterygoid plexus.
  • Palatal abscess (lateral incisor/palatal root of 1st molar).
⭐: Canine/infratemporal infection can reach the cavernous sinus → cavernous sinus thrombosis (emergency).

• Submental (lower incisors): midline chin swelling.
  • Sublingual (apices above mylohyoid – premolars/1st molar): raised floor of mouth.
  • Submandibular (apices below mylohyoid – 2nd/3rd molar): swelling at the lower border, may obscure the angle.
  • Buccal (mandibular molars).
  • Masticator group: masseteric, pterygomandibular, temporal — present with marked trismus; pterygomandibular space also relevant to a failed IANB.

• Bilateral cellulitis of submandibular + sublingual + submental spaces — usually from a lower molar.
  • Brawny, board-like ("woody") floor of mouth, raised/protruding tongue, drooling, dysphagia, "hot potato" voice.
  • Airway emergency → secure airway (may need awake fibreoptic/tracheostomy), IV antibiotics, urgent surgical decompression of all involved spaces, treat the source.

• Lateral (para)pharyngeal → retropharyngeal → "danger space" → mediastinitis (high mortality).
  • Cavernous sinus thrombosis (from upper anterior/canine/infratemporal spread): proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, fever.
  • Necrotising fasciitis: rapidly spreading, crepitus, systemic toxicity — surgical emergency.
  • Brain abscess, sepsis, airway loss.

1. Remove the cause — extraction, pulp extirpation/RCT, or drain the source.
  2. Establish drainage — incise & drain pus (dependent drainage, place a drain), or open through the tooth.
  3. Support the patient — analgesia, hydration, nutrition, treat systemic upset.
  4. Antibiotics as an adjunct (not a substitute for drainage) — empirical then guided by culture & sensitivity.
  5. Reassess; airway and systemic monitoring for severe cases.
⭐: "Pus somewhere, pus nowhere, pus under a flap" — find and drain the pus; antibiotics alone fail.

• First-line: amoxicillin / penicillin V; add metronidazole for anaerobic cover; co-amoxiclav for broader cover.
  • Penicillin allergy: clindamycin (good bone penetration) or a macrolide.
  • Severe/hospital: IV therapy, broaden per culture; consider source-control surgery first.

• Mandible >> maxilla (poorer collateral blood supply).
  • Acute suppurative: pain, swelling, pus, fever, loose teeth, lip paraesthesia; X-ray lags (radiolucency after ~10 days).
  • Chronic: sequestrum (dead bone) + involucrum (new bone), sinus tracts, "moth-eaten" bone.
  • Garré's (chronic with proliferative periostitis): "onion-skin" periosteal new bone in young patients.
  • Predisposing: irradiated bone (ORN), bisphosphonates (MRONJ), diabetes, immunosuppression.
  • Treatment: drainage, sequestrectomy/debridement, prolonged antibiotics, treat the source; hyperbaric O₂ for ORN.

• Actinomycosis: chronic, multiple sinuses discharging "sulfur granules"; treat with prolonged high-dose penicillin.
  • Candidiasis: pseudomembranous (wipeable white plaques), erythematous, angular cheilitis — in immunosuppressed/denture wearers.
  • Pericoronitis: inflammation of the operculum over a partially erupted (usually lower 3rd molar) tooth; manage with irrigation/debridement, treat trauma from the opposing tooth, antibiotics if spreading/systemic; later definitive extraction.

study.h: S1. Classification of the fascial spaces
study.html:
Spaces are classified by region and by whether they are primary (infected directly from a tooth) or secondary (involved by spread from a primary space).

GroupSpaces
Maxillary (upper)Canine · Buccal · Infratemporal
Mandibular primary (lower)Submental · Sublingual · Submandibular · Buccal
Masticator (secondary)Submasseteric (masseteric) · Pterygomandibular · Temporal (superficial & deep)
Deep cervical / neckLateral pharyngeal (parapharyngeal) · Retropharyngeal · 'Danger' space · Pretracheal · Carotid sheath
⭐ Determinant of spread: the position of the root apex relative to the muscle attachment (mylohyoid, buccinator, mentalis) and the thinnest cortical plate.

study.h: S2. Maxillary spaces — tooth, sign, spread
study.html:
SpaceFrom which teethSign / danger
CanineMaxillary canine (long root above the muscle)Swelling of the upper lip/nasolabial fold; loss of the nasolabial groove → may spread to the eye/cavernous sinus
BuccalMaxillary premolars/molars (apex above buccinator)Cheek swelling
InfratemporalMaxillary 3rd molar / PSA regionDeep; can reach the cavernous sinus via the pterygoid plexus

study.h: S3. Mandibular spaces & the mylohyoid rule
study.html:
The mylohyoid line decides where a lower molar infection points:

  • Apex ABOVE the mylohyoid line (anteriors, premolars, 1st molar) → sublingual space (raised floor of mouth).
  • Apex BELOW the mylohyoid line (2nd & 3rd molars) → submandibular space (swelling at the lower border/angle).
  • Submental (lower incisors, below the mentalis) → midline chin swelling.
  • Buccal (mandibular premolars/molars, apex below buccinator) → cheek swelling.

The sublingual and submandibular spaces communicate around the posterior free border of mylohyoid — infection passes between them.

• Pterygomandibular space (between medial pterygoid & ramus): from lower 3rd molars or a contaminated IAN block → marked trismus, little external swelling.
  • Submasseteric & temporal spaces: trismus, swelling over the ramus/temple.
  • Lateral (para)pharyngeal space: medial tonsillar/pharyngeal bulge, dysphagia → gateway to the retropharyngeal space and the carotid sheath.
  • Retropharyngeal & 'danger' space: lead directly to the mediastinum (mediastinitis, high mortality).

• Ludwig's angina = bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular + sublingual + submental spaces → 'woody' floor of mouth, raised tongue, airway emergency.
  • Escalation: masticator/submandibular → lateral pharyngeal → retropharyngeal → danger space → mediastinum.
  • Upper anterior/canine/infratemporal → cavernous sinus thrombosis via valveless veins.
  • Other dangers: necrotising fasciitis, carotid-sheath involvement, airway loss, sepsis.

quiz.q: A rapidly spreading infection with crepitus and skin necrosis is:
The principle 'antibiotics are an adjunct, not a substitute' means:
Osteomyelitis affects the mandible more than the maxilla because the mandible has:
o: A poorer/less collateral blood supply & dense cortex

quiz.q: In chronic osteomyelitis, dead separated bone is called the:
'Onion-skin' periosteal new bone in a young patient suggests:
Multiple sinuses discharging 'sulfur granules' indicate:
Actinomycosis is treated with:
Pseudomembranous candidiasis appears as:
Pericoronitis is inflammation of the:
o: Operculum/soft tissue over a partially erupted tooth

quiz.q: Initial management of acute pericoronitis includes:
o: Irrigation/debridement under the operculum ± relieving the opposing tooth

quiz.q: A palatal abscess is most often from the:
o: Lateral incisor or palatal root of an upper molar

quiz.q: The infratemporal space is most relevant to infection from the:
Cellulitis is best described as:
A submasseteric/masticator space abscess characteristically causes:
The lower 2nd/3rd molar apices usually lie below the mylohyoid, so infection points to the:
The 'danger space' is clinically important because it provides a route to the:
A patient with a spreading facial infection, raised temperature and difficulty swallowing should be:
o: Admitted; airway/systemic assessment + IV antibiotics + drainage

quiz.q: The single most reliable way to resolve a periapical abscess is:
o: Drainage + remove the cause (extraction or RCT)

quiz.q: Co-amoxiclav is used in odontogenic infection because it:
Acute suppurative osteomyelitis early radiograph typically shows:
o: Little change for ~10 days, then 'moth-eaten' lucency

quiz.q: Hyperbaric oxygen is a useful adjunct particularly in:
Angular cheilitis is commonly associated with:
A child with bilateral parotid swelling and systemic symptoms most likely has:
Pus pointing intra-orally should be drained by:
o: A dependent incision (and a drain if needed)

quiz.q: The commonest cause of a deep neck-space infection is:
In a diabetic with a spreading facial infection you should also:
The key difference between a sinus tract (chronic) and acute abscess is:
o: Sinus drains chronically with less acute pain

quiz.q: A diabetic man has rapidly spreading bilateral submandibular swelling, a raised tongue, drooling, a muffled voice and difficulty swallowing. The FIRST priority is:
o: Start IV antibiotics and review in the morning
Secure/protect the airway (prepare for awake fibreoptic intubation or tracheostomy)
Take an OPG before doing anything
Extract the causative tooth under local anaesthesia
quiz.e: This is Ludwig's angina; the immediate threat to life is airway obstruction from the elevated tongue and floor-of-mouth swelling, so airway control comes before everything else.
w: A — antibiotics are essential but do not address the imminent airway obstruction, and 'review in the morning' is dangerous
C — imaging must not delay airway management in an obstructing patient
D — operating under LA without first securing the airway risks losing it
quiz.ty: Ludwig's angina = airway first (then IV antibiotics + surgical decompression + source control).

quiz.q: A patient has a tender, diffuse, firm facial swelling that is red and warm but NOT fluctuant, with no pus on aspiration. The MOST appropriate management is:
o: Antibiotics + remove/treat the source, with review for any developing collection
Long-term antibiotics alone without treating the tooth
quiz.e: A diffuse, non-fluctuant swelling without pus is cellulitis (pre-suppurative); treat with antibiotics and source control, and re-assess because it may localise into an abscess needing drainage.
w: A — there is no pus yet to drain; incising cellulitis achieves little
C — untreated cellulitis spreads and may become life-threatening
D — antibiotics alone without removing the dental cause allow recurrence
quiz.ty: Cellulitis (diffuse, no pus) = antibiotics + source control + re-assess; abscess (fluctuant pus) = incise & drain.

quiz.q: An untreated infection from an upper canine causes swelling of the upper lip and lower eyelid, and the patient now develops proptosis, fever and eye-movement problems. The feared complication is:
quiz.e: Spread from the canine/upper anterior region via the valveless angular/ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus produces cavernous sinus thrombosis (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, fever) — a true emergency.
w: A — Ludwig's angina arises from lower molars and affects the floor of mouth, not the orbit
C — dry socket is a localised post-extraction problem
D — simple sinusitis does not cause proptosis and ophthalmoplegia
quiz.ty: Upper anterior/canine infection → cavernous sinus thrombosis via valveless veins (proptosis, ophthalmoplegia).

quiz.q: An infection from a lower second molar whose root apices lie BELOW the mylohyoid line will most likely point to the:
quiz.e: When the apices are below the mylohyoid attachment, pus tracks into the submandibular space; apices above mylohyoid drain into the sublingual space.
w: A — the sublingual space is involved when apices are ABOVE the mylohyoid line
C — the canine space relates to the maxillary canine
D — the maxillary buccal space is unrelated to a lower molar
quiz.ty: Mylohyoid line decides it: apices above → sublingual; below → submandibular.

quiz.q: A patient with a deep molar infection has severe trismus and can barely open the mouth, with little visible facial swelling. The space MOST likely involved is:
quiz.e: Marked trismus with little external swelling indicates involvement of the muscles of mastication in the masticator space.
w: A — buccal-space infection causes obvious cheek swelling, not predominant trismus
C — submental infection causes midline chin swelling
D — canine-space infection causes upper lip/peri-orbital swelling
quiz.ty: Severe trismus with minimal external swelling = masticator (pterygomandibular) space.

quiz.q: A patient with a spreading neck infection becomes toxic with dysphagia, neck stiffness and chest pain; imaging shows gas and fluid tracking into the chest. The life-threatening complication is:
quiz.e: Spread through the lateral pharyngeal/retropharyngeal 'danger space' into the mediastinum causes mediastinitis, which carries high mortality and needs urgent surgical and intensive care.
w: B — simple cellulitis does not track into the mediastinum with systemic toxicity
C — pericoronitis is a localised operculum infection
D — dry socket is a localised post-extraction problem
quiz.ty: Deep neck infection → retropharyngeal/danger space → mediastinitis (high mortality).

quiz.q: A patient with a true penicillin allergy has a spreading odontogenic infection. The MOST appropriate antibiotic, also valued for bone penetration, is:
quiz.e: In genuine penicillin allergy, clindamycin is a good choice for odontogenic infections and penetrates bone well (useful if osteomyelitis is a concern).
w: A — amoxicillin is a penicillin and contraindicated in true allergy
C — cephalosporins carry a cross-reactivity risk and should not be given 'without caution'
D — nystatin is an antifungal, not relevant to a bacterial odontogenic infection
quiz.ty: Penicillin allergy → clindamycin (good bone penetration).

quiz.q: Weeks after inadequate treatment of a mandibular infection, a patient has chronic pain, a discharging sinus and a radiograph showing a piece of dead bone surrounded by new bone. This describes:
quiz.e: Chronic suppurative osteomyelitis is defined by a sequestrum (dead bone) within an involucrum (new surrounding bone) with sinus tracts; management combines prolonged antibiotics with removal of the sequestrum and the source.
w: A — acute cellulitis is a soft-tissue spreading infection without dead bone
C — a radicular cyst is a non-infective epithelial-lined cavity at a non-vital apex
D — dry socket is an acute post-extraction osteitis, not chronic with a sequestrum
quiz.ty: Dead bone (sequestrum) + new shell (involucrum) + sinus = chronic osteomyelitis → debride + prolonged antibiotics.

quiz.q: A patient has multiple chronic skin sinuses over the jaw discharging pus that contains yellowish 'sulfur granules'. The diagnosis and treatment are:
quiz.e: Sulfur granules discharging through multiple sinuses are characteristic of actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii), which requires prolonged high-dose penicillin.
w: A — TB does not classically produce sulfur granules in this pattern
C — candidiasis is a mucosal fungal infection, not sinus tracts with granules
D — a short course fails actinomycosis, which needs weeks-to-months of treatment
quiz.ty: Sulfur granules + multiple sinuses = actinomycosis → prolonged high-dose penicillin.

quiz.q: A systemically toxic patient has a rapidly spreading facial infection with skin discoloration, crepitus on palpation and pain out of proportion to the signs. The priority is:
o: Oral antibiotics and review in 48 hours
Urgent surgical debridement + IV antibiotics + resuscitation (treat as necrotising fasciitis)
Incision and drainage of a small pocket only
quiz.e: Crepitus, rapid spread, systemic toxicity and pain out of proportion suggest necrotising fasciitis, a surgical emergency requiring aggressive debridement, IV antibiotics and resuscitation.
w: A — oral antibiotics and delay are dangerous in a rapidly necrotising infection
C — limited drainage is inadequate for necrotising fasciitis
D — this is a bacterial necrotising process, not fungal
quiz.ty: Crepitus + rapid spread + toxicity + pain out of proportion = necrotising fasciitis → urgent debridement.

quiz.q: A 23-year-old has pain, swelling and bad taste around a partially erupted lower third molar, with the upper molar traumatising the operculum. Initial management is:
o: Immediate surgical removal of the lower third molar that day
Local debridement/irrigation under the operculum, relieve trauma from the opposing tooth, analgesia ± antibiotics if spreading; definitive extraction later
quiz.e: Acute pericoronitis is managed first with local measures (irrigation/debridement, relieving the traumatic occlusion) and analgesia, with antibiotics only if spreading; definitive extraction is planned once acute symptoms settle.
w: A — extracting in the acute phase is usually avoided; settle the acute episode first
C — antibiotics alone without local measures or addressing trauma are insufficient
D — leaving acute pericoronitis untreated risks spread
quiz.ty: Acute pericoronitis: local debridement + relieve the traumatic occlusion first; antibiotics only if spreading; extract later.

quiz.q: A patient with an abscess has been on the correct antibiotic for three days but is not improving and the swelling is now fluctuant. The BEST next step is:
o: Switch to a different antibiotic and wait
Incise and drain the collection and ensure the source is treated
quiz.e: An established fluctuant collection will not resolve on antibiotics alone; it must be drained and the dental cause removed — antibiotics are an adjunct.
w: A — changing antibiotics without draining pus repeats the original error
C — an antifungal is irrelevant to a bacterial abscess
D — stopping treatment abandons source control
quiz.ty: Antibiotics failing + fluctuant pus = drain it (and treat the cause). Antibiotics are an adjunct to drainage.

quiz.q: Infection from a lower FIRST molar whose root apices lie ABOVE the mylohyoid line will point to which space?
quiz.e: Apices above the mylohyoid line drain into the sublingual space (raised floor of mouth); apices below it drain into the submandibular space.
w: A — the submandibular space is involved when apices are BELOW the mylohyoid line
C — the submental space relates to the lower incisors
D — the buccal space relates to spread lateral to the buccinator
quiz.ty: Mylohyoid line: apex above → sublingual; below → submandibular.

quiz.q: Which space, when infected, produces MARKED trismus with little external facial swelling and is also relevant to a contaminated inferior alveolar nerve block?
quiz.e: The pterygomandibular space (between the medial pterygoid and the ramus) causes trismus with minimal external swelling and is entered during an IAN block.
w: A — the buccal space causes obvious cheek swelling, not predominant trismus
C — the submental space causes midline chin swelling
D — the canine space causes upper lip/peri-orbital swelling
quiz.ty: Trismus + minimal external swelling = pterygomandibular (masticator) space.

quiz.q: A deep neck infection in a toxic patient threatens life MOST directly by spreading from the lateral pharyngeal and retropharyngeal spaces to the:
quiz.e: The retropharyngeal/'danger' space communicates inferiorly with the mediastinum, so descending necrotising mediastinitis is the feared, high-mortality complication.
w: A — orbital spread is from upper anterior/canine routes, not the retropharyngeal space
C — the parotid is not the lethal deep-neck pathway
D — the scalp is not in this pathway
quiz.ty: Lateral pharyngeal → retropharyngeal → danger space → mediastinitis.

quiz.q: Which set of spaces is bilaterally involved in Ludwig's angina?
quiz.e: Ludwig's angina is a bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual and submental spaces, producing a woody floor of mouth and an airway emergency.
w: A — these are maxillary/deep spaces, not the Ludwig's group
C — these are the masticator spaces (cause trismus)
D — these are deep cervical spaces, not the Ludwig's floor-of-mouth group
quiz.ty: Ludwig's = bilateral submandibular + sublingual + submental (airway emergency).

pearls: Marked trismus localises infection to the masticator (pterygomandibular/masseteric) space.
Upper anterior/canine and infratemporal infections can reach the cavernous sinus via the valveless pterygoid/facial venous system — a true emergency.
The deadly escalation is lateral pharyngeal → retropharyngeal → 'danger space' → mediastinitis; a toxic patient with dysphagia and neck stiffness needs urgent imaging and admission.
First-line is penicillin/amoxicillin; add metronidazole for anaerobic cover; use clindamycin in true penicillin allergy (good bone penetration).
Chronic osteomyelitis is defined by dead bone: a sequestrum surrounded by new involucrum, with sinus tracts.
Multiple discharging sinuses with 'sulfur granules' point to actinomycosis and need prolonged high-dose penicillin, not a short course.
mistakes: Forgetting the mylohyoid line determines sublingual vs submandibular spread.
Not recognising that marked trismus with little swelling means a masticator (pterygomandibular) space.
Missing the lateral pharyngeal → retropharyngeal → mediastinum escalation in a toxic patient.
Overlooking the canine/infratemporal route to the cavernous sinus.
Treating Ludwig's angina as a local swelling rather than an airway emergency.
Assuming spaces are isolated — they communicate (sublingual↔submandibular; pterygomandibular↔lateral pharyngeal).
Relying on antibiotics without draining the involved spaces and removing the cause.
Failing to assess the airway and systemic status in multi-space infection.
Giving a short antibiotic course for actinomycosis/osteomyelitis (both need prolonged treatment).
Treating osteomyelitis with antibiotics alone without removing the sequestrum/source.
Mistaking necrotising fasciitis for ordinary cellulitis and delaying debridement.
Not adding anaerobic cover (metronidazole) when indicated.
Forgetting hyperbaric oxygen as an adjunct in refractory/irradiated cases.
facts: Spaces are primary (infected directly from a tooth) or secondary (involved by spread).
Maxillary spaces: canine, buccal, infratemporal.
Mandibular primary spaces: submental, sublingual, submandibular, buccal.
Masticator (secondary) spaces: submasseteric, pterygomandibular, temporal (superficial & deep).
Deep cervical spaces: lateral pharyngeal, retropharyngeal, danger space, pretracheal, carotid sheath.
Mylohyoid line: apex above → sublingual; apex below → submandibular.
Lower 2nd/3rd molars (apices below mylohyoid) → submandibular space.
Canine space infection → loss of the nasolabial fold; risk to the eye/cavernous sinus.
Pterygomandibular space infection → marked trismus (also relevant to a failed IAN block).
Sublingual & submandibular spaces communicate around the posterior border of mylohyoid.
Ludwig's angina = bilateral submandibular + sublingual + submental → airway emergency.
Deep neck escalation: lateral pharyngeal → retropharyngeal → danger space → mediastinum.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis: from upper anterior/canine/infratemporal via valveless veins.
Boundaries hint: buccinator separates the buccal space; mylohyoid separates sublingual from submandibular.
Carotid sheath contents at risk in deep neck infection: carotid, internal jugular vein, vagus.
Early/acute infections: facultative aerobic streptococci; later/established: anaerobes (Prevotella, Fusobacterium).
First-line antibiotic: penicillin/amoxicillin; add metronidazole for anaerobes; co-amoxiclav for broader cover.
Penicillin allergy: clindamycin (good bone penetration).
Stages: inoculation → cellulitis (diffuse, no pus) → abscess (fluctuant pus) → resolution.
Cellulitis = diffuse, non-fluctuant, no pus → antibiotics + source control; abscess → incise & drain.
Buccinator separates the buccal space; mylohyoid separates sublingual from submandibular.
Infratemporal/upper-anterior infection → cavernous sinus via the pterygoid plexus (valveless veins).
Osteomyelitis: mandible >> maxilla (poorer collateral supply); sequestrum (dead bone) + involucrum (new bone).
Garré's osteomyelitis = chronic with proliferative periostitis ('onion-skin') in young patients.
Acute osteomyelitis radiograph lags ~10 days before lucency appears.
Actinomycosis: 'sulfur granules', multiple sinuses → prolonged high-dose penicillin.
Candidiasis: wipeable white plaques (pseudomembranous) in immunosuppressed/denture wearers.
Pericoronitis: operculum inflammation over a partially erupted lower 3rd molar; local measures first.
Necrotising fasciitis: rapid spread + crepitus + pain out of proportion → surgical emergency.
Most deep neck-space infections are odontogenic (a lower molar).
Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct in osteoradionecrosis/refractory osteomyelitis.
mnemonics: Deep spread path: Lateral pharyngeal → Retropharyngeal → Danger space → Mediastinum.
Osteomyelitis hallmark 'Sequestrum + Involucrum' (dead bone + new shell).
Maxillary spaces 'CBI': Canine, Buccal, Infratemporal.
Mandibular primary spaces 'S-S-S-B': Submental, Sublingual, Submandibular, Buccal.
Mylohyoid rule: Above → Sublingual; Below → Submandibular.
Deep neck escalation 'LR-D-M': Lateral pharyngeal → Retropharyngeal → Danger space → Mediastinum.

study.html:
• Definition: a white patch that cannot be wiped off and is not diagnosable as another condition — a diagnosis of exclusion.
  • Types: homogeneous (lower risk) vs non-homogeneous / speckled / nodular / verrucous (higher risk). Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is high-risk/multifocal.
  • High-risk sites: floor of mouth, ventrolateral tongue.
  • Overall malignant transformation ~3–5% (higher for non-homogeneous & dysplastic).

• Red velvety patch — highest malignant potential; most already show severe dysplasia / carcinoma in situ / invasive SCC on biopsy.
  • Any non-homogeneous or erythroplakic lesion → biopsy mandatory.

• Oral submucous fibrosis: a premalignant condition from areca/betel nut; juxta-epithelial fibrosis → blanching, burning, progressive trismus, stiff mucosa.
  • Lichen planus: Wickham's striae; the erosive/atrophic form carries a small malignant risk and needs monitoring.
  • Other premalignant conditions: sideropenic dysphagia (Plummer-Vinson), discoid lupus, dyskeratosis congenita, actinic cheilitis (lip).

• Epithelial dysplasia (mild/moderate/severe → carcinoma in situ) is the key histological predictor of transformation.
  • Risk factors: tobacco (smoked/smokeless), alcohol (synergistic), betel, sunlight (lip), HPV, chronic irritation.
  • Management: remove cause (stop tobacco/betel), biopsy to grade dysplasia, excise high-grade lesions, and long-term review with re-biopsy of changing lesions.
⭐: Erythroplakia > leukoplakia for malignant risk; degree of dysplasia drives management.

quiz.q: Erythroplakia often histologically shows:
quiz.e: Frequently dysplasia or carcinoma in situ.

quiz.q: Homogeneous leukoplakia compared to speckled has:
Highest malignant potential oral lesion:
Highest-risk leukoplakia type:
Tobacco + alcohol act:
Definitive step for a suspicious patch:
Best histological predictor of malignant change:
Plummer-Vinson (sideropenic dysphagia) deficiency:
Erythroplakia histology often shows:
The erosive/atrophic form with malignant risk is:
Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia is:
A homogeneous leukoplakia compared with speckled has:
Management of OSMF includes:
Discoid lupus erythematosus is a:
The most important management principle of premalignant lesions:
A 55-year-old smoker has a well-demarcated, red, velvety patch on the floor of the mouth that does not wipe off. Compared with a white patch, this lesion is:
o: Lower risk and can be observed
The highest-risk lesion — biopsy promptly (often already dysplasia/CIS)
A fungal infection to treat with antifungals
quiz.e: A red velvety non-wipeable patch is erythroplakia, which carries the highest malignant potential and frequently shows severe dysplasia or carcinoma in situ on biopsy.
w: A — erythroplakia is higher risk than leukoplakia and must not be merely observed
C — a persistent indurated red patch is not assumed to be benign inflammation
D — it does not wipe off and is not candidiasis
quiz.ty: Erythroplakia = highest malignant potential → biopsy promptly.

quiz.q: A betel-nut chewer has progressive limitation of mouth opening, blanched stiff buccal mucosa and a burning sensation. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
quiz.e: Areca/betel nut causes oral submucous fibrosis, a premalignant CONDITION characterised by juxta-epithelial fibrosis, blanching, burning and progressive trismus.
w: A — leukoplakia is a localised white patch, not generalised fibrosis with trismus
C — lichen planus shows Wickham's striae, not blanching fibrosis from betel
D — erythroplakia is a red patch, not fibrosis
quiz.ty: Betel/areca + trismus + blanching + burning = oral submucous fibrosis (a premalignant condition).

quiz.q: A persistent white patch cannot be scraped off and no other diagnosis fits. The single most important next step is:
o: Biopsy to assess for epithelial dysplasia
quiz.e: Leukoplakia is a diagnosis of exclusion; biopsy is essential because the grade of dysplasia (not the appearance) determines the risk and management.
w: A — antifungals are for candidiasis (which wipes off), not a fixed leukoplakia
C — discharging a persistent leukoplakia without histology is unsafe
D — antibiotics have no role in a non-infective white patch
quiz.ty: Persistent leukoplakia → biopsy to grade dysplasia (the histology drives management).

quiz.q: A white patch on the buccal mucosa WIPES OFF leaving an erythematous base in an immunosuppressed patient. This is MOST likely:
quiz.e: A wipeable white plaque is pseudomembranous candidiasis — by definition leukoplakia cannot be wiped off.
w: A — leukoplakia does not wipe off
C — erythroplakia is a red patch, not a wipeable white plaque
D — OSMF is fibrosis with trismus, not a wipeable plaque
quiz.ty: A white patch that wipes off = candidiasis, NOT leukoplakia.

quiz.q: Which single factor best predicts malignant transformation of an oral leukoplakia on biopsy?
quiz.e: The histological degree of epithelial dysplasia (mild → moderate → severe → carcinoma in situ) is the key predictor of transformation.
w: A — size correlates loosely but is not the key predictor
C — age is a risk factor but not the histological predictor
D — hyperkeratosis alone is not the predictor; dysplasia is
quiz.ty: Degree of epithelial dysplasia is the best histological predictor of malignant change.

pearls: Distinguish a lesion (local, e.g., leukoplakia) from a condition (generalised, e.g., OSMF, lichen planus, sideropenic dysphagia).
Oral submucous fibrosis is caused by areca/betel nut and presents with progressive trismus, blanching and a burning mouth.
A white patch that wipes off is not leukoplakia — it is usually candidiasis.
Management is always: remove the cause (stop tobacco/betel/alcohol), biopsy to grade dysplasia, excise high-grade lesions, and review long-term.
mistakes: Failing to biopsy a non-homogeneous or persistent suspicious patch.
Treating a premalignant lesion without addressing the causative habit.
Confusing a lesion (leukoplakia) with a condition (OSMF).
Relying on toluidine blue/adjuncts instead of a biopsy.
Reassuring and discharging instead of long-term review with re-biopsy of changing lesions.
Missing the higher dysplasia risk of chronic hyperplastic (candidal) leukoplakia.
Overlooking actinic cheilitis of the lip as premalignant.
Assuming homogeneous and non-homogeneous leukoplakia carry the same risk.
Forgetting iron-deficiency (sideropenic dysphagia) as a premalignant condition.
Mistaking a lichenoid (drug/amalgam) reaction for idiopathic lichen planus without history.
Not recognising erosive (not reticular) lichen planus as the form with malignant risk.
Underestimating proliferative verrucous leukoplakia (multifocal, high transformation).
facts: Leukoplakia types: homogeneous (lower risk) vs non-homogeneous/speckled/nodular/verrucous (higher risk).
Proliferative verrucous leukoplakia (PVL): multifocal, high transformation risk, often elderly women.
Highest-risk sites: floor of mouth and ventrolateral tongue.
Overall leukoplakia transformation ~3–5% (higher for non-homogeneous/dysplastic).
Erythroplakia = a red velvety patch with the HIGHEST malignant potential (often severe dysplasia/CIS/invasive SCC).
Erythroleukoplakia (speckled) is a mixed high-risk lesion.
OSMF: areca/betel nut → juxta-epithelial fibrosis, blanching, palpable fibrous bands, burning to spicy food, progressive trismus.
OSMF is essentially irreversible; manage by stopping the habit, intralesional steroids, physiotherapy, surgery for severe trismus.
Lichen planus is T-cell mediated; reticular type (Wickham's striae) is commonest, usually bilateral buccal.
The erosive/atrophic lichen planus carries the small malignant risk (reticular is low risk).
A lichenoid reaction (to a drug or amalgam) is a differential for lichen planus.
Epithelial dysplasia grading: mild (lower third), moderate (to middle third), severe/CIS (upper third to full thickness).
Dysplasia features: nuclear pleomorphism, ↑ nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, hyperchromatism, loss of polarity, abnormal/↑ mitoses, drop-shaped rete ridges.
Risk factors: tobacco (smoked & smokeless), alcohol (synergistic with tobacco), betel quid, sunlight (lip), HPV-16, chronic candida, iron deficiency.
Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis ('candidal leukoplakia') has a higher dysplasia risk.
Sideropenic dysphagia (Plummer-Vinson/Paterson-Kelly) = iron deficiency + dysphagia → post-cricoid/oral cancer risk.
Discoid lupus erythematosus and dyskeratosis congenita are recognised premalignant conditions.
Actinic cheilitis (solar keratosis of the lip) is premalignant — from chronic sun exposure.
Any non-homogeneous or erythroplakic/persistent lesion → mandatory biopsy.
Toluidine blue and other adjuncts AID site selection but do not replace biopsy.
Management of dysplasia: remove the cause, excise/laser high-grade lesions, long-term review with re-biopsy of changing lesions.
Field cancerisation explains multiple primaries and second-primary risk in exposed mucosa.
The degree of dysplasia (not the colour/size) is the best predictor of malignant transformation.
A white patch that WIPES off is candidiasis, not leukoplakia (by definition).
Homogeneous leukoplakia has a lower transformation risk than speckled/non-homogeneous.
Smokeless tobacco/snuff causes a characteristic keratosis at the site of placement.
Frictional keratosis and morsicatio (cheek-biting) are benign white lesions to exclude before diagnosing leukoplakia.
mnemonics: OSMF cause = Areca/Betel; hallmark = trismus + blanching + burning.
Management 'Cause–Biopsy–Excise–Review' (treat the habit, grade the dysplasia, remove high-grade, follow up).

study.html:
• Warfarin: do NOT routinely stop; check INR ≤24–72 h before; proceed with simple extractions if INR < ~3.5–4.0 using local haemostasis.
  • DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): for higher-bleeding-risk procedures, miss/delay the morning dose per protocol; no routine reversal needed.
  • Aspirin/clopidogrel: usually continue; local measures control bleeding.
  • Local haemostasis: sutures, oxidized cellulose/gelatin, tranexamic acid mouthwash, pressure.
⭐: Stopping anticoagulation risks thrombosis/stroke — far worse than manageable dental bleeding.

• Haemophilia A (factor VIII) / B (factor IX): liaise with haematology; factor replacement ± desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild A; tranexamic acid; avoid IANB (deep bleed) — use infiltration/intraligamentary.
  • von Willebrand disease: DDAVP, vWF/factor concentrate, tranexamic acid.
  • Thrombocytopenia: platelet count guides surgery (generally >50×10⁹/L for extractions).
  • Liver disease & vitamin-K deficiency impair clotting factor synthesis.

• Risk of infection, delayed healing, periodontal disease.
  • Morning appointments, don't let the patient skip meals/medication; aim good control (HbA1c) before elective surgery.
  • Hypoglycaemia is the acute emergency (sweating, confusion) → give oral glucose (or IV/IM glucagon if unconscious).
  • Consider antibiotic cover for surgery in poorly controlled diabetics.

• Long-term corticosteroids → adrenal suppression; major surgical stress may precipitate an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis (hypotension, collapse) — may need steroid cover.
  • Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism: avoid adrenaline; risk of thyroid storm with infection/stress.
  • Hypothyroidism: sensitivity to sedatives/opioids.

• Liver: impaired clotting (↓ factors), reduced metabolism of amide LAs and many drugs → reduce dose; bleeding risk; avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
  • Renal failure / dialysis: treat on the day after dialysis (heparin worn off, less uraemic bleeding); adjust drug doses; bleeding tendency, anaemia, hypertension; avoid nephrotoxic NSAIDs.

• Elective treatment best in the second trimester; urgent care any time.
  • Avoid the supine position late in pregnancy (supine hypotensive syndrome from IVC compression) → left lateral tilt.
  • Safe: paracetamol, penicillins, lidocaine. Avoid: NSAIDs (esp. 3rd trimester), tetracyclines (tooth staining), metronidazole (caution 1st trimester), elective radiographs (shield/defer).

• Asthma: have the patient's inhaler available; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin in sensitive patients; stress can trigger attacks.
  • Epilepsy: ensure compliance with medication; minimise triggers; manage a seizure by protecting the airway/patient, time it, give oxygen.
  • Allergy/anaphylaxis: identify true allergies; anaphylaxis → adrenaline IM 0.5 mg (1:1000), airway, oxygen, call for help.

• MRONJ (bisphosphonates, denosumab, antiangiogenics): avoid extractions where possible; prevention with pre-treatment dental clearance; conservative management of established necrosis.
  • HIV / transplant / chemotherapy: infection risk, mucositis, candidiasis; coordinate timing of dental care with counts (e.g., neutrophils, platelets).
⭐: The recurring principle — most medical conditions don't contraindicate care; they modify how and when you do it (timing, drug choice, haemostasis, antibiotic/steroid cover, liaison).

DOAC before higher-risk extraction:
A 70-year-old on warfarin (INR 2.4 today) for atrial fibrillation needs a single lower premolar extracted. The BEST plan is:
o: Ask the GP to stop warfarin for 5 days, then extract
Proceed atraumatically with sutures + oxidized cellulose ± tranexamic acid, without stopping warfarin
quiz.e: For a simple extraction with INR in the therapeutic range (<~3.5-4), the anticoagulant is continued and bleeding is controlled with local measures, because stopping it risks stroke.
w: A — stopping warfarin in an AF patient risks thromboembolic stroke
C — heparin bridging is unnecessary and increases bleeding for a minor procedure
D — deliberately under-anticoagulating an AF patient exposes them to clot risk
quiz.ty: Simple extraction + INR <~3.5-4 → don't stop warfarin; use local haemostasis.

quiz.q: A patient with a prosthetic heart valve needs an extraction. The correct prophylaxis is:
o: Amoxicillin 2 g orally one hour before (clindamycin 600 mg if penicillin-allergic)
Metronidazole at the time of extraction
quiz.e: A prosthetic valve is a high-risk cardiac condition; an extraction breaches the gingiva, so single-dose amoxicillin 2 g one hour before is indicated.
w: A — high-risk cardiac patients having gingival-breaching procedures do need prophylaxis
C — a post-operative week-long course is not the prophylaxis regimen
D — metronidazole is not the standard IE prophylaxis agent
quiz.ty: High-risk cardiac + gingival-breaching procedure → amoxicillin 2 g 1 h before (clindamycin if allergic).

quiz.q: Mid-appointment a diabetic patient who skipped breakfast becomes sweaty, tremulous and confused. The immediate action is:
o: Give fast-acting oral glucose (or IM glucagon/IV glucose if unconscious)
quiz.e: These are hypoglycaemia symptoms; conscious patients are treated with fast-acting oral glucose, and unconscious patients with IM glucagon or IV glucose.
w: A — insulin would deepen hypoglycaemia and could be fatal
C — continuing treatment ignores a developing emergency
D — adrenaline is for anaphylaxis/cardiac arrest, not hypoglycaemia
quiz.ty: Diabetic + sweaty/confused after skipping food = hypoglycaemia → give glucose (never insulin).

quiz.q: A steroid-dependent patient (long-term prednisolone) is scheduled for a major surgical extraction under sedation. The key peri-operative consideration is:
o: Stop the steroid the night before
Provide steroid cover to prevent an adrenal (Addisonian) crisis
quiz.e: Chronic steroids suppress the adrenal axis; the stress of major surgery can precipitate an adrenal crisis (hypotension/collapse), so supplemental steroid cover may be needed.
w: A — stopping the steroid abruptly worsens adrenal insufficiency
C — insulin is irrelevant unless the patient is diabetic and hyperglycaemic
D — local anaesthesia is safe and necessary
quiz.ty: Long-term steroids + major surgery → consider steroid cover (adrenal crisis risk).

quiz.q: A woman in her first trimester requests elective extraction of an asymptomatic tooth. The MOST appropriate advice is:
o: Extract now and prescribe an NSAID for pain
Defer elective treatment to the second trimester; if treating, use paracetamol/penicillin and avoid NSAIDs (late) and tetracycline
quiz.e: Elective dental care is best in the second trimester; safe analgesia/antibiotics are paracetamol and penicillins, while NSAIDs (especially late) and tetracyclines are avoided.
w: A — NSAIDs are avoided in pregnancy (especially the third trimester)
C — routine GA is unnecessary and adds risk
D — tetracycline is contraindicated (tooth discoloration)
quiz.ty: Elective dental care in the 2nd trimester; avoid NSAIDs (late) and tetracycline; left-lateral tilt.

quiz.q: A patient on IV zoledronate for bone metastases needs a hopeless molar removed. The dominant concern and approach are:
o: High MRONJ risk — exhaust conservative options, involve the oncology team, and use the most atraumatic technique if extraction is unavoidable
Give a single antibiotic dose and extract without further thought
quiz.e: IV bisphosphonates carry a high risk of medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw; extraction is avoided where possible and, if unavoidable, performed as atraumatically as possible with specialist input.
w: A — IV bisphosphonates are the highest-risk MRONJ group, not routine
C — implant surgery is contraindicated in high-MRONJ-risk patients
D — a single antibiotic dose does not abolish MRONJ risk; the decision is whether to extract at all
quiz.ty: IV bisphosphonates = high MRONJ risk → avoid extraction if possible; never place an implant.

pearls: In a diabetic, hypoglycaemia is the acute emergency: keep appointments short and morning, and never let the patient skip a meal or their medication.
Long-term steroids cause adrenal suppression — major surgical stress may precipitate an adrenal crisis, so steroid cover may be needed.
Plan dental care in the second trimester; avoid NSAIDs late in pregnancy and tetracyclines throughout; use the left-lateral tilt to avoid supine hypotension.
IV bisphosphonates and head/neck radiotherapy are the high-risk groups for osteonecrosis — avoid extractions where possible and treat doubtful teeth before radiotherapy.
In bleeding disorders, liaise with haematology, arrange factor cover/DDAVP and tranexamic acid, and avoid inferior alveolar nerve blocks.
mistakes: Routinely stopping warfarin/DOACs for a simple extraction (thrombosis/stroke risk).
Giving IE prophylaxis to low-risk patients or withholding it from genuinely high-risk ones.
Letting a diabetic skip a meal before an appointment and precipitating hypoglycaemia.
Forgetting steroid cover for a steroid-dependent patient having major surgery.
Using NSAIDs in late pregnancy or prescribing tetracycline to a pregnant patient/child.
Extracting in an IV-bisphosphonate or irradiated patient without considering osteonecrosis.
Performing an IAN block in a haemophiliac without factor cover.
Treating a dialysis patient ON the dialysis day (heparinised) instead of the day after.
Giving full-dose adrenaline in significant cardiac disease.
Mistaking hypoglycaemia for anxiety and not giving glucose.
Avoiding all treatment in a controlled epileptic instead of minimising triggers.
Ignoring drug interactions of adrenaline (TCA/MAOI/non-selective β-blockers/cocaine).
facts: Defer elective surgery ~6 months after a myocardial infarction.
IE prophylaxis: amoxicillin 2 g (child 50 mg/kg) 1 h before; clindamycin 600 mg if penicillin-allergic.
IE prophylaxis is for HIGH-risk cardiac (prosthetic valve, previous IE, certain congenital disease) undergoing gingival/periapical-breaching procedures.
Significant cardiac disease: limit adrenaline to ≤0.04 mg (~2 cartridges 1:100,000).
Angina: have GTN available; stop and treat chest pain.
Warfarin: don't routinely stop for a simple extraction if INR < ~3.5–4; use local haemostasis.
DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): miss/delay the dose per protocol for higher-bleeding-risk procedures; no routine reversal.
Aspirin/clopidogrel: usually continue; control bleeding locally.
Local haemostatics: sutures, oxidized cellulose, gelatin sponge, tranexamic acid mouthwash, pressure.
Haemophilia A = factor VIII deficiency; B = factor IX; manage with factor cover ± DDAVP + tranexamic acid; avoid IAN blocks.
von Willebrand disease: DDAVP, vWF/factor concentrate, tranexamic acid.
Thrombocytopenia: generally need platelets > 50×10⁹/L for extractions.
Liver disease impairs clotting-factor synthesis and amide metabolism → reduce dose; bleeding risk.
Diabetes: risk of infection and delayed healing; morning appointments; don't skip meals/medication.
Hypoglycaemia is the acute diabetic emergency → oral glucose (IM glucagon/IV glucose if unconscious).
Long-term steroids → adrenal suppression → may need steroid cover for major surgery (adrenal crisis).
Uncontrolled hyperthyroidism: avoid adrenaline (thyroid storm risk).
Renal/dialysis: treat the day AFTER dialysis (heparin worn off, less uraemic bleeding); adjust drug doses; avoid NSAIDs.
Pregnancy: elective care in the 2nd trimester; left-lateral tilt to avoid supine hypotension.
Pregnancy drugs: safe = paracetamol, penicillin, lidocaine; avoid NSAIDs (late), tetracycline (throughout).
Asthma: have the inhaler available; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin if sensitive.
Epilepsy: ensure medication compliance; manage a seizure by protecting the airway/patient and giving oxygen.
Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (1:1000) + airway + oxygen.
MRONJ: bisphosphonates/denosumab/antiangiogenics → avoid extractions where possible; pre-treatment dental clearance.
Osteoradionecrosis: avoid extractions in irradiated bone; extract doubtful teeth BEFORE radiotherapy.
Immunosuppression (HIV/transplant/chemo): infection risk, mucositis, candidiasis; time care with blood counts.
ASA classification grades the patient's systemic fitness (I–V).
Most conditions modify timing/drugs/haemostasis/cover — they rarely contraindicate care outright.
mnemonics: Adrenaline limit in cardiac disease ≤0.04 mg (~2 cartridges 1:100,000).
Pregnancy 'avoid' = NSAIDs (late) + Tetracycline; treat in the 2nd trimester; left-lateral tilt.
Haemophilia: AVOID IAN block; use factor cover + tranexamic acid.

study.html:
A cyst = epithelium-lined pathological cavity (usually fluid/semi-fluid).

GroupExamples
Odontogenic — inflammatoryRadicular (periapical), residual, paradental
Odontogenic — developmentalDentigerous, eruption, OKC, lateral periodontal/botryoid, gingival, glandular, calcifying (Gorlin)
Non-odontogenicNasopalatine duct, nasolabial
Pseudocysts (no epithelium)Solitary (simple/traumatic) bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst, Stafne defect

• Most common odontogenic cyst; inflammatory, from epithelial rests of Malassez stimulated by periapical inflammation of a non-vital tooth.
  • Well-defined corticated round/oval radiolucency at the apex; tooth non-vital.
  • Residual cyst = a radicular cyst left behind after extraction of the offending tooth.

• Dentigerous: most common developmental cyst; encloses the crown of an unerupted tooth, attached at the CEJ (commonly lower 3rd molar / canine). Well-defined pericoronal radiolucency.
  • Potential complications: displacement/resorption, rarely ameloblastoma/SCC in the wall.
  • Eruption cyst: soft-tissue dentigerous variant over an erupting tooth (often in children); usually resolves.

• From dental lamina (rests of Serres); grows along the bone (antero-posteriorly) with little expansion; highest recurrence of jaw cysts.
  • Histology: parakeratinised stratified squamous epithelium, palisaded basal cells, corrugated surface, thin friable wall, satellite/daughter cysts.
  • Aspirate: low soluble protein (<4 g/dL), keratin (caseous).
  • Multiple OKCs → Gorlin (nevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome.
  • Treatment: enucleation ± Carnoy's solution/peripheral ostectomy, or marsupialisation/decompression for large lesions, due to recurrence.

• Lateral periodontal cyst: lateral root surface of vital premolars/canines; botryoid = multilocular variant.
  • Calcifying odontogenic cyst (Gorlin): contains ghost cells, may calcify.
  • Glandular odontogenic cyst: aggressive, can recur.
  • Nasopalatine duct cyst: midline anterior maxilla, "heart-shaped" radiolucency; most common non-odontogenic cyst.
  • Nasolabial cyst: soft-tissue, nasolabial fold (no bony cavity).

• Solitary (simple/traumatic) bone cyst: empty/blood-filled, no lining; scalloping up between roots; often resolves after surgical exploration.
  • Aneurysmal bone cyst: blood-filled spaces, rapid "blow-out" expansion.
  • Stafne defect: not a cyst — a lingual mandibular depression containing salivary gland, below the IAN canal near the angle (incidental).

Management of cysts

  • Enucleation (remove the whole lining) — most cysts; send for histology.
  • Marsupialisation/decompression — large cysts, or to protect vital structures (IAN, unerupted tooth), allowing shrinkage then enucleation.
  • Aspirate before opening if a vascular lesion is suspected.

quiz.q: The definitive treatment for most jaw cysts is:
quiz.e: Remove the lining; send for histology.

quiz.q: A well-defined, corticated, round radiolucency surrounds the apex of a discoloured upper central incisor that does NOT respond to vitality testing. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
quiz.e: An apical corticated radiolucency on a NON-VITAL tooth is a radicular cyst, an inflammatory cyst from the rests of Malassez.
w: A — a dentigerous cyst surrounds the crown of an UNERUPTED tooth, not the apex of an erupted non-vital one
C — an OKC is typically a posterior multilocular lesion not centred on a non-vital apex
D — a nasopalatine cyst is midline between vital central incisors
quiz.ty: Apical corticated radiolucency + NON-VITAL tooth = radicular cyst.

quiz.q: A pericoronal radiolucency around an impacted lower third molar is enucleated; histology reports an ameloblastic epithelial lining. This is BEST regarded as:
o: A simple dentigerous cyst — no further action
A unicystic ameloblastoma — needs appropriate follow-up/treatment, not simple discharge
quiz.e: Ameloblastic lining in a 'dentigerous-looking' cyst is a unicystic ameloblastoma; recognising it matters because management and follow-up differ from a simple cyst.
w: A — the ameloblastic lining means it is not a simple dentigerous cyst
C — a radicular cyst is periapical on a non-vital tooth
D — an odontoma is a calcified hamartoma, not a cystic lining
quiz.ty: A 'dentigerous cyst' with ameloblastic lining = unicystic ameloblastoma — always send the lining for histology.

quiz.q: A 25-year-old has a multilocular radiolucency that has grown along the body of the mandible with little bony expansion, and it recurred after previous simple enucleation. Aspirate shows low soluble protein and keratin. The diagnosis is:
quiz.e: Growth along bone with little expansion, high recurrence and a keratin-rich, low-protein aspirate are classic OKC; treatment adds Carnoy's/peripheral ostectomy because of recurrence, and multiple OKCs suggest Gorlin syndrome.
w: A — radicular cysts are unilocular periapical lesions on non-vital teeth
C — dentigerous cysts are pericoronal and expansile, not antero-posteriorly growing with recurrence
D — a solitary bone cyst has no epithelial lining/keratin and rarely recurs
quiz.ty: AP growth, minimal expansion, high recurrence, keratin aspirate = OKC (multiple → Gorlin).

pearls: Aspirating an OKC yields low soluble protein (<4 g/dL) and keratin — a useful bedside clue.
A midline 'heart-shaped' radiolucency between the upper central incisors (both vital) is a nasopalatine duct cyst — the commonest non-odontogenic cyst.
For a large cyst threatening the IAN or an unerupted tooth, decompression/marsupialisation first lets it shrink before definitive enucleation.
Always send the cyst lining for histopathology — a clinically benign cyst can harbour a keratocyst or ameloblastoma.
mistakes: Enucleating an OKC simply and expecting no recurrence.
Forgetting that multiple OKCs signal Gorlin syndrome.
Aggressively enucleating a huge cyst next to the IAN instead of decompressing it first.
Discarding the lining instead of sending it for histopathology.
Confusing a true cyst with a pseudocyst (no epithelial lining).
Mistaking a Stafne defect for a pathological cyst.
Not recognising the botryoid (multilocular) lateral periodontal cyst.
Forgetting the ghost cells of the calcifying odontogenic (Gorlin) cyst.
Overlooking the malignant potential within a dentigerous cyst wall.
Operating on a large mandibular cyst without considering pathological fracture risk.
Failing to vitality-test adjacent teeth before surgery.
Biopsying a vascular lesion mistaken for a cyst without prior imaging.
facts: Radicular cyst = commonest odontogenic cyst; from rests of Malassez stimulated by pulpal necrosis.
Radicular cyst tooth is NON-VITAL; well-defined corticated round radiolucency at the apex.
Residual cyst = a radicular cyst remaining after extraction of the offending tooth.
Dentigerous cyst = commonest developmental cyst; encloses the crown of an unerupted tooth, attached at the CEJ.
Dentigerous cyst wall may rarely give rise to ameloblastoma, SCC or intra-osseous mucoepidermoid carcinoma.
Eruption cyst = a soft-tissue dentigerous variant over an erupting tooth (children); usually resolves.
OKC arises from the dental lamina (rests of Serres).
OKC histology: parakeratinised stratified squamous, palisaded hyperchromatic basal cells, corrugated surface, thin friable wall, daughter (satellite) cysts.
OKC grows antero-posteriorly along the bone with little expansion → highest recurrence of jaw cysts.
OKC aspirate: soluble protein < 4 g/dL with keratin (caseous).
Multiple OKCs → Gorlin (nevoid basal cell carcinoma) syndrome (also BCCs, rib anomalies, falx calcification, palmar pits).
OKC treatment: enucleation ± Carnoy's solution/peripheral ostectomy, or marsupialisation/decompression for large lesions.
Lateral periodontal cyst: lateral root surface of a VITAL premolar/canine; botryoid type = multilocular.
Calcifying odontogenic cyst (Gorlin cyst): contains ghost cells; may be associated with an odontoma.
Glandular odontogenic cyst: aggressive, recurs, contains mucous/glandular cells.
Nasopalatine duct cyst: midline anterior maxilla, 'heart-shaped' radiolucency, vital incisors; commonest non-odontogenic cyst.
Nasolabial cyst: soft-tissue cyst of the nasolabial fold (no bony cavity).
Pseudocysts have NO epithelial lining: solitary (simple/traumatic) bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst, Stafne defect.
Solitary bone cyst: empty/blood-filled, scallops up between the roots, often resolves after surgical exploration.
Aneurysmal bone cyst: blood-filled spaces with rapid 'blow-out' expansion.
Stafne defect: a lingual mandibular depression containing salivary gland, below the IAN canal near the angle (incidental, asymptomatic).
Enucleation (Partsch II) = remove the whole lining; marsupialisation (Partsch I) = open and decompress.
Decompression shrinks a large cyst before definitive enucleation and protects the IAN/unerupted teeth.
Always send the cyst lining for histopathology (it may harbour an OKC or ameloblastoma).
A large mandibular cyst can predispose to a pathological fracture.
Differential of a pericoronal radiolucency: dentigerous cyst, unicystic ameloblastoma, OKC, AOT.
Vitality testing is the quickest way to separate a radicular (non-vital) from a developmental (vital) cyst.
Gingival cyst of the newborn (Bohn's nodules / Epstein pearls) is a benign self-resolving lesion.
Aspirate a lesion before opening if a vascular cause is suspected.
Marsupialisation is preferred when enucleation would damage vital structures or for very large cysts.
mnemonics: Multiple OKCs → Gorlin (NBCC) syndrome.
Nasopalatine duct cyst = midline maxilla, Heart-shaped, vital teeth.

study.html:
• >90% are squamous cell carcinoma (SCC); variants: verrucous carcinoma (low-grade, exophytic), basaloid, spindle-cell.
  • Field cancerisation: whole mucosa exposed to carcinogens → multiple primary tumours & high second-primary risk.
  • Premalignant precursors: leukoplakia, erythroplakia (highest risk), OSMF, lichen planus (erosive).

• Non-healing ulcer >3 weeks with rolled, indurated margins; or a red/white patch, exophytic mass, or unexplained swelling.
  • Pain (late), bleeding, loose teeth, ill-fitting denture, dysphagia, referred otalgia, numbness, neck lump (nodal metastasis), trismus.
  • Common sites: lateral border of tongue, floor of mouth, retromolar, lip.
⭐ Red flags: ulcer >3 weeks, induration, fixation, unexplained neck node, numb lip/chin → urgent referral & biopsy.

• Diagnosis: incisional biopsy (histopathology) of the suspicious area + margin.
  • Imaging: MRI (soft tissue/tongue), CT (bone/neck/chest), OPG, PET-CT for staging; FNAC/USS for neck nodes.
  • TNM: T tumour size/depth of invasion, N nodal involvement (number/size/laterality/ENE), M distant metastasis. Stage combines T+N+M.

• Local invasion (muscle, bone), lymphatic spread to cervical nodes levels I–V (predictable by site), and late haematogenous spread (commonly lungs).
  • Nodal (lymph-node) involvement is the single most important prognostic factor; extranodal extension worsens prognosis.

• Multidisciplinary team. Modalities: surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy — often combined by stage.
  • Early (I–II): single modality (surgery OR radiotherapy). Advanced (III–IV): combined surgery + adjuvant chemoradiotherapy.
  • Primary resection with adequate margins ± mandibulectomy; neck dissection for nodal disease or elective for high-risk necks.
  • Reconstruction: local/regional flaps or free flaps (e.g., radial forearm for soft tissue, free fibula for mandible).

• Acute: mucositis, dysgeusia, dermatitis. Chronic: xerostomia (salivary damage), radiation caries, trismus, fibrosis.
  • Osteoradionecrosis (ORN): hypovascular/hypocellular/hypoxic irradiated bone heals poorly; avoid extractions in irradiated bone — extract needed teeth before radiotherapy; hyperbaric O₂/pentoxifylline as adjuncts.

• Prognosis depends on stage and nodal status; early detection dramatically improves survival.
  • Prevention: tobacco/alcohol cessation, treat premalignant lesions, opportunistic screening (examine the whole mucosa), biopsy suspicious lesions.
  • Regular follow-up for recurrence and second primaries; manage dry mouth & dental disease.
⭐: Definitive diagnosis is always histopathology; the most important determinant of outcome is whether the neck nodes are involved.

o: Prescribe antiseptic mouthwash and review in 2 months
Urgent referral and an incisional biopsy to exclude squamous cell carcinoma
Excise the whole lesion immediately in the chair
Reassure — it is a traumatic ulcer
quiz.e: A non-healing indurated ulcer at a high-risk site in a high-risk patient must be biopsied urgently to exclude SCC; incisional biopsy gives the diagnosis before planning definitive treatment.
w: A — delaying a suspicious ulcer for 2 months risks progression
C — chair-side excision of an undiagnosed possible cancer compromises definitive surgery
D — assuming a traumatic ulcer without biopsy is unsafe given the red flags
quiz.ty: Non-healing indurated ulcer >3 weeks at a high-risk site → urgent incisional biopsy.

quiz.q: For a patient with confirmed oral SCC, which factor MOST strongly determines prognosis?
quiz.e: Nodal status is the single most important prognostic factor; extranodal extension worsens it further.
w: A — age influences fitness for treatment but is not the dominant prognostic factor
C — surface colour does not determine prognosis
D — smoking is a risk factor, not the key prognostic determinant once cancer is present
quiz.ty: Nodal (lymph-node) involvement is the single most important prognostic factor in oral SCC.

quiz.q: A patient who had radiotherapy to the mandible for oral cancer now needs a lower molar removed. The MAIN concern and approach are:
o: Osteoradionecrosis risk — manage atraumatically, consider hyperbaric oxygen, and ideally such teeth are removed before radiotherapy
Give a long antibiotic course and extract carelessly
quiz.e: Irradiated bone is hypovascular and heals poorly; extraction risks osteoradionecrosis, so doubtful teeth should be removed before radiotherapy and any later extraction is atraumatic with adjuncts.
w: A — routine extraction in irradiated bone is exactly what causes ORN
C — implants in irradiated bone are high-risk and not the answer here
D — careless extraction increases ORN risk
quiz.ty: Irradiated jaw → ORN risk: extract doubtful teeth BEFORE radiotherapy; later extractions atraumatic ± HBO.

pearls: Tobacco and alcohol act synergistically; HPV-16 drives oropharyngeal cancer in younger, often non-smoking patients.
Field cancerisation means the whole exposed mucosa is at risk — look for and follow up second primaries.
Definitive diagnosis is histopathological — image the neck/primary, but the biopsy makes the diagnosis.
Prevent osteoradionecrosis: extract doubtful teeth BEFORE radiotherapy and avoid extractions in irradiated bone afterwards.
mistakes: Forgetting a 'numb chin'/lip without a dental cause can signal malignancy.
Extracting teeth in an irradiated jaw and precipitating osteoradionecrosis.
Reassuring a patient with a persistent red/white patch without biopsy.
Missing second primaries due to incomplete mucosal examination/follow-up.
Chair-side excision of an undiagnosed possible cancer (compromising definitive surgery).
Underestimating the prognostic weight of nodal status/extranodal extension.
Forgetting to extract doubtful teeth BEFORE radiotherapy.
Assuming all white/red lesions are benign without biopsy.
Not arranging neck imaging/FNAC for a suspicious node.
Confusing verrucous carcinoma (low-grade) management with aggressive SCC.
Overlooking HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer in a young non-smoker.
Neglecting tobacco/alcohol cessation counselling.
facts: Other risks: betel/areca quid, sunlight (lip), HPV-16 (oropharynx), immunosuppression, chronic trauma, poor diet.
HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer affects younger, often non-smoking patients and has a better prognosis.
Premalignant precursors: erythroplakia (highest), leukoplakia, OSMF, erosive lichen planus.
SCC variants: verrucous carcinoma (low-grade, exophytic, rarely metastasises), basaloid, spindle-cell.
Field cancerisation → multiple primary tumours and a high second-primary risk.
Red flags: non-healing ulcer >3 weeks, induration, rolled margins, fixation, bleeding, neck node, referred otalgia, numbness.
Diagnosis is by incisional biopsy (histopathology).
Staging is by TNM: T (size/depth of invasion), N (nodes), M (distant metastasis).
Depth of invasion is incorporated into modern T staging.
Lymphatic spread is to cervical nodes levels I–V (predictable by primary site).
Nodal (lymph-node) involvement is the single most important prognostic factor; extranodal extension worsens it.
Distant metastasis is mainly to the lungs.
Investigations: MRI (soft tissue/tongue), CT (bone/neck/chest), OPG, PET-CT for staging; USS-FNAC for neck nodes.
Treatment modalities: surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy — combined by stage.
Early (stage I–II): single modality; advanced (III–IV): surgery + adjuvant chemoradiotherapy.
Surgery: wide local excision (clear margins) ± mandibulectomy; neck dissection for nodal disease or elective high-risk necks.
Reconstruction: radial forearm flap (soft tissue), free fibula flap (mandible), pectoralis major (regional).
Radiotherapy effects: mucositis, xerostomia, radiation caries, trismus, fibrosis.
Osteoradionecrosis: irradiated bone is hypovascular/hypocellular/hypoxic and heals poorly.
Prevent ORN: extract doubtful teeth BEFORE radiotherapy; avoid extractions in irradiated bone; HBO/pentoxifylline adjuncts.
A 'numb chin' without a dental cause can be the first sign of malignancy/metastasis.
Prognosis depends on stage and nodal status; early detection markedly improves survival.
Prevention: tobacco/alcohol cessation, treat premalignant lesions, opportunistic mucosal screening.
Cervical node levels: I submental/submandibular, II–IV jugular chain, V posterior triangle.
Verrucous carcinoma rarely metastasises and is treated mainly by surgery.
Lip SCC (lower lip, sun-exposed) generally has a better prognosis than intra-oral SCC.
Regular follow-up detects recurrence and second primaries.
mnemonics: Risk 'TAB-S-H': Tobacco, Alcohol, Betel, Sunlight (lip), HPV.
Pre-RT clearance prevents ORN (extract before radiotherapy).

study.html:
• Winter's (angulation): mesioangular (commonest, usually easiest), vertical, distoangular (often hardest in the mandible), horizontal, transverse.
  • Pell & Gregory: depth relative to occlusal plane = A/B/C; relationship of the distal crown to the ramus/2nd molar = Class 1/2/3 (3 = within ramus, hardest).

• Difficulty rises with depth, distoangular/horizontal angulation, class 3, curved/divergent roots, dense bone, older patient.
  • Radiographic signs of close IAN relation (on OPG): darkening/notching of the root, diversion of the canal, interruption of the white lines of the canal, deflection of roots. If present → CBCT and consider coronectomy.

• Remove for: recurrent pericoronitis, unrestorable caries (tooth or distal of 2nd molar), pathology (cyst/tumour), resorption of the adjacent tooth, fracture line, pre-orthognathic/pre-radiotherapy.
  • Avoid prophylactic removal of asymptomatic, disease-free impactions (NICE).
  • Relative contraindications: extremes of age/comorbidity where risk outweighs benefit.

• LA ± sedation/GA; buccal mucoperiosteal flap (broad base), protect the lingual tissues.
  • Bone removal (buccal gutter) with an irrigated bur; section the tooth (crown/roots) to deliver along the path of least resistance with elevators.
  • Debride the socket, smooth bone, irrigate, achieve haemostasis, suture.

• Deliberate removal of the crown only, leaving vital roots, when roots are intimately related to the IAN canal — to reduce nerve injury risk.
  • Contraindicated if the tooth is non-vital/infected, mobile, or horizontally impacted along the nerve.
  • Roots may later migrate away from the nerve.

• Most are neuropraxia (temporary); recovery over weeks–months. Persisting >6 months suggests axonotmesis/neurotmesis.
  • Lingual nerve injury risk with lingual flap retraction/distolingual bone; IAN risk with deep close roots.
  • Document sensation; review; refer for microsurgical repair if indicated for persistent neurotmesis.

• 2nd most commonly impacted; often palatal.
  • Localise with the parallax/SLOB rule (Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal) or CBCT.
  • Management options: interceptive removal of the deciduous canine, surgical exposure + orthodontic traction (open/closed technique), surgical removal, or observation (autotransplantation in selected cases).

• Intra-op: nerve injury, fracture (root, alveolus, mandible, tuberosity for upper 8s), displacement (upper 8 into sinus/infratemporal fossa; lower root into the canal/floor of mouth), haemorrhage, oroantral communication.
  • Post-op: pain, swelling, trismus, dry socket (common after lower 8s), infection, bleeding.
  • Post-op care: analgesia, ice, soft diet, gentle warm saline rinses after 24 h, avoid smoking.
⭐: Mesioangular = commonest & usually easiest; distoangular = often the most difficult lower 8; always assess IAN proximity before surgery.

quiz.e: Distoangular lower third molars are usually the most difficult because the path of withdrawal runs into the ascending ramus; mesioangular is usually the easiest.
w: A — mesioangular is the commonest and usually the easiest

D — buccal tilt alone is not the classic 'most difficult' answer
quiz.ty: Distoangular = generally the most difficult lower 8; mesioangular = commonest/easiest.

quiz.q: A palatally impacted maxillary canine needs surgical exposure. The correct way to determine its bucco-palatal position from two periapical films is the:
quiz.e: The parallax/SLOB rule (Same Lingual, Opposite Buccal) — or CBCT — localises an impacted canine bucco-palatally before exposure.
w: A — TNM is cancer staging, not localisation
C — Winter's lines assess third-molar depth, not canine position
D — ALARA is a radiation-protection principle, not a localisation method
quiz.ty: Localise an impacted canine with parallax (SLOB) or CBCT before exposure.

pearls: Coronectomy (remove the crown, leave vital roots) is for roots intimately related to the IAN — but not if the tooth is infected, non-vital or mobile.
Localise an impacted maxillary canine with the parallax (SLOB) rule or CBCT before exposing it.
NICE: do not remove asymptomatic, disease-free impactions prophylactically.
An upper third molar can be displaced into the maxillary sinus or the infratemporal fossa — control the tooth and direction of force.
mistakes: Performing a coronectomy on an infected or mobile tooth.
Removing asymptomatic, disease-free impactions prophylactically.
Damaging the lingual nerve by poor lingual flap/retractor placement.
Extracting in the acute phase of pericoronitis instead of settling it first.
Forgetting CBCT when OPG shows close IAN signs.
Choosing an open exposure for a deep palatal canine where a closed technique is better.
Not warning the patient about IAN/lingual nerve injury before lower 3rd molar surgery.
Mislabelling a distoangular impaction as easy.
Leaving a mesiodens that is obstructing incisor eruption.
Inadequate bone removal/sectioning leading to fracture by force.
Forgetting dry socket is the commonest complication after lower 3rd molars.
Failing to localise an impacted canine (SLOB/CBCT) before exposure.
facts: Pell & Gregory = depth relative to the occlusal plane (A/B/C) + relationship to the ramus/2nd molar (class 1/2/3).
Pell & Gregory class 3 = the crown is within the ramus (most difficult access).
Difficulty rises with depth, distoangular/horizontal angulation, class 3, curved/divergent roots, dense bone, older age.
Radiographic signs of close IAN relation: darkening/notching of the root, diversion of the canal, interruption of the canal's white lines, deflection of roots.
If IAN-proximity signs are present → CBCT and consider coronectomy.

Indications to remove a 3rd molar: recurrent pericoronitis, unrestorable caries (tooth or distal of 2nd molar), cyst/tumour, resorption of the adjacent tooth, fracture line, pre-orthognathic/pre-radiotherapy.
NICE: avoid prophylactic removal of asymptomatic, disease-free impactions.
Surgical technique: buccal mucoperiosteal flap (broad base), protect the lingual tissues, bone removal with an irrigated bur, tooth sectioning, debride, suture.
Coronectomy = remove the crown, leave vital roots, when roots are intimately related to the IAN canal.
Coronectomy is contraindicated if the tooth is non-vital/infected, mobile, or horizontal along the nerve.
Nerves at risk in lower 3rd molar surgery: inferior alveolar and lingual.
Most third-molar nerve injuries are neuropraxia (recover); persistence >6 months suggests axonotmesis/neurotmesis.
Lingual nerve injury risk with lingual flap retraction/distolingual bone removal.
Pericoronitis = inflammation of the operculum over a partially erupted tooth (usually lower 3rd molar).
Acute pericoronitis: local debridement/irrigation + relieve the traumatic occlusion; antibiotics only if spreading; extract later.
The maxillary canine is the 2nd most commonly impacted tooth and is often palatal.
Localise an impacted canine with the parallax (SLOB) rule or CBCT.
Impacted canine options: interceptive removal of the deciduous canine, surgical exposure + orthodontic traction, removal, or autotransplantation.
Exposure techniques: open (window) for superficial teeth; closed (bonded chain, flap replaced) for deep/palatal teeth.
Upper 3rd molar removal risks displacement into the maxillary sinus or infratemporal fossa.
Lower 3rd molar roots can be displaced into the IAN canal or the submandibular/sublingual space.
A mesiodens is a midline supernumerary tooth that may block or divert incisor eruption.
Most common post-op complication after a lower 3rd molar = dry socket.
Transmigration = an impacted canine that migrates across the midline.
Coronectomy roots may later migrate away from the IAN canal.
Winter's lines (white/amber/red) help assess impaction depth/difficulty.
Post-op care: analgesia, ice, soft diet, warm saline rinses after 24 h, avoid smoking.
mnemonics: IAN-proximity signs: Darkening, Diversion of canal, Loss of white lines → CBCT.
Upper 8 displacement: Sinus or Infratemporal fossa; Lower 8 root: Canal or Submandibular space.

study.html:
• Largest paranasal sinus (antrum of Highmore); respiratory ciliated lining; the ostium drains high on the medial wall (against gravity).
  • Floor relates to premolar/molar apices; pneumatisation after extraction lowers the floor toward the ridge.

• OAC = fresh communication; OAF = epithelialised chronic tract.
  • Diagnose: Valsalva (air/bubbles), nasal regurgitation of fluids, echo on suction, blunt probe (gently).
  • By size: <2 mm encourage a clot; 2–6 mm figure-8 suture ± dressing; >6 mm formal flap closure.

• Buccal advancement (Rehrmann) flap — commonest; periosteal scoring to advance; may reduce sulcus depth.
  • Palatal rotation/transposition flap — robust, keratinised, good for posterior defects.
  • Buccal fat pad — for larger posterior defects.
  • Cover with antibiotics, decongestants, and sinus precautions (no nose-blowing/straws).

• Odontogenic sinusitis: usually unilateral, foul-smelling; from periapical infection, OAF, or displaced root/foreign body. Treat the dental cause + sinus management.
  • Root/tooth displaced into the antrum: confirm radiographically; retrieve via Caldwell-Luc or endoscopic approach; do not blindly instrument.
  • Other: mucous retention cysts (dome-shaped, often incidental), antroliths.
