After removing an upper first molar you suspect an oro-antral communication. The quickest reliable bedside test to confirm it is:
o: The Valsalva (gentle nose-holding/blowing) test looking for air/bubbling at the socket
quiz.e: The Valsalva test demonstrates air or bubbling through the socket, confirming a communication with the antrum.
w: A — percussion assesses periodontal/periapical tenderness, not a sinus communication
C — vitality testing is irrelevant for an empty socket
D — a bite test assesses cracked teeth, not an OAC
quiz.ty: Confirm an OAC with the Valsalva test (air/bubbling).

quiz.q: A 4 mm oro-antral communication is confirmed with healthy surrounding tissue. The MOST appropriate management is:
o: Place a figure-of-eight suture, give antibiotics, a decongestant and sinus precautions
Raise a large buccal advancement flap immediately
Pack the socket open to drain the sinus
quiz.e: A 2-6 mm OAC is managed by supporting the clot with a figure-of-eight suture plus antibiotics, decongestant and sinus precautions; most heal.
w: A — even small communications need review and precautions
C — a large flap is reserved for defects >6 mm and is unnecessary here
D — packing open invites a chronic fistula
quiz.ty: OAC 2-6 mm → figure-of-eight suture + antibiotics + precautions; >6 mm → flap.

quiz.q: A patient has unilateral nasal congestion and a foul-smelling discharge that started after an upper molar problem, with tenderness over the cheek. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
quiz.e: Unilateral, foul-smelling maxillary sinusitis following a dental problem is odontogenic; management treats the dental source plus the sinus.
w: A — allergic rhinitis is usually bilateral and not foul-smelling
C — viral sinusitis is typically bilateral and self-limiting without a dental trigger
D — migraine does not cause a foul nasal discharge
quiz.ty: Unilateral foul-smelling maxillary sinusitis = odontogenic until proven otherwise → treat the dental cause.

pearls: A unilateral, foul-smelling 'sinusitis' is odontogenic until proven otherwise — find and treat the dental cause.
A root lost into the antrum is confirmed radiographically and retrieved via a Caldwell-Luc or endoscopic approach, never by blind suction through the socket.
Give sinus precautions after any OAC: no nose-blowing, straws or smoking, and sneeze with the mouth open.
An established (epithelialised) oro-antral fistula will not close by suture alone — excise the tract and close with a flap (buccal advancement/Rehrmann, palatal, or buccal fat pad).
mistakes: Trying to close an established epithelialised OAF with a suture alone.
Omitting sinus precautions after creating an OAC.
Using a large flap for a tiny (<2 mm) communication that would clot.
Forgetting to confirm a displaced root's location radiographically before surgery.
Perforating the Schneiderian membrane during a sinus lift without repair.
Overlooking pneumatisation when planning posterior maxillary implants.
Missing invasive fungal sinusitis in a diabetic/immunocompromised patient.
Mistaking an incidental mucous retention cyst for significant pathology.
Not giving decongestants/treating the dental cause in odontogenic sinusitis.
Closing an OAF without excising the epithelial tract first.
Failing to warn the patient of sinus precautions and follow-up.
facts: OAC = a fresh socket-to-antrum communication; OAF = an epithelialised chronic tract.
Diagnose an OAC: bubbling of blood/air at the socket, nasal regurgitation of fluids, the Valsalva test, a hollow note on suction.
OAC management by size: <2 mm encourage a clot; 2–6 mm figure-of-eight suture; >6 mm a flap.
Flap options for a large OAC/OAF: buccal advancement (Rehrmann), palatal rotation, or buccal fat pad.
An established OAF needs excision of the epithelialised tract PLUS flap closure.
Do NOT repeatedly probe a suspected OAC (it enlarges it and pushes infection into the sinus).
Sinus precautions: no nose-blowing, no straws, no smoking, sneeze with the mouth open.
A root displaced into the antrum is retrieved via Caldwell-Luc or an endoscopic approach (never blind suction).
Confirm a displaced root radiographically before retrieval.
Odontogenic (dental) sinusitis is typically unilateral and foul-smelling.
Treat odontogenic sinusitis by addressing the dental cause plus sinus management.
A mucous retention cyst is a dome-shaped antral-floor opacity, often incidental.
An antrolith is a calcified mass within the sinus.
Cilia move mucus toward the ostium.
Imaging: CT or an occipitomental (Waters') view assesses antral pathology.
Posterior maxillary teeth (premolars/molars) are most related to the sinus floor.
Pneumatisation reduces available bone for posterior maxillary implants.
A sinus lift (direct lateral window or indirect osteotome) augments deficient posterior maxillary height for implants.
Schneiderian membrane perforation is the main complication of a sinus lift.
Acute sinusitis features: cheek pain/pressure, tenderness, nasal discharge, postnasal drip.
Antibiotics + decongestants are used for sinusitis alongside treating any dental cause.
The maxillary artery and its branches supply the sinus region.
The infraorbital nerve (V2) runs in the roof/floor-of-orbit region above the sinus.
A wide OAC left untreated epithelialises into a persistent oro-antral fistula.
Caldwell-Luc accesses the antrum through an anterior (canine fossa) bony window.
Beware fungal sinusitis in immunocompromised/diabetic patients (invasive disease).
mnemonics: Root in antrum → Caldwell-Luc / endoscopic.
Sinus precautions: no Nose-blowing, Straws, Smoking.

study.html:
• With reduction: disc displaced (usually antero-medial) at rest, reduces on opening → reciprocal click; opening usually normal.
  • Without reduction (closed lock): disc does not reduce → limited opening (~25–30 mm), deviation to the affected side, no click.
  • Wilkes staging describes progression from early reducible displacement to late degeneration.

• Most common cause of TMJ-region pain; muscular, related to parafunction/bruxism, stress, malocclusion; more in women.
  • Signs: muscle tenderness, dull preauricular ache, limited opening, clicking; imaging is normal (no joint pathology).
  • Treatment: conservative first — reassurance, soft diet, jaw rest, NSAIDs, occlusal splint, physiotherapy, stress management; very rarely surgery.

• Condyle moves anterior to the articular eminence and cannot self-reduce (open lock); often after wide yawn/opening.
  • Reduction: Hippocratic method — downward then backward pressure on the posterior teeth (thumbs on external oblique ridges).
  • Recurrent dislocation: conservative measures, autologous blood injection, or surgery (eminectomy, eminence augmentation).
  • Subluxation = self-reducing hypermobility.

• Fusion restricting movement: true (intra-articular, bony/fibrous) vs false (extra-articular, e.g., coronoid hyperplasia, fibrosis, myositis ossificans).
  • Causes: childhood trauma (condylar), infection (otitis/osteomyelitis), previous surgery.
  • Consequences in children: restricted opening, facial asymmetry/retrognathia ("bird face"), impaired feeding/hygiene.
  • Treatment: surgical release — gap or interpositional arthroplasty, aggressive physiotherapy to prevent re-ankylosis; reconstruct as needed.

• Osteoarthritis: degenerative; crepitus, flattening/osteophytes, pain on loading in older patients.
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: bilateral, autoimmune, may cause anterior open bite from condylar resorption.
  • Juvenile idiopathic arthritis can disturb mandibular growth.

• Brief, severe, electric-shock pain in a V division, with cutaneous trigger zones; often due to vascular compression of the nerve root.
  • First-line drug: carbamazepine (oxcarbazepine alternative).
  • Refractory: microvascular decompression, or ablative procedures (glycerol/balloon/radiofrequency rhizotomy, gamma knife).
  • Red flags (young patient, bilateral, sensory loss) → exclude MS/tumour with MRI.

• Atypical (persistent idiopathic) facial pain: chronic, poorly localised, no organic cause; managed with tricyclics/reassurance.
  • Glossopharyngeal neuralgia: throat/ear pain triggered by swallowing.
  • Giant cell (temporal) arteritis: elderly, temporal headache, jaw claudication, raised ESR — urgent steroids to prevent blindness.
  • Burning mouth syndrome; cluster headache; dental/sinus causes.

• Imaging: OPG (screening), MRI (disc/soft tissue — best for internal derangement), CT (bony ankylosis/trauma).
  • Stepwise care: conservative (splint, NSAIDs, physio) → minimally invasive (arthrocentesis, arthroscopy) → open surgery (disc repair/removal, eminectomy, joint replacement) for refractory cases.
⭐: Start with reversible/conservative therapy for almost all TMD; reserve surgery for clear structural disease unresponsive to it.

flashcards.a: Brief, severe, electric-shock, with trigger zones.

o: Bilateral TMJ dislocation — reduce by downward then backward pressure on the posterior teeth
Bilateral condylar tumour — refer for biopsy
quiz.e: An open lock after wide opening with pre-auricular hollows is anterior TMJ dislocation; reduce by the Hippocratic method.
w: A — a fracture causes malocclusion/mobility, not a simple post-yawn open lock
C — MPDS is chronic muscular pain, not an acute open lock
D — a tumour does not present as an acute reducible dislocation

quiz.q: A 30-year-old has intermittent preauricular pain with a reproducible reciprocal click on opening and closing, and a normal range of opening. The MOST likely problem is:
quiz.e: A reciprocal click with preserved opening indicates anterior disc displacement that reduces on opening (with reduction).
w: B — displacement without reduction causes limited opening and NO click
C — ankylosis causes fixed restriction, not clicking
D — septic arthritis presents with an acutely hot, painful, restricted joint and systemic signs
quiz.ty: Reciprocal click + normal opening = disc displacement WITH reduction.

quiz.q: A 72-year-old has a unilateral temporal headache, pain in the jaw on chewing (jaw claudication), scalp tenderness and an ESR of 90. The priority action is:
o: Reassure and give a soft diet
Start high-dose corticosteroids urgently (giant cell/temporal arteritis) to prevent blindness
quiz.e: Jaw claudication, temporal headache and a high ESR in an elderly patient indicate giant cell arteritis; urgent steroids are started to prevent irreversible visual loss.
w: A — reassurance risks blindness from an untreated vasculitis
C — carbamazepine is for trigeminal neuralgia, not arteritis
D — a splint does not treat a vasculitis
quiz.ty: Elderly + jaw claudication + temporal headache + raised ESR = giant cell arteritis → urgent steroids.

pearls: Childhood condylar trauma is the classic cause of TMJ ankylosis — early mobilisation prevents it.
Trigeminal neuralgia is brief, severe, electric-shock pain with trigger zones; first-line drug is carbamazepine, with microvascular decompression for refractory cases.
In an elderly patient, jaw claudication with a temporal headache and a raised ESR is giant cell (temporal) arteritis — start steroids urgently to prevent blindness.
Reserve TMJ surgery for clear structural disease that has failed conservative therapy.
mistakes: Prolonged intermaxillary fixation of a condylar fracture (promotes ankylosis), especially in children.
Missing giant cell arteritis (jaw claudication + raised ESR) and risking blindness.
Treating trigeminal neuralgia as a dental problem and doing irreversible dentistry.
Forgetting to exclude a sinister cause (young/bilateral, sensory loss) in 'neuralgia'.
Mistaking septic arthritis for simple MPDS.
Not recognising rheumatoid arthritis causing an anterior open bite.
Failing early mobilisation after a condylar fracture (ankylosis risk).
Using carbamazepine for myofascial pain instead of neuralgia.
Reducing a dislocation with the wrong vector (must be down then back).
Choosing open TMJ surgery before trying conservative/minimally invasive steps.
Overlooking parafunction/bruxism as the driver of MPDS.
Ordering CT instead of MRI to assess the disc.
facts: Main ligament: lateral (temporomandibular); accessory: stylomandibular & sphenomandibular.
TMJ nerve supply: auriculotemporal + masseteric branches (both V3).
TMJ arterial supply: superficial temporal & maxillary arteries.
Normal interincisal opening ≈ 40 mm.
Most TMJ-region pain is myofascial pain dysfunction (MPDS) — muscular, with normal imaging.
MPDS is linked to parafunction/bruxism and stress; commoner in women.
MPDS management is conservative first: reassurance, soft diet, NSAIDs, occlusal splint, physiotherapy.
Disc displacement WITH reduction = reciprocal click, normal opening.
Disc displacement WITHOUT reduction = closed lock, limited opening (~25–30 mm), no click.
Wilkes staging describes progression of internal derangement.
Acute dislocation = condyle anterior to the articular eminence (open lock), cannot self-reduce.
Reduce a dislocation by the Hippocratic method (downward then backward pressure on the posterior teeth).
Recurrent dislocation: autologous blood injection or surgery (eminectomy).
Subluxation = self-reducing hypermobility.
TMJ ankylosis: true (intra-articular, bony/fibrous) vs false (extra-articular).
Ankylosis usually follows childhood condylar trauma or infection; early mobilisation prevents it.
Childhood ankylosis → restricted opening + facial asymmetry/retrognathia ('bird face').
Ankylosis surgery: gap or interpositional arthroplasty + aggressive physiotherapy.
Osteoarthritis: degenerative, crepitus, flattening/osteophytes, older patients.
Rheumatoid arthritis: bilateral, autoimmune, may cause anterior open bite from condylar resorption.
Septic arthritis: acutely hot, painful, restricted joint with systemic signs.
Trigeminal neuralgia: brief, severe, electric-shock pain in a V division with trigger zones.
Trigeminal neuralgia first-line drug = carbamazepine; refractory → microvascular decompression.
Young/bilateral trigeminal neuralgia with sensory loss → MRI to exclude MS/tumour.
Giant cell (temporal) arteritis: elderly, temporal headache, jaw claudication, raised ESR → urgent steroids (prevent blindness).
Atypical (persistent idiopathic) facial pain: chronic, poorly localised, no organic cause.
Imaging: MRI is best for the disc/internal derangement; CT for bony ankylosis/trauma.
Treatment ladder: conservative → arthrocentesis/arthroscopy → open surgery for refractory structural disease.
mnemonics: MPDS first-line = Conservative (Splint, NSAIDs, Soft diet, Reassurance).
Trigeminal neuralgia drug = Carbamazepine; refractory = Microvascular decompression.
Elderly + jaw claudication + raised ESR = Giant cell arteritis → urgent steroids.

study.html:
• Acute bacterial (parotid): in dehydrated/elderly/post-op, reduced flow → ascending Staph aureus; painful swelling, pus from duct. Treat: rehydrate, antibiotics, sialagogues, massage.
  • Mumps: viral (paramyxovirus); bilateral parotid swelling, systemic; complications orchitis/meningitis.
  • Chronic/recurrent sialadenitis: often obstructive (stone/stricture).

• ~80% in the submandibular gland/Wharton's duct (mucous alkaline saliva + uphill tortuous duct); mostly radiopaque.
  • Classic: mealtime pain & swelling that settles between meals.
  • Investigate: lower true occlusal radiograph, ultrasound, sialography, or sialendoscopy.
  • Treat: sialagogues/massage/hydration; intraoral stone removal; sialendoscopy; gland excision if recurrent/damaged.

• Mucocele: mucous extravasation cyst, usually lower lip from minor-gland trauma; treat by excision with the feeding gland.
  • Ranula: from the sublingual gland in the floor of mouth; "plunging" ranula herniates through mylohyoid into the neck.
  • Sjögren's syndrome: autoimmune; dry eyes + dry mouth (sicca), ± connective tissue disease (secondary); raised risk of MALT lymphoma; anti-Ro/La, labial gland biopsy.
  • Necrotising sialometaplasia: benign ulcer (palate) that mimics malignancy — self-healing.

Rule of thumb: the larger the gland, the more likely a tumour is benign; small glands (e.g., palate) → higher malignancy chance. ~80% of parotid tumours are benign.

TumourKey features
Pleomorphic adenomaMost common; parotid; benign but recurs if incompletely excised; small malignant potential
Warthin's (adenolymphoma)Parotid, older males, may be bilateral; smoking-related
Mucoepidermoid carcinomaMost common malignant; variable grade
Adenoid cystic carcinomaPerineural invasion, late lung metastases, poor long-term prognosis
Acinic cell carcinomaLow-grade, parotid

• Ultrasound (first-line) ± FNAC for masses; MRI for deep-lobe/parapharyngeal extent; CT for stones/bone.
  • Sialography for ductal pathology (avoid in acute infection); sialendoscopy is diagnostic + therapeutic.
  • Never do an excisional/incisional biopsy of a suspected major salivary malignancy in the clinic — risk of tumour seeding & facial-nerve injury; plan formal surgery.

• Parotidectomy: superficial/total; the facial nerve is the key structure to identify and preserve.
  • Frey's syndrome: gustatory sweating from auriculotemporal nerve misdirection after parotid surgery.
  • Submandibular gland excision risks: lingual, hypoglossal, and marginal mandibular (facial) nerves.
  • Other: salivary fistula, sialocele, numbness of the ear lobe (great auricular nerve).

• Xerostomia (dry mouth): drugs (anticholinergics, antidepressants), Sjögren's, radiotherapy, dehydration; complications: caries, candidiasis, difficulty with dentures. Manage with saliva substitutes/sialagogues, fluoride, hydration.
  • Sialosis: bilateral painless non-neoplastic enlargement (diabetes, alcoholism, bulimia, malnutrition).
⭐: Submandibular = stones; parotid = tumours (mostly benign) & mumps; minor glands = higher malignancy risk.

w: A — a tumour causes a persistent painless mass, not mealtime obstruction
C — mumps is a bilateral viral parotid swelling with systemic symptoms
D — Sjögren's causes dry mouth/eyes, not mealtime obstructive swelling
quiz.ty: Mealtime pain/swelling of one gland = obstructive sialolithiasis (usually submandibular, radiopaque).

quiz.q: A slow-growing, painless, mobile mass is found in the superficial parotid. The MOST likely diagnosis and the key surgical risk are:
o: Pleomorphic adenoma; injury to the facial nerve
quiz.e: The commonest parotid tumour is a pleomorphic adenoma; the facial nerve runs through the parotid and is the key structure to protect during excision (which must be adequate to avoid recurrence).
w: B — mucoepidermoid is the commonest malignant tumour, but the parotid surgical risk is the facial nerve, not the lingual
C — Warthin's occurs in older males, and the at-risk nerve in the parotid is still the facial, not the hypoglossal
D — adenoid cystic is less common, and the parotid surgical risk is the facial nerve
quiz.ty: Commonest parotid tumour = pleomorphic adenoma; the facial nerve is the key structure to protect.

quiz.q: A salivary malignancy is reported as having extensive perineural invasion with a tendency to late lung metastases. This is characteristic of:
quiz.e: Adenoid cystic carcinoma classically shows perineural invasion and late distant (lung) metastases, giving a poor long-term prognosis.
w: A — pleomorphic adenoma is benign (small malignant potential), not perineural
C — Warthin's is a benign tumour
D — a mucocele is a benign mucous extravasation cyst
quiz.ty: Perineural invasion + late lung metastases = adenoid cystic carcinoma.

pearls: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is notorious for perineural invasion and late lung metastases — long-term prognosis is poor despite slow growth.
The facial nerve is the structure to identify and protect in any parotid surgery; Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating) is a recognised sequela.
Do not perform an incisional/excisional biopsy of a suspected major-gland malignancy in the clinic — image and plan formal surgery to avoid seeding and nerve injury.
Dry eyes plus dry mouth (sicca) is Sjögren's syndrome, which carries an increased risk of MALT lymphoma.
mistakes: Forgetting that small-gland (palatal) tumours have a higher malignancy rate.
Missing perineural spread of adenoid cystic carcinoma.
Performing sialography during acute infection.
Overlooking Sjögren's (and its lymphoma risk) in a patient with sicca symptoms.
Mistaking necrotising sialometaplasia (benign) for a malignancy.
Forgetting the facial nerve is the key structure in parotid surgery.
Not warning about Frey's syndrome after parotid surgery.
Assuming all gland enlargement is neoplastic (consider mumps, sialosis, sialadenitis).
Not recognising mealtime swelling as obstructive sialolithiasis.
Forgetting the lingual/hypoglossal/marginal mandibular nerves in submandibular excision.
Confusing a mucocele (lower lip) with a ranula (floor of mouth/sublingual).
Treating an obstructive stone with antibiotics alone without relieving the obstruction.
facts: Hundreds of minor salivary glands line the oral mucosa (palate, lips, cheeks).
~80% of salivary calculi are in the submandibular gland/Wharton's duct (mucous, alkaline saliva, uphill tortuous duct).
Most salivary stones are radiopaque.
Sialolithiasis: pain and swelling at mealtimes that settles between meals.
Investigate stones: lower true occlusal radiograph, ultrasound, sialography, or sialendoscopy.
Stone treatment: sialagogues/massage/hydration, intraoral removal, sialendoscopy, gland excision if recurrent.
Acute bacterial parotitis: dehydrated/elderly, reduced flow, ascending Staph aureus; pus from the duct.
Mumps = viral parotitis (paramyxovirus), bilateral, systemic; complications orchitis/meningitis.
Chronic/recurrent sialadenitis is often obstructive (stone/stricture).
Sjögren's syndrome: autoimmune dry eyes + dry mouth (sicca); anti-Ro/La; labial gland biopsy; increased MALT lymphoma risk.
Mucocele = mucous extravasation cyst, usually the lower lip, from minor-gland trauma.
Ranula = mucous cyst from the sublingual gland in the floor of mouth; 'plunging' ranula herniates through mylohyoid into the neck.
Necrotising sialometaplasia: a benign self-healing palatal ulcer that mimics malignancy.
Rule: the larger the gland, the more likely a tumour is benign; smaller glands → higher malignancy chance.
~80% of parotid tumours are benign.
Pleomorphic adenoma = commonest salivary tumour (parotid); benign but recurs if incompletely excised.
Warthin's tumour (adenolymphoma): parotid, older males, smoking-related, may be bilateral.
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma = commonest malignant salivary tumour; graded low to high.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma: perineural invasion, late lung metastases, poor long-term prognosis.
Acinic cell carcinoma: low-grade, usually parotid.
Investigations: ultrasound (first-line) ± FNAC; MRI for deep-lobe/parapharyngeal extent; CT for stones/bone.
Avoid sialography during acute infection.
Never do a clinic incisional/excisional biopsy of a suspected major-gland malignancy (seeding & facial-nerve risk).
Parotidectomy: the facial nerve is the key structure to identify and preserve.
Frey's syndrome: gustatory sweating from auriculotemporal-nerve misdirection after parotid surgery.
Submandibular gland excision risks: lingual, hypoglossal and marginal mandibular (facial) nerves.
Xerostomia causes: drugs (anticholinergics/antidepressants), Sjögren's, radiotherapy, dehydration → caries/candidiasis.
Sialosis: bilateral painless non-neoplastic enlargement (diabetes, alcoholism, bulimia, malnutrition).
mnemonics: Commonest tumour = Pleomorphic adenoma (parotid); commonest malignant = Mucoepidermoid.
Adenoid cystic = Perineural invasion + late Lung mets.
Parotid surgery danger = Facial nerve; sequela = Frey's (gustatory sweating).

study.html: Bone grafts/ridge preservation or implants for severe resorption. Order: hard tissue procedures before soft tissue.

• Aim: a broad, U-shaped, smooth ridge with adequate sulcus depth, healthy keratinised mucosa, no sharp bone/undercuts or interfering frena, correct ridge relationship.
  • Examine ridge form, undercuts, tori, frenal attachments, denture-bearing mucosa; plan hard-tissue procedures before soft-tissue ones.

• Alveoloplasty (recontour ridge after extractions), alveolectomy, removal of sharp interseptal/labial bone.
  • Removal of tori (palatinus/mandibularis) and exostoses when they interfere with a denture.
  • Mylohyoid ridge reduction, genial tubercle reduction, tuberosity reduction (bony or fibrous) to create inter-arch space.

• Frenectomy for a high frenal attachment that unseats a denture.
  • Vestibuloplasty to deepen the sulcus and increase the denture-bearing area.
  • Excision of denture-induced hyperplasia (epulis fissuratum), papillary hyperplasia of the palate, and correction of a flabby (mobile) ridge.

• For severe resorption: ridge augmentation (onlay grafts, GBR) or, increasingly, implant-retained overdentures/fixed prostheses.
  • Implants have reduced the need for many traditional preprosthetic procedures.

flashcards.a: Deepen the sulcus to increase denture-bearing area.

flashcards.q: Hard or soft tissue surgery first?

o: Reducing the need for many traditional procedures

quiz.q: A long-term denture wearer has a folded, fibrous overgrowth in the labial sulcus that fits the denture flange. The diagnosis and management are:
o: Epulis fissuratum (denture-induced hyperplasia) — excise AND correct/replace the ill-fitting denture
quiz.e: A fibrous overgrowth conforming to a denture flange is epulis fissuratum; treatment excises the tissue and addresses the causative denture, otherwise it recurs.
w: A — although any chronic lesion warrants vigilance, the classic flange-related fold is denture hyperplasia, and biopsy confirms benignity
C — it will persist while the denture trauma continues
D — a torus is a bony, not a soft-tissue, lesion
quiz.ty: Epulis fissuratum = denture-induced hyperplasia → excise AND fix the denture.

quiz.q: When preparing a mouth for a complete denture, the correct sequence is to:
o: Deepen the sulcus first, then recontour bone
Recontour bone/remove interfering tori (hard tissue) BEFORE soft-tissue procedures

Place implants only, never prepare tissue
quiz.e: Hard-tissue procedures (alveoloplasty, tori removal) precede soft-tissue procedures (frenectomy, vestibuloplasty) so the soft-tissue result is built on the final bony contour.
w: A — soft-tissue deepening before bony recontouring may need redoing
C — sequencing matters for a predictable result
D — implants are an option but tissue preparation still follows a sequence when needed
quiz.ty: Preprosthetic sequence: hard-tissue procedures before soft-tissue.

pearls: Remove tori and exostoses only when they interfere with the prosthesis.
Implants have replaced many traditional preprosthetic procedures — consider them before extensive ridge surgery.
mistakes: Over-reducing bone and compromising ridge height for the denture.
Ignoring denture stomatitis/candida under the fitting surface.
Not deepening an inadequate sulcus (poor denture retention).
Forgetting ridge/socket preservation at the time of extraction.
Performing a frenectomy without addressing the denture instability cause.
Choosing extensive ridge surgery when implants would serve better.
Failing to smooth the final bony contour before closure.
Overlooking a fibrous (flabby) ridge under a denture.
Not planning hard- and soft-tissue steps in the correct order.
Leaving a prominent genial tubercle/mylohyoid ridge that interferes.
Recontouring bone roughly and leaving an irregular surface under the denture.
Ignoring the inter-arch space when a fibrous tuberosity is enlarged.
facts: Simple alveoloplasty (finger pressure/bone file) vs interseptal (Dean's) alveoloplasty (collapse the interseptal bone).
Alveolectomy = removal of alveolar bone; remove sharp interseptal/labial bone.
Torus palatinus: bony exostosis in the midline of the hard palate.
Torus mandibularis: bony exostosis on the lingual mandible near the premolars.
Remove tori/exostoses only when they interfere with the prosthesis.
Mylohyoid ridge reduction and genial tubercle reduction when they are prominent after resorption.
Tuberosity reduction may be bony or fibrous, to create inter-arch space.
Frenectomy: for a high labial or lingual frenal attachment that unseats a denture.
Vestibuloplasty: deepens the sulcus to increase the denture-bearing area (may use a mucosal/skin graft).
Epulis fissuratum (denture-induced hyperplasia): excise AND correct the ill-fitting denture.
Papillary hyperplasia of the palate: denture + candida related; manage hygiene/antifungal ± excision.
A flabby (mobile fibrous) ridge should be corrected/excised.
Denture stomatitis: candida under the fitting surface; treat hygiene, soak the denture, antifungal.
Ideal residual ridge: broad, rounded, U-shaped, no sharp undercuts.
A knife-edge ridge or severe undercut needs recontouring or augmentation.
Ridge augmentation for severe resorption: onlay grafts or GBR.
Ridge/socket preservation grafting after extraction limits resorption.
Implants have replaced many traditional preprosthetic procedures (implant-retained over/fixed prostheses).
Principles: preserve bone, atraumatic technique, smooth final contour, healthy keratinised mucosa.
Examine ridge form, undercuts, tori, frenal attachments and the denture-bearing mucosa when planning.
Genial tubercles can become prominent and interfere as the mandible resorbs.
A pendulous/fibrous maxillary tuberosity reduces inter-arch space and is reduced surgically.
mnemonics: Goal ridge = Broad, U-shaped, no sharp undercuts.
Denture lesions: Epulis fissuratum & Papillary hyperplasia (correct the denture too).

study.html:
• TADs / mini-implants: skeletal anchorage; placed in attached gingiva/interradicular bone.
  • Corticotomy / PAOO: accelerate tooth movement (regional acceleratory phenomenon).
  • Surgical exposure timing coordinated with the orthodontist.

• Most often the maxillary canine (commonly palatal). Localise with parallax/SLOB or CBCT.
  • Open technique: window left, pack/heal, then bond; suits superficial/buccal teeth.
  • Closed technique: bond a bracket/gold chain, replace the flap, apply orthodontic traction — preferred for deep/palatal teeth and aesthetics.

• A thick fibrous labial frenum can cause/maintain a midline diastema; frenectomy is usually done after orthodontic space closure to reduce relapse.
  • Removal of a mesiodens/supernumerary that blocks or diverts incisor eruption.
  • Exposure/removal decisions coordinated with the orthodontist.

• Temporary anchorage devices (mini-implants/screws): skeletal anchorage; placed in attached gingiva/interradicular bone; failure linked to mobile mucosa, inflammation, root contact.
  • Corticotomy / PAOO: surgical injury triggers the regional acceleratory phenomenon → faster tooth movement.
  • Surgical assistance for ankylosed teeth (luxation/transplantation) and exposure timing.

quiz.e: Free the ankylosed tooth or replace it.

quiz.q: A deeply placed palatal impacted maxillary canine needs surgical exposure with orthodontic traction. The technique giving the best aesthetic/periodontal outcome is:
o: Open exposure with a window left to heal
Closed exposure: bond a bracket/gold chain and reposition the flap, then apply traction
quiz.e: For deep/palatal canines a closed technique (bonded attachment under a repositioned flap) protects the soft tissue and gives a better result than an open window.
w: A — open exposure of a deep palatal tooth gives poorer aesthetics/periodontal outcome
C — extraction sacrifices a strategically important tooth unnecessarily
D — indefinite waiting risks resorption of adjacent roots and cyst formation
quiz.ty: Deep/palatal impacted canine → closed exposure (bonded chain + repositioned flap) for traction.

quiz.q: A persistent midline diastema is maintained by a thick fibrous labial frenum. Frenectomy is BEST timed:
o: After orthodontic space closure (to reduce relapse)
quiz.e: Frenectomy for a diastema is usually performed after orthodontic closure so the scar consolidates the closed space and reduces relapse.
w: A — operating first can leave scar tissue that hinders closure
C — a thick frenum can maintain a diastema
D — timing relates to the ortho plan, not an arbitrary age
quiz.ty: Diastema frenectomy is timed AFTER orthodontic space closure to reduce relapse.

pearls: Place temporary anchorage devices in attached gingiva/interradicular bone; failure is linked to mobile mucosa, inflammation and root contact.
Do a frenectomy for a persistent midline diastema AFTER orthodontic space closure to reduce relapse.
mistakes: Leaving a mesiodens that is obstructing incisor eruption.
Failing to localise the impacted tooth (SLOB/CBCT) before surgery.
Damaging adjacent roots when placing a TAD (no inter-radicular planning).
Bonding an attachment that detaches because of poor moisture control.
Not coordinating exposure timing with the orthodontist.
Attempting expansion surgically in the wrong patient (SARPE indication).
Forgetting interceptive deciduous-canine removal can guide an ectopic canine.
Operating on an ankylosed tooth expecting normal movement without addressing the ankylosis.
Overlooking autotransplantation as an option for some impactions.
Ignoring periodontal/aesthetic consequences of an open palatal exposure.
Not warning about the prolonged combined surgical-orthodontic timeline.
facts: Open exposure (a window left to heal) suits superficial/buccal teeth.
Closed exposure (bond a bracket/gold chain, reposition the flap, then apply traction) suits deep/palatal teeth and gives a better aesthetic/periodontal result.
A thick fibrous labial frenum can cause/maintain a midline diastema.
Frenectomy for a diastema is usually performed AFTER orthodontic space closure (to reduce relapse).
A mesiodens (midline supernumerary) may block or divert incisor eruption and is removed.
Temporary anchorage devices (TADs/mini-implants) provide skeletal anchorage for tooth movement.
TADs are placed in attached gingiva / interradicular bone; failure is linked to mobile mucosa, inflammation and root contact.
Corticotomy / periodontally accelerated osteogenic orthodontics (PAOO) speeds movement via the regional acceleratory phenomenon (RAP).
Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE) is used in skeletally mature patients to widen the maxilla.
Interceptive removal of a retained deciduous canine can help guide an ectopic permanent canine.
Surgical exposure timing is coordinated with the orthodontist's traction plan.
An ankylosed tooth may be surgically luxated or transplanted to allow movement.
Distraction osteogenesis can correct skeletal discrepancies alongside orthodontics.
Autotransplantation is an option for some unfavourable impacted teeth.
Exposure aims to bond an attachment for controlled orthodontic traction along the correct path.
Failure to localise the tooth (SLOB/CBCT) risks the wrong surgical approach.
Frenectomy techniques include simple excision and Z-plasty.
A supernumerary may be conical (mesiodens) or tuberculate; tuberculate ones commonly prevent eruption.
mnemonics: TAD site = attached gingiva / interradicular bone.
Mesiodens blocking eruption → remove.

study.html:
• Three properties: osteogenesis (living cells form bone — autograft only), osteoinduction (BMPs recruit cells), osteoconduction (scaffold).
  • Autograft = gold standard (all three); donor sites: iliac crest, ramus/symphysis (intraoral), calvarium, fibula (vascularised).
  • Allograft (human), xenograft (e.g., Bio-Oss, bovine), alloplast (synthetic: HA, β-TCP, bioglass) — osteoconductive ± inductive.
  • Non-vascularised grafts heal by creeping substitution; large defects need vascularised bone.

• Ladder: secondary healing → primary closure → skin graft → local flap → regional flap → free (microvascular) flap.
  • Free fibula = workhorse for mandibular reconstruction (long bone + skin paddle, segmental osteotomies).
  • Radial forearm (thin soft tissue), DCIA/iliac crest (bulky bone), anterolateral thigh; pectoralis major = pedicled regional flap.

• Free flaps need microvascular anastomosis to neck vessels; monitor flap perfusion post-op.
  • Distraction osteogenesis: gradual bone lengthening via an osteotomy + distractor (latency → activation → consolidation).
  • Prosthetic rehabilitation: obturators for maxillary defects, implants in reconstructed bone.

• Restore form and function: continuity, occlusion, oral competence, swallowing/speech, facial contour, and a foundation for dental rehabilitation.
  • Stage with the resection/oncologic plan; consider radiotherapy effects on healing.

After a segmental mandibulectomy for tumour, the surgeon needs to restore mandibular continuity with vascularised bone. The workhorse flap is the:
quiz.e: The free fibula flap supplies a long segment of vascularised bone (with a skin paddle) that can be osteotomised to shape, making it the workhorse for mandibular reconstruction.
w: A — the radial forearm flap is thin soft tissue, not the main bone flap for the mandible
C — pectoralis major is a pedicled soft-tissue flap, not vascularised bone
D — a skin graft cannot restore bony continuity
quiz.ty: Segmental mandibular reconstruction → free fibula osteocutaneous flap.

quiz.q: Which property is present in an AUTOGRAFT but NOT in an allograft or xenograft?
quiz.e: Only an autograft carries living osteogenic cells (osteogenesis); allografts/xenografts can be osteoconductive ± inductive but are not osteogenic.
w: A — osteoconduction (scaffold) is shared by other graft types
B — osteoinduction can be provided by some processed grafts/BMP
D — radiopacity is not a biological graft property
quiz.ty: Only autograft is osteogenic (living cells); all provide osteoconduction, some osteoinduction.

pearls: Climb the reconstructive ladder only as far as needed: secondary healing → primary closure → graft → local → regional → free flap.
Free flaps depend on a microvascular anastomosis — monitor flap perfusion closely after surgery.
Maxillary defects are often rehabilitated with an obturator; implants can be placed into reconstructed bone for dental rehabilitation.
mistakes: Grafting bone without a vascular bed, stability and soft-tissue cover.
Using a non-vascularised graft for a large/irradiated continuity defect.
Ignoring dental rehabilitation (implants/obturator) in the reconstructive plan.
Mismatching donor flap to the defect (bone vs soft tissue needs).
Forgetting distraction osteogenesis as an option for bone lengthening.
Not staging reconstruction with the oncology/radiotherapy timeline.
Overlooking the obturator option for maxillary defects.
Confusing osteoinduction (BMP) and osteoconduction (scaffold).
Using a split-thickness graft where a full-thickness graft is needed for quality.
Compromising margins to preserve tissue for reconstruction.
Placing a bulky flap where a thin pliable one is needed (or vice versa).
Delaying definitive reconstruction without a clear staged plan.
facts: Autograft donor sites: iliac crest, ramus/symphysis (intraoral), calvarium, fibula (vascularised).
Allograft = human donor bone; xenograft = animal (e.g., Bio-Oss/bovine); alloplast = synthetic (HA, β-TCP, bioglass).
Osteoinduction is mediated by bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs).
Non-vascularised grafts heal by creeping substitution; large/irradiated defects need vascularised bone.
Reconstructive ladder: secondary healing → primary closure → skin graft → local flap → regional flap → free (microvascular) flap.
Local flaps: advancement, rotation, transposition.
Regional (pedicled) flaps: pectoralis major, deltopectoral, temporalis.
Free (microvascular) flaps: radial forearm (thin soft tissue), free fibula (bone), DCIA/iliac crest (bulky bone), anterolateral thigh, latissimus dorsi, scapula.
The free fibula flap is the workhorse for segmental mandibular reconstruction (long bone + skin paddle, multiple osteotomies).
The radial forearm flap is favoured for soft-tissue (e.g., floor of mouth/tongue) defects.
Free flaps require a microvascular anastomosis to neck vessels.
Post-operative free-flap monitoring (colour, capillary refill, Doppler) detects vascular compromise early.
Distraction osteogenesis lengthens bone gradually: latency → activation → consolidation.
Maxillary/palatal defects are often rehabilitated with an obturator prosthesis.
Implants can be placed into reconstructed (e.g., fibula) bone for dental rehabilitation.
Skin grafts: split-thickness (larger areas, contracts more) vs full-thickness (better quality, limited size).
Reconstruction is staged with the oncologic resection plan and radiotherapy timing.
Radiotherapy impairs graft/flap healing (hypovascular bed).
Choose the lowest rung of the ladder that achieves the reconstructive goal.
Bone grafts need a vascular bed, stability and soft-tissue cover to succeed.
Composite (osteocutaneous) flaps provide bone and soft tissue together.
Guided bone regeneration uses a barrier membrane to exclude soft tissue from a bony defect.
mnemonics: Ladder: 2ry healing → primary closure → graft → local → regional → free flap.
Maxillary defect rehab = Obturator.

study.html:
• Indications: failed/non-retreatable orthograde RCT with persistent periapical pathology, blocked canal/post precluding retreatment, broken instrument beyond the apex, need for periapical biopsy, large cyst with a root involved.
  • Contraindications: untreatable/unrestorable tooth, vertical root fracture, poor access, unfavourable proximity to vital structures without control, poor periodontal support.

• Flap designs: sulcular full-thickness, submarginal (Ochsenbein-Luebke), or semilunar (limited) — broad base, on sound bone.
  • Resect ~3 mm of the apex (removes most lateral canals/apical ramifications & deltas) with a shallow bevel (minimises exposed dentinal tubules/leakage).

• Prepare a class-I cavity ~3 mm deep along the canal axis, ideally with ultrasonic retro-tips.
  • Retrograde filling material: MTA (best — biocompatible, seals well, sets in moisture), Super-EBA/IRM; amalgam is now obsolete for this.

• Hemisection (remove one root + its crown portion of a lower molar), root amputation (remove a root, keep the crown), bicuspidisation.
  • Intentional replantation: extract, seal the apex extra-orally, replant.
  • Perforation repair (MTA). Periapical curettage alone is insufficient without sealing the canal.

Removal of a root, retaining the crown.

quiz.e: Separating mandibular molar roots into two units.

quiz.q: Periapical curettage alone (without retro-seal) is:
o: Often insufficient if canal not sealed

quiz.q: Apical surgery may also serve to:

Root-end preparation is ideally done with:
quiz.e: Ultrasonic, ~3 mm along the canal axis.

A tooth with a well-placed but failed root filling has persistent apical pathology and cannot be retreated orthogradely because of a well-fitting post. The MOST appropriate surgical option is:
o: Apicectomy with root-end resection (~3 mm) and an MTA retrograde filling
Periapical curettage alone without sealing the canal
quiz.e: When orthograde retreatment is impractical (e.g., a post) and periapical disease persists, apicectomy with a 3 mm root-end resection and an MTA retro-seal is indicated.
w: A — the tooth may be saved by apical surgery rather than extracted
C — curettage without sealing the canal usually fails
D — persistent pathology should be treated, not merely observed
quiz.ty: Failed, non-retreatable RCT + persistent periapical disease → apicectomy + MTA retrograde seal (resect ~3 mm).

quiz.q: Apical surgery is being considered, but examination/imaging reveals a vertical root fracture. The correct decision is:

Place a retrograde MTA filling anyway
quiz.e: A vertical root fracture has a hopeless prognosis and contraindicates apical surgery; the tooth is extracted.
w: A — apicectomy will not address a fractured root
C — a retro-seal does not fix a fractured root
D — curettage does not treat the fracture
quiz.ty: Vertical root fracture contraindicates apical surgery → extract.

pearls: MTA is the modern retrograde filling material of choice (biocompatible, seals well, sets in moisture); amalgam is obsolete for this.
A vertical root fracture is a contraindication to apical surgery — the tooth should be extracted.
Periapical curettage alone, without sealing the canal, is usually insufficient.
mistakes: Relying on periapical curettage without sealing the canal apically.
Operating without first considering orthograde retreatment.
Not resecting enough apex (leaving apical ramifications).
Ignoring proximity to the IAN canal/sinus/mental foramen.
Failing to achieve haemostasis before placing the retrograde filling.
Poor flap design compromising the blood supply/healing.
Not sending a periapical lesion for histology when indicated.
Performing apical surgery on an unrestorable tooth.
Forgetting magnification/ultrasonic tips that improve outcomes.
Choosing hemisection/amputation without sound endodontic and periodontal prognosis.
Misjudging case selection (poor periodontal support/access).
facts: Resect about 3 mm of the apex (removes most lateral canals and apical ramifications/deltas).
Use a SHALLOW bevel to minimise exposed dentinal tubules and apical leakage.
Prepare a root-end cavity ~3 mm deep along the canal axis, ideally with ultrasonic retro-tips.
Retrograde filling material of choice = MTA (biocompatible, seals well, sets in moisture).
Other retro-fillings: Super-EBA, IRM; amalgam is now obsolete.
Periapical curettage alone (without sealing the canal) is usually insufficient.
Apical surgery can provide a tissue diagnosis (biopsy) of a periapical lesion.
Hemisection = removal of one root plus its crown portion (mandibular molars).
Root amputation = removal of a root while retaining the crown.
Bicuspidisation = separating the roots of a mandibular molar into two units.
Intentional replantation = extract, seal the apex extra-orally, then replant.
Perforation repair is performed with MTA.
Magnification (loupes/microscope) and ultrasonic tips improve modern apical (endodontic micro-) surgery success.
Success depends on a complete apical seal, removal of the pathology and good case selection.
Achieve haemostasis in the bony crypt before placing the retrograde filling.
Guided tissue regeneration may aid healing of large through-and-through periapical defects.
Always consider orthograde retreatment before resorting to apical surgery.
A vertical root fracture has a hopeless prognosis → extraction, not apicectomy.
Anatomical proximity (IAN canal, maxillary sinus, mental foramen) must be assessed before apical surgery.
MTA's setting in a moist field makes it ideal for a wet surgical crypt.
mnemonics: Contraindication = Vertical Root Fracture.
Hemisection (root+crown portion) vs Root amputation (root only, keep crown).

study.html:
The 8 cranial (braincase) bones

  • Frontal (1)
  • Parietal (2 — paired)
  • Occipital (1)
  • Temporal (2 — paired)
  • Sphenoid (1)
  • Ethmoid (1)
Note: Only the parietal and temporal bones are paired; the rest are single midline bones.

The 14 facial bones

  • Zygomatic (2)
  • Maxilla (2)
  • Nasal (2)
  • Lacrimal (2)
  • Palatine (2)
  • Inferior nasal concha (2)
  • Vomer (1)
  • Mandible (1)
Note: Only the vomer and mandible are single; all others are paired.

Bones forming the anterior cranial fossa

  • Orbital plates of the frontal bone
  • Cribriform plate of the ethmoid
  • Lesser wings + part of the body of the sphenoid

Bones forming the middle cranial fossa

  • Body & greater wings of the sphenoid
  • Squamous & petrous parts of the temporal bones

Bones forming the posterior cranial fossa

  • Occipital bone
  • Petrous & mastoid parts of the temporal bones
  • Part of the body of the sphenoid (clivus)

StructureFunction
Cranial fossae (stepped floor)Cradle the brain in three descending tiers, each shaped to its lobe, limiting bulk displacement.
DiploëProvides a lightweight yet strong sandwich construction and houses red marrow + diploic venous channels.
ForaminaConduits that allow nerves and vessels to pass between the cranial cavity and the face, orbit, nose and neck.
Pterion regionThin lateral wall overlying the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery — a surgical/traumatic landmark.
Crista galli (ethmoid)Bony ridge anchoring the falx cerebri (anterior attachment of the dural fold).

Inner table vs Outer table: The inner table is thinner and more brittle, so it may fracture even when the outer table looks intact — important in head trauma.

Vault ossification vs Base ossification: Vault bones ossify in MEMBRANE (intramembranous); base bones ossify in CARTILAGE (endochondral).

Foramen ovale (V3) vs Foramen rotundum (V2): Ovale transmits the mandibular nerve + lesser petrosal; rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve. Mnemonic 'Standing Room Only' = Sup. orbital fissure → Rotundum → Ovale carry V1, V2, V3.

1. The middle meningeal artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.
  2. The maxillary nerve (V2) leaves the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum.
  3. The mandibular nerve (V3) leaves through the foramen ovale.
  4. The internal acoustic meatus transmits the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves.
  5. The hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

Anterior fossa — precise foramina (anterior → posterior)

  • Foramen cecum — emissary vein to superior sagittal sinus
  • Cribriform plate perforations — olfactory nerve filaments (CN I)
  • Anterior ethmoidal foramen — anterior ethmoidal n. & vessels
  • Posterior ethmoidal foramen — posterior ethmoidal n. & vessels

Middle fossa — precise foramina (medial → lateral, each side)

  • Optic canal — CN II + ophthalmic artery
  • Superior orbital fissure — CN III, IV, V1, VI + superior ophthalmic vein
  • Foramen rotundum — CN V2 (maxillary)
  • Foramen ovale — CN V3 (mandibular) + lesser petrosal n. + accessory meningeal a.
  • Foramen spinosum — middle meningeal artery & vein + meningeal branch of V3
  • Foramen lacerum — internal carotid a. crosses its superior aspect; nothing fully traverses it

Posterior fossa — precise foramina

  • Internal acoustic meatus — CN VII, CN VIII, labyrinthine artery
  • Jugular foramen — CN IX, X, XI; inferior petrosal & sigmoid sinuses → internal jugular vein
  • Hypoglossal canal — CN XII
  • Condylar canal — emissary vein
  • Foramen magnum — medulla/spinal cord junction, vertebral arteries, spinal roots of CN XI, dural veins

Layers of the calvaria (scalp-side → brain-side)

  • Outer table of compact bone
  • Diploë (cancellous bone with red marrow & diploic veins)
  • Inner table of compact bone (thinner, more brittle)

Sphenoid bone — its named parts

  • Body (contains sphenoid sinus + sella turcica)
  • Greater wings (×2)
  • Lesser wings (×2)
  • Pterygoid processes (×2 — medial & lateral plates)

StructureFunction
Sella turcica (sphenoid body)Houses the pituitary gland; the diaphragma sellae roofs it and is pierced by the infundibulum.
Petrous temporal boneHouses the internal ear; its sharp crest separates the middle from the posterior cranial fossa and supports the tentorium cerebelli & superior petrosal sinus.
Clivus (basisphenoid + basiocciput)Sloping surface supporting the pons & medulla; related to the basilar venous plexus.
Grooves on the inner tableMark the courses of the middle meningeal vessels and the dural venous sinuses (transverse, sigmoid, superior sagittal).
Diploic & emissary veinsValveless channels connecting scalp veins ↔ dural sinuses — a route for extracranial infection to reach the meninges.

Superior orbital fissure vs Optic canal: The fissure transmits CN III, IV, V1, VI + superior ophthalmic vein; the optic canal transmits ONLY CN II + ophthalmic artery. They are separated by the optic strut of the lesser wing.

Foramen spinosum vs Foramen ovale: Spinosum (postero-lateral) transmits the middle meningeal artery; ovale (antero-medial to it) transmits V3. Spinosum lies just posterolateral to ovale — a constant relationship.

Foramen lacerum vs Carotid canal: Nothing passes vertically through lacerum (its lower end is cartilage-filled in life); the internal carotid artery enters the carotid canal and runs ACROSS the upper part of lacerum, not through it.

Pterion vs Asterion: Pterion = H-shaped junction (frontal, parietal, sphenoid greater wing, temporal squama) overlying the anterior middle meningeal artery. Asterion = junction of parietal, occipital & temporal (mastoid) overlying the transverse–sigmoid sinus junction.

1. The anterior division of the middle meningeal artery grooves the inner table at the pterion, ~4 cm above the midpoint of the zygomatic arch — the classic site of extradural haemorrhage.
  2. The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI plus the sigmoid sinus continuing as the internal jugular vein; the inferior petrosal sinus enters its anteromedial part.
  3. The lesser petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic from CN IX, destined for the otic ganglion) leaves the middle fossa through the foramen ovale.
  4. The greater petrosal nerve (from CN VII) runs forward on the floor of the middle fossa toward the foramen lacerum to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal.
  5. The optic canal lies within the lesser wing of the sphenoid and transmits CN II together with the ophthalmic artery (a branch of the internal carotid).

scenarios.title: The Clear Nasal Drip After Trauma
scenarios.vignette: A 24-year-old man is struck across the forehead in a fall. He has nosebleeds and a persistent clear, watery discharge from one nostril that tests positive for glucose.
scenarios.q: Where is the fracture, and which structures are torn?
scenarios.a: An anterior cranial fossa fracture through the CRIBRIFORM PLATE of the ethmoid. The fracture tears the adherent meninges (and mucoperiosteum), allowing cerebrospinal fluid to leak into the nose (CSF rhinorrhoea) alongside bleeding. Glucose-positive nasal fluid confirms CSF.
pearls: Cribriform plate fracture → CSF rhinorrhoea
Risk of ascending meningitis along the olfactory nerve sheaths
Anosmia may follow if olfactory filaments are sheared

scenarios.title: The Lucid Interval
scenarios.vignette: A young man is struck on the temple with a bat. After a brief dazed moment he recovers fully ('lucid interval'), then over the next hour develops a worsening headache, drowsiness and weakness of the opposite side of the body. A skull film shows a fracture line crossing the pterion.
scenarios.q: What is the diagnosis, the precise vessel, and why the lucid interval?
scenarios.a: Extradural (epidural) haemorrhage from the ANTERIOR DIVISION of the MIDDLE MENINGEAL ARTERY, torn where it grooves the inner table at the pterion. The arterial blood slowly strips the dura from the skull; the lucid interval reflects the time taken for the expanding haematoma to raise intracranial pressure and compress the underlying motor cortex, producing contralateral weakness.
pearls: Pterion overlies the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery
Arterial bleed → deterioration after a lucid interval
Contralateral signs from pressure on the precentral gyrus
Burr hole placed ~4 cm above the zygomatic arch midpoint

quiz.q: How many bones form the cranium (braincase), excluding the facial skeleton?
quiz.e: 8 cranial bones: frontal (1), parietal (2), occipital (1), temporal (2), sphenoid (1), ethmoid (1).

quiz.q: Which cranial fossa houses the cerebellum?
quiz.e: The posterior cranial fossa holds the cerebellum, pons and medulla.

quiz.q: The thinnest part of the lateral wall of the skull is the:
quiz.e: The pterion is the thinnest part of the side of the skull and overlies the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery.

quiz.q: Which suture lies between the two parietal bones?
quiz.e: The sagittal suture runs in the midline between the two parietal bones.

quiz.q: The middle meningeal artery enters the cranial cavity through the:
quiz.e: The middle meningeal artery (a branch of the maxillary artery) enters through the foramen spinosum.

quiz.q: Which structures pass through the foramen ovale?
quiz.e: Foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3) and the lesser petrosal nerve.

quiz.q: The maxillary nerve (V2) leaves the middle cranial fossa via the:
quiz.e: V2 exits through the foramen rotundum; V1 uses the superior orbital fissure and V3 the foramen ovale.

quiz.q: The internal acoustic meatus transmits which two cranial nerves?
quiz.e: The facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves traverse the internal acoustic meatus with the labyrinthine artery.

quiz.q: Vault bones of the skull develop by which type of ossification?
quiz.e: Vault bones ossify in membrane (intramembranous); base bones ossify in cartilage (endochondral).

quiz.q: A linear fracture crossing the pterion most endangers the:
o: Anterior division of the middle meningeal artery
quiz.e: The pterion overlies the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery — the classic source of extradural haemorrhage.

quiz.q: Which nerve destined for the otic ganglion exits the skull through the foramen ovale alongside V3?
quiz.e: The lesser petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic from CN IX) passes through the foramen ovale to reach the otic ganglion.

quiz.q: The optic canal lies within which part of the sphenoid and transmits the ophthalmic artery with CN II?
quiz.e: The optic canal lies within the lesser wing of the sphenoid and transmits CN II plus the ophthalmic artery.

quiz.q: The asterion overlies the junction of which two dural venous sinuses?
quiz.e: The asterion (parietal–occipital–mastoid junction) overlies the transverse–sigmoid sinus junction — a neurosurgical landmark.

quiz.q: Regarding the foramen lacerum, which statement is correct?
o: The mandibular nerve passes vertically through it
The internal carotid artery runs across its superior surface
It transmits the middle meningeal artery
quiz.e: In life the foramen lacerum is closed inferiorly by cartilage; the internal carotid artery crosses its upper aspect rather than passing fully through it.

flashcards.a: Anterior division of the middle meningeal artery
CN VII + CN VIII + labyrinthine artery
CN IX, X, XI; sigmoid sinus → internal jugular vein

flashcards.q: Number of cranial vs facial bones?
Which skull table is thinner & more brittle?

flashcards.a: Superior orbital fissure → Rotundum → Ovale carry V1, V2, V3

pearls: Optic canal = CN II + ophthalmic artery ONLY. Everything else orbital goes through the superior orbital fissure.
Inner table is the brittle one — fractures hide under an intact outer table.
mistakes: Myth: The middle meningeal artery enters through the foramen ovale. Truth: It enters through the foramen SPINOSUM. The foramen ovale transmits V3.
Myth: The internal carotid artery passes straight up through the foramen lacerum. Truth: It runs ACROSS the superior surface of the lacerum; the foramen's lower end is closed by cartilage in life.
Myth: All skull bones ossify in cartilage. Truth: Only the cranial BASE ossifies in cartilage; the VAULT ossifies in membrane.

study.html:
Sensory/Motor/Both — mnemonic

  • 'Some Say Marry Money But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More'
  • S/M letters give: Sensory(I,II,VIII), Motor(III,IV,VI,XI,XII), Both(V,VII,IX,X)

Nerves carrying parasympathetic fibres (4)

  • III → ciliary ganglion (pupil & lens)
  • VII → pterygopalatine & submandibular ganglia (tears & saliva)
  • IX → otic ganglion (parotid saliva)
  • X → thoracic & abdominal viscera

The four parasympathetic ganglia of the head

  • Ciliary ganglion (CN III)
  • Pterygopalatine ganglion (CN VII)
  • Submandibular ganglion (CN VII)
  • Otic ganglion (CN IX)

Nerves exiting via the jugular foramen

  • IX Glossopharyngeal
  • X Vagus
  • XI Accessory

Nerves entering the orbit via superior orbital fissure

  • III Oculomotor
  • IV Trochlear
  • V1 Ophthalmic branches
  • VI Abducent

StructureFunction
CN III OculomotorMoves most eye muscles, raises the upper lid, constricts the pupil and accommodates the lens.
CN IV TrochlearSupplies superior oblique → turns the eye down and out.
CN VI AbducentSupplies lateral rectus → abducts the eye.
CN V TrigeminalSensation of the whole face + motor to the muscles of mastication.
CN VII FacialMuscles of facial expression, taste to the anterior tongue, and secretion of tears and saliva.
CN XI AccessorySupplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.

CN V (trigeminal) vs CN VII (facial): Trigeminal = SENSATION of the face + motor to mastication. Facial = MOVEMENT of facial expression + taste & glands. The face 'feels' with V and 'moves' with VII.

UMN facial lesion vs LMN facial lesion: Upper motor neuron lesions SPARE the forehead (bilateral cortical supply); lower motor neuron lesions (Bell's palsy) paralyse the WHOLE half of the face including the forehead.

CN IX vs CN X: Both supply the pharynx, but IX is mainly SENSORY there (gag afferent) plus motor to stylopharyngeus, while X is mainly MOTOR (gag efferent) to almost all pharyngeal & laryngeal muscles.

1. The trochlear nerve (IV) supplies the superior oblique muscle.
  2. The abducent nerve (VI) supplies the lateral rectus muscle.
  3. The accessory nerve (XI) supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
  4. Cranial nerves IX, X and XI all leave the skull through the jugular foramen.

Functional components of CN VII (facial)

  • Branchial motor → muscles of facial expression, stapedius, stylohyoid, posterior digastric
  • Parasympathetic → lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual, nasal & palatine glands
  • Special sensory (taste) → anterior two-thirds of the tongue (via chorda tympani)
  • General sensory → small area of external ear

Functional components of CN IX (glossopharyngeal)

  • Branchial motor → stylopharyngeus (only muscle)
  • Parasympathetic → parotid gland (via otic ganglion)
  • Visceral sensory → carotid sinus & body
  • General sensory → posterior third of tongue, pharynx, middle ear, auditory tube
  • Special sensory (taste) → posterior third of tongue

Functional components of CN X (vagus)

  • Branchial motor → pharynx, larynx, palate (except stylopharyngeus & tensor veli palatini)
  • Parasympathetic → thoracic & abdominal viscera to the splenic flexure
  • Visceral sensory → pharynx, larynx, viscera, aortic bodies
  • General sensory → external ear, dura of posterior fossa
  • Special sensory (taste) → epiglottis & root of tongue

The three branches of the trigeminal nerve & their exits

  • V1 Ophthalmic → superior orbital fissure (sensory only)
  • V2 Maxillary → foramen rotundum (sensory only)
  • V3 Mandibular → foramen ovale (sensory + the entire motor root)

StructureFunction
CN III parasympatheticEdinger–Westphal nucleus → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae (miosis) and ciliary muscle (accommodation).
CN VII greater petrosalParasympathetic via pterygopalatine ganglion → lacrimal gland and the mucous glands of nose and palate.
CN IX tympanic branch (Jacobson)Forms the lesser petrosal nerve → otic ganglion → secretomotor to the parotid via the auriculotemporal nerve.
CN X recurrent laryngealMotor to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid; sensory to the larynx below the vocal folds.
CN XI cranial rootJoins the vagus to supply the palate, pharynx and larynx; the spinal root supplies SCM and trapezius.

CN III palsy vs Horner's syndrome: CN III palsy → ptosis + a DILATED 'down-and-out' pupil. Horner's (sympathetic loss) → partial ptosis + a CONSTRICTED pupil. Opposite pupils.

Cricothyroid (external laryngeal) vs Other intrinsic laryngeal muscles (recurrent laryngeal): All intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of X except cricothyroid, supplied by the external laryngeal branch.

Hypoglossal (XII) lesion vs Vagus (X) palatal lesion: In XII lesions the protruded tongue deviates TOWARD the lesion; in X lesions the uvula deviates AWAY from the lesion.

Spinal root of XI vs Cranial root of XI: The spinal root supplies SCM & trapezius; the cranial root joins the vagus and is functionally part of it (palate/pharynx/larynx).

1. The only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) is stylopharyngeus.
  2. The lesser petrosal nerve carries IX's parasympathetic fibres to the otic ganglion for the parotid gland.
  3. The chorda tympani (a branch of VII) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
  4. The trigeminal motor root travels only with V3 and supplies the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid, anterior digastric, tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini.
  5. The dorsal nucleus of the vagus provides parasympathetic supply to thoracic and abdominal viscera down to the left colic (splenic) flexure.
