scenarios.title: The Deviating Tongue
scenarios.vignette: Following a stab wound to the neck, a patient is asked to stick out the tongue. It deviates to the right; over weeks the right half becomes wrinkled and wasted.
scenarios.q: Which nerve is injured and why does the tongue point that way?
scenarios.a: The RIGHT hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). The right genioglossus is paralysed, so the intact left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side — the tip deviates TOWARD the lesion. Chronic denervation produces wasting and wrinkling of that half.
pearls: Tongue points toward the side of the XII lesion
Genioglossus is the protruding muscle
XII supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus

scenarios.title: Hoarseness and a Bovine Cough
scenarios.vignette: A patient with a left lung apex tumour develops a hoarse voice and a weak, non-explosive ('bovine') cough. Laryngoscopy shows a left vocal cord fixed near the midline.
scenarios.q: Which nerve is involved and why is the left side affected by a chest lesion?
scenarios.a: The left RECURRENT LARYNGEAL NERVE, a branch of the vagus (X). On the left it loops under the arch of the aorta, so a mediastinal/lung-apex mass can compress it. Loss of intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid) leaves the cord paramedian, causing hoarseness and an ineffective cough.
pearls: Left recurrent laryngeal loops under the aortic arch
Supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid
Mediastinal disease → left cord palsy

quiz.q: Which cranial nerves are purely sensory?
quiz.e: Olfactory (I), Optic (II) and Vestibulocochlear (VIII) are purely sensory.

quiz.q: The vagus nerve is which numbered cranial nerve?
Which cranial nerve moves the tongue?
quiz.e: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) supplies the tongue muscles.

quiz.q: How many cranial nerves are classed as mixed?
quiz.e: Four are mixed: V, VII, IX and X.

quiz.q: The superior oblique muscle is supplied by:
quiz.e: The trochlear nerve (IV) supplies superior oblique.

quiz.q: Cranial nerves IX, X and XI exit the skull through the:
quiz.e: All three pass through the jugular foramen.

quiz.q: A lower motor neuron facial nerve lesion affects the forehead because:
o: The forehead has bilateral cortical supply only in UMN lesions
The whole half of the face is paralysed in LMN lesions
The forehead is supplied by the trigeminal
quiz.e: An LMN (Bell's) lesion paralyses the entire half of the face; UMN lesions spare the forehead.

quiz.q: Which cranial nerve carries parasympathetic fibres to the parotid gland?
quiz.e: CN IX, via the lesser petrosal nerve and otic ganglion, supplies the parotid.

quiz.q: The only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve is:
quiz.e: Stylopharyngeus is the sole muscle supplied by CN IX.

quiz.q: The trigeminal motor root travels exclusively with which division?
quiz.e: The motor root joins V3 to supply the muscles of mastication and others.

quiz.q: In a unilateral hypoglossal lesion the protruded tongue deviates:
quiz.e: It deviates toward the lesion side because the contralateral genioglossus is unopposed.

quiz.q: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by a branch of which nerve?
quiz.e: The chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (VII), carries this taste.

quiz.q: Which cranial nerve's dorsal nucleus supplies abdominal viscera to the splenic flexure?
quiz.e: The vagus (X) supplies foregut and midgut derivatives to the left colic (splenic) flexure.

flashcards.q: Only muscle supplied by CN IX?

pearls: Stylopharyngeus is the ONLY muscle of CN IX.
Tongue deviates TOWARD an XII lesion; uvula deviates AWAY from an X lesion.
Parotid = glossopharyngeal (otic ganglion). Submandibular/sublingual = facial (chorda tympani).
mistakes: Myth: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies several pharyngeal muscles. Truth: It supplies only ONE muscle — stylopharyngeus. The rest are by the vagus (pharyngeal plexus).
Myth: In a hypoglossal lesion the tongue deviates away from the lesion. Truth: It deviates TOWARD the lesion side.

Myth: Parasympathetic fibres to the parotid travel in the facial nerve. Truth: They travel in the GLOSSOPHARYNGEAL nerve (IX) via the otic ganglion. The facial nerve serves the submandibular & sublingual glands.

study.html:
The two layers of the dura mater

  • Endosteal layer (periosteum of the inner skull)
  • Meningeal layer (the true dura, continuous with spinal dura)
Note: The two layers separate in places to enclose the dural venous sinuses.

The four dural infoldings (septa)

  • Falx cerebri (between the cerebral hemispheres)
  • Tentorium cerebelli (over the cerebellum)
  • Falx cerebelli (between cerebellar hemispheres)
  • Diaphragma sellae (roof over the pituitary)

The meningeal spaces

  • Extradural — potential space between skull and dura
  • Subdural — potential space between dura and arachnoid
  • Subarachnoid — true CSF-filled space between arachnoid and pia

Contents of the cavernous sinus

  • In the lateral wall: CN III, IV, V1, V2
  • Passing through the blood: internal carotid artery + CN VI

StructureFunction
Dural septaSubdivide the cranial cavity and restrict rotatory displacement of the brain.
Dural venous sinusesEndothelial-lined channels between dural layers draining venous blood and CSF toward the internal jugular vein.
Arachnoid granulationsProject into the superior sagittal sinus to return CSF to the venous blood.
Subarachnoid spaceCushions the brain with CSF and transmits the cerebral vessels and cranial nerve roots.

Extradural haemorrhage vs Subdural haemorrhage: Extradural is ARTERIAL (middle meningeal artery), rapid, follows a pterion fracture. Subdural is VENOUS (bridging veins), slower, and may be chronic.

Endosteal dura vs Meningeal dura: The endosteal layer is the inner periosteum and stops at the foramen magnum; the meningeal layer is the true dura that continues into the spinal canal and forms the septa.

Falx cerebri vs Tentorium cerebelli: The falx is a vertical sheet between the hemispheres; the tentorium is a horizontal tent over the cerebellum separating it from the occipital lobes.

1. The dura mater has two layers: an outer endosteal and an inner meningeal layer.
  2. The middle meningeal artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.
  3. Arachnoid granulations return cerebrospinal fluid to the superior sagittal sinus.
  4. The cavernous sinus communicates with the facial vein through the ophthalmic veins.

Dural venous sinus drainage chain

  • Superior sagittal sinus → confluence → right transverse sinus
  • Inferior sagittal sinus → straight sinus → left transverse sinus
  • Transverse → sigmoid → internal jugular vein
  • Cavernous → superior & inferior petrosal sinuses → transverse / IJV

Sources of each haemorrhage type

  • Extradural: anterior division of the middle meningeal artery
  • Subdural: superior cerebral (bridging) veins at the sagittal sinus
  • Subarachnoid: ruptured berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis
  • Intracerebral: lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery

Cavernous sinus connections (clinical routes)

  • Anteriorly: superior & inferior ophthalmic veins (from the facial vein)
  • Posteriorly: petrosal sinuses
  • Via emissary veins: pterygoid venous plexus
  • Across the midline: intercavernous sinuses

StructureFunction
Middle meningeal arteryChief blood supply to the dura; its anterior branch grooves the pterion and is the source of extradural haemorrhage.
Cavernous sinusReceives ophthalmic & cerebral veins and transmits the ICA and CN VI; a hub linking facial veins to the dural sinuses.
Emissary veinsValveless connections between scalp veins and dural sinuses — a route for extracranial infection to reach the meninges.
Tentorium cerebelliSeparates the cerebrum from the cerebellum; its free edge is where the midbrain and CN III may be compressed (uncal herniation).

Cavernous sinus wall (III, IV, V1, V2) vs Cavernous sinus lumen (ICA + VI): Four nerves sit in the lateral wall; only the abducent nerve and the internal carotid artery pass through the blood itself — so VI is affected early in cavernous sinus pathology.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage vs Intracerebral haemorrhage: Subarachnoid (ruptured berry aneurysm) → sudden thunderclap headache + neck stiffness + bloody CSF. Intracerebral (lenticulostriate vessel) → focal deficit such as contralateral hemiplegia from internal capsule damage.

Superior sagittal sinus drainage vs Straight sinus drainage: The superior sagittal sinus usually drains to the RIGHT transverse sinus; the straight sinus drains to the LEFT — a frequently tested asymmetry.

1. Extradural haemorrhage arises from the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery at the pterion.
  2. Subdural haemorrhage arises from the superior cerebral veins where they enter the superior sagittal sinus.
  3. The abducent nerve (CN VI) runs through the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery, making it vulnerable early in cavernous sinus thrombosis.
  4. A ruptured berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis is the usual cause of spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  5. The straight sinus drains the great cerebral vein and inferior sagittal sinus into the left transverse sinus.

TypeBleeding sourceKey clinical clue
ExtraduralAnterior division, middle meningeal a.Lucid interval, then deterioration
SubduralSuperior cerebral (bridging) veinsSlow onset; elderly/alcoholic; may be chronic
SubarachnoidRuptured berry aneurysmSudden 'worst-ever' headache, neck stiffness
IntracerebralLenticulostriate branch of MCAFocal deficit (e.g. hemiplegia)

SinusLocationDrains into
Superior sagittalUpper border of falx cerebriRight transverse sinus
Inferior sagittalFree lower border of falxStraight sinus
StraightFalx–tentorium junctionLeft transverse sinus
TransverseAttached margin of tentoriumSigmoid sinus
SigmoidBehind the mastoid antrumInternal jugular vein
CavernousBeside the body of the sphenoidPetrosal sinuses → IJV

LayerFeature
Dura materTough outer layer; two layers (periosteal + meningeal) that split to enclose venous sinuses; forms folds (falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli).
Arachnoid materThin avascular layer; subarachnoid space beneath it holds CSF; arachnoid granulations return CSF to the venous sinuses.
Pia materDelicate layer adherent to the brain surface, following every gyrus and sulcus.

study.h: Dural folds & venous sinuses — more on the brain
study.html:
• Falx cerebri — sickle-shaped midline fold between the two cerebral hemispheres; encloses the superior sagittal sinus (top) and inferior sagittal sinus (free edge).
  • Tentorium cerebelli — tent over the cerebellum separating it from the occipital lobes; its free edge bounds the tentorial notch through which the midbrain passes.
  • Cavernous sinus — beside the sphenoid body; in its wall: CN III, IV, V1, V2; passing through it: ICA and CN VI (VI is the most medial and most at risk).
  • Confluence of sinuses → transverse → sigmoid → internal jugular vein — the main venous outflow.
⭐ Tentorial herniation: a supratentorial mass pushes the uncus through the tentorial notch, compressing CN III (fixed dilated pupil) and the midbrain.

TypeVesselCT shape
ExtraduralMiddle meningeal artery (pterion)Biconvex / lens (lentiform), does not cross sutures
SubduralBridging cerebral veinsCrescent (concave), crosses sutures
SubarachnoidBerry aneurysm (circle of Willis)Blood in sulci/cisterns; 'thunderclap' headache

scenarios.title: The Lucid Interval
scenarios.vignette: A man is struck on the temple, briefly loses consciousness, recovers, then an hour later becomes drowsy with weakness of the opposite limbs. A fracture crosses the pterion.
scenarios.q: What is bleeding, and why the delay?
scenarios.a: An EXTRADURAL haemorrhage from the anterior division of the middle meningeal artery torn at the pterion. The lucid interval is the time the arterial haematoma takes to enlarge and raise intracranial pressure, after which it compresses the motor cortex producing contralateral weakness.
pearls: Pterion overlies the anterior middle meningeal artery
Arterial bleed → deterioration after a lucid interval
Contralateral signs from cortical compression

scenarios.title: The Painful Red Eye with Fever
scenarios.vignette: Following an infected boil on the upper lip, a patient develops a swollen, protruding eye, drooping lid, fever and an inability to abduct that eye.
scenarios.q: What is the diagnosis and the anatomical route?
scenarios.a: CAVERNOUS SINUS THROMBOSIS. Infection from the danger area of the face passed via the valveless facial vein → superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus. Involvement of the structures in the sinus explains the signs: proptosis and lid swelling (venous congestion), and lateral rectus palsy from compression of the abducent nerve (CN VI), which lies within the sinus lumen.
pearls: Facial vein is valveless → retrograde spread
CN VI is affected first (lies in the sinus, not the wall)
Danger area = nose, upper lip, medial eye

scenarios.title: Lucid Interval After a Temple Blow
scenarios.vignette: A boxer is struck on the temple, briefly dazed, then recovers and chats normally. An hour later he becomes drowsy with a worsening headache and weakness of the opposite arm. CT shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) bleed.
scenarios.q: Type of haemorrhage and the vessel?
scenarios.a: Extradural (epidural) haemorrhage from the MIDDLE MENINGEAL ARTERY torn at the pterion. Arterial blood strips the dura off the skull; the lens shape reflects the firm dural attachment at sutures. The 'lucid interval' is the time before the expanding clot raises intracranial pressure and compresses the motor cortex (contralateral weakness).
pearls: Biconvex/lens shape, does not cross sutures
Middle meningeal artery at the pterion
Lucid interval then deterioration

scenarios.title: The Slowly Confused Elderly Man
scenarios.vignette: An elderly man on warfarin becomes gradually confused and unsteady over three weeks after a minor fall he barely remembers. CT shows a crescent-shaped collection over the hemisphere that crosses suture lines.
scenarios.q: Diagnosis and the bleeding source?
scenarios.a: Chronic subdural haematoma from torn BRIDGING (cerebral) VEINS crossing from the cortex to the dural sinuses. Brain atrophy in the elderly stretches these veins, so trivial trauma tears them; the venous, low-pressure bleed accumulates slowly. The crescent shape crosses sutures because it is deep to the dura (subdural), unlike an extradural.
pearls: Crescent shape, crosses sutures
Bridging veins; elderly, anticoagulated
Slow, fluctuating course

scenarios.title: The Worst Headache of My Life
scenarios.vignette: A 45-year-old woman collapses with a sudden 'thunderclap' headache, neck stiffness and photophobia. CT shows blood in the basal cisterns.
scenarios.q: Type of haemorrhage and the usual cause?
scenarios.a: Subarachnoid haemorrhage, usually from a ruptured BERRY (saccular) ANEURYSM of the circle of Willis (commonly at the anterior communicating or posterior communicating artery). Blood spreads in the CSF of the subarachnoid space, irritating the meninges (neck stiffness, photophobia). A CT-negative but strongly suspected case needs a lumbar puncture looking for xanthochromia.
pearls: Thunderclap headache + meningism
Berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis
Xanthochromia on LP if CT is negative

scenarios.title: The Fixed Dilated Pupil
scenarios.vignette: A patient with a large traumatic clot becomes deeply drowsy; the right pupil is now wide and unreactive, and the left limbs are weak.
scenarios.q: What herniation is occurring and which nerve is compressed?
scenarios.a: Uncal (transtentorial) herniation: the expanding supratentorial mass pushes the medial temporal lobe (uncus) through the tentorial notch. This compresses the ipsilateral CN III (parasympathetic fibres first → fixed dilated pupil) and the midbrain/cerebral peduncle (contralateral weakness). It is a neurosurgical emergency.
pearls: Uncus herniates through the tentorial notch
CN III compressed → fixed dilated pupil (same side)
Midbrain compression → contralateral weakness

scenarios.title: Clear Fluid From the Nose After a Frontal Blow
scenarios.vignette: After a blow to the forehead a patient has a persistent clear, glucose-positive watery drip from one nostril and has lost the sense of smell.
scenarios.q: Where is the fracture and which meningeal/neural structures are torn?
scenarios.a: Fracture of the CRIBRIFORM PLATE of the ethmoid (anterior cranial fossa). It tears the adherent dura/arachnoid → CSF rhinorrhoea (glucose-positive), and shears the olfactory nerve filaments → anosmia. There is a risk of ascending meningitis along the torn meningeal sheaths.
pearls: Cribriform plate fracture → CSF rhinorrhoea + anosmia
Glucose-positive fluid confirms CSF
Risk of ascending meningitis

quiz.q: How many layers of meninges cover the brain?
quiz.e: Three: dura, arachnoid and pia mater.

quiz.q: Cerebrospinal fluid is found in which space?
quiz.e: CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia.

quiz.q: Which haemorrhage classically follows a blow to the pterion?
quiz.e: Extradural haemorrhage from the middle meningeal artery.

quiz.q: The dura mater consists of which two layers?
quiz.e: An outer endosteal (periosteal) layer and an inner meningeal layer.

quiz.q: Subdural haemorrhage results from tearing of:
quiz.e: Bridging veins entering the superior sagittal sinus tear, producing a venous subdural bleed.

quiz.q: Which dural fold lies between the two cerebral hemispheres?
quiz.e: The falx cerebri is the vertical midline fold between the hemispheres.

quiz.q: Arachnoid granulations return CSF to which sinus?
quiz.e: They project into the superior sagittal sinus.

quiz.q: Which structures lie in the LATERAL WALL of the cavernous sinus?
quiz.e: The wall contains III, IV, V1 and V2; the ICA and CN VI pass through the lumen.

quiz.q: Which cranial nerve is affected earliest in cavernous sinus thrombosis?
quiz.e: CN VI lies free within the sinus lumen beside the ICA, so it is compressed first.

quiz.q: The straight sinus typically drains into the:
quiz.e: The straight sinus usually drains into the left transverse sinus.

quiz.q: Spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage is most often due to:
o: Ruptured berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis
quiz.e: A ruptured congenital berry aneurysm on the circle of Willis is the classic cause.

flashcards.a: Falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, falx cerebelli, diaphragma sellae

flashcards.q: Extradural haemorrhage — vessel and CT shape?
flashcards.a: Middle meningeal artery; biconvex/lens, does not cross sutures.

flashcards.q: Subdural haemorrhage — vessel and CT shape?
flashcards.a: Bridging cerebral veins; crescent, crosses sutures.
Ruptured berry aneurysm of the circle of Willis.

flashcards.q: What passes through the cavernous sinus (not its wall)?
flashcards.a: Internal carotid artery and CN VI.

flashcards.q: Which CN are in the wall of the cavernous sinus?
Uncal herniation compresses which nerve first?
Falx cerebri encloses which sinus at its upper margin?

pearls: Facial vein is valveless → danger-area infection can reach the cavernous sinus.
Lens = extradural (artery, no suture crossing); crescent = subdural (vein, crosses sutures); cisternal = subarachnoid (aneurysm).
Cavernous sinus wall = III, IV, V1, V2; lumen = ICA + VI (VI most vulnerable).
Fixed dilated pupil + drowsiness = uncal herniation compressing CN III — call neurosurgery.
mistakes: Myth: The subdural space is a real fluid-filled space. Truth: It is only a POTENTIAL space; CSF is in the subarachnoid space.
Myth: The middle meningeal artery enters through the foramen ovale. Truth: It enters through the foramen SPINOSUM.
Myth: Both transverse sinuses receive the superior sagittal sinus. Truth: The superior sagittal usually drains to the RIGHT transverse; the straight sinus to the LEFT.

study.html:
The six extra-ocular muscles

  • Superior rectus
  • Inferior rectus
  • Medial rectus
  • Lateral rectus
  • Superior oblique
  • Inferior oblique

Nerve supply of the eye muscles (mnemonic LR6 SO4)

  • Lateral rectus → Abducent (VI)
  • Superior oblique → Trochlear (IV)
  • All the rest → Oculomotor (III)

The tear (lacrimal) drainage pathway

  • Lacrimal gland → conjunctival sac
  • Puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac
  • Nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus of the nose

StructureFunction
Lateral rectusTurns the eye outward (abduction) — supplied by VI.
Medial rectusTurns the eye inward (adduction) — supplied by III.
Superior obliqueTurns the eye down and out (used looking down, e.g. reading) — supplied by IV.
Levator palpebrae superiorisRaises the upper eyelid — supplied by III (with a sympathetic smooth-muscle part).

Lateral rectus (VI) vs Superior oblique (IV): LR6 SO4: the lateral rectus is the only muscle supplied by VI, the superior oblique the only one by IV; every other eye muscle is III.

Levator palpebrae superioris vs Orbicularis oculi: Levator (III) OPENS the eye; orbicularis oculi (VII) CLOSES it. Different nerves, opposite actions.

1. The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducent nerve (VI).
  2. The superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (IV).
  3. All other extra-ocular muscles are supplied by the oculomotor nerve (III).
  4. The nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the inferior meatus of the nose.
  5. Levator palpebrae superioris raises the upper eyelid and is supplied by CN III.

Structures passing through the superior orbital fissure

  • Oculomotor (III)
  • Trochlear (IV)
  • Ophthalmic (V1) branches (lacrimal, frontal, nasociliary)
  • Abducent (VI)
  • Superior ophthalmic vein

Components of the pupillary light reflex

  • Afferent: optic nerve (II)
  • Efferent: parasympathetic via oculomotor (III) → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae

Smooth muscles inside/around the eye

  • Sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, III) — constricts pupil
  • Dilator pupillae (sympathetic) — dilates pupil
  • Ciliary muscle (parasympathetic, III) — accommodation
  • Superior tarsal muscle (sympathetic) — helps hold the lid up

StructureFunction
Sphincter pupillaeConstricts the pupil in bright light and accommodation (parasympathetic, III).
Dilator pupillaeDilates the pupil in dim light or fear (sympathetic).
Ciliary muscleContracts to thicken the lens for near vision (accommodation, parasympathetic III).
Superior tarsal muscleA small sympathetic muscle assisting lid elevation; its loss causes the partial ptosis of Horner's syndrome.

CN III palsy vs Horner's syndrome: CN III palsy gives a DILATED pupil with ptosis and a 'down-and-out' eye; Horner's gives a CONSTRICTED pupil with partial ptosis (sympathetic loss).

Sphincter pupillae vs Dilator pupillae: Sphincter constricts the pupil (parasympathetic, III); dilator widens it (sympathetic). They oppose each other.

1. The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, IV, V1 branches, VI and the superior ophthalmic vein.
  2. The afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is the optic nerve and the efferent limb is the parasympathetic component of the oculomotor nerve.
  3. The sphincter pupillae (parasympathetic, III) constricts the pupil; the dilator pupillae (sympathetic) dilates it.
  4. The superior oblique muscle is tested by asking the patient to look down and in; weakness causes difficulty descending stairs.
  5. Horner's syndrome (sympathetic loss) gives ptosis, miosis and anhidrosis; CN III palsy gives a dilated pupil with ptosis.

MuscleActionNerve
Lateral rectusAbducts (out)Abducent (VI)
Medial rectusAdducts (in)Oculomotor (III)
Superior rectusElevates (up)Oculomotor (III)
Inferior rectusDepresses (down)Oculomotor (III)
Superior obliqueDown & outTrochlear (IV)
Inferior obliqueUp & outOculomotor (III)
Levator palpebrae sup.Raises upper lidOculomotor (III)

study.h: Autonomic supply of the eye — in full
study.html:
PathwayOrigin → ganglion → effect
Parasympathetic (constrict)Edinger-Westphal nucleus → CN III → ciliary ganglion → short ciliary nn. → sphincter pupillae + ciliary muscle (accommodation)
Sympathetic (dilate)Hypothalamus → ciliospinal centre (T1) → superior cervical ganglion → plexus on ICA → long ciliary nn. → dilator pupillae + superior tarsal (Müller's)
SensoryNasociliary (V1) → long & short ciliary nn. → cornea (afferent of corneal reflex)
⭐ Corneal reflex: afferent = V1 (nasociliary), efferent = VII (orbicularis oculi). A wisp of cotton → both eyes blink.

study.h: Lacrimal gland — its winding nerve supply
study.html:
Parasympathetic (secretomotor) tears travel a famously long road: VII → greater petrosal n. → nerve of pterygoid canal → pterygopalatine ganglion → (hitch a ride on V2 → zygomatic → zygomaticotemporal → lacrimal nerve of V1) → lacrimal gland.

⭐: "Crocodile tears" = misdirected regeneration of these fibres after a facial-nerve lesion: the patient tears when they eat.

scenarios.title: The Eye That Looks 'Down and Out'
scenarios.vignette: A patient is found with a drooping right upper eyelid. When the lid is lifted, the right eye is rotated downward and outward, and the pupil is dilated and unreactive to light.
scenarios.q: Which nerve is paralysed and why each sign?
scenarios.a: A complete OCULOMOTOR (CN III) palsy. III supplies most eye muscles, so the unopposed lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV) pull the eye 'down and out'. Loss of levator palpebrae superioris causes the ptosis, and loss of the parasympathetic fibres to sphincter pupillae leaves the pupil dilated and unreactive ('blown' pupil).
pearls: III supplies all eye muscles except LR (VI) and SO (IV)
'Down and out' eye + ptosis + dilated pupil = III palsy
A fixed dilated pupil after head injury is an ominous sign

scenarios.title: The Cotton Wisp That Won't Blink
scenarios.vignette: After a head injury a patient does not blink when you touch the cornea of the right eye, but touching the LEFT cornea makes BOTH eyes blink.
scenarios.q: Localise the lesion using the corneal reflex pathway.
scenarios.a: The corneal reflex has an afferent limb in the ophthalmic nerve (V1, via nasociliary) and an efferent limb in the facial nerve (VII) to orbicularis oculi. Touching the LEFT cornea gives a normal consensual blink in both eyes, so both facial nerves work. Touching the RIGHT cornea gives NO blink at all — so the RIGHT afferent (V1) is the lesion. If VII were the problem, the affected side would fail to blink no matter which cornea was touched.
pearls: Corneal reflex: afferent V1, efferent VII
Test each side; compare direct vs consensual
No blink touching one side = that side's V1 (afferent) lost

scenarios.title: The Small Pupil, Drooping Lid and Dry Face
scenarios.vignette: A man with a lung apex tumour has a slightly drooping right upper lid, a constricted right pupil, and a dry (non-sweating) right side of the face. The eye looks slightly sunken.
scenarios.q: Name the syndrome and the muscle responsible for the ptosis.
scenarios.a: Horner's syndrome — interruption of the sympathetic supply (here by a Pancoast tumour of the lung apex). Signs: partial ptosis (loss of the sympathetic SUPERIOR TARSAL/Müller's muscle), miosis (loss of dilator pupillae), anhidrosis (loss of sweating) and apparent enophthalmos. It is the sympathetic mirror-image of a CN III palsy.
pearls: Ptosis here = superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle, NOT levator
Miosis + ptosis + anhidrosis = Horner's
Pancoast tumour is a classic cause

scenarios.title: Down-and-Out with a Blown Pupil
scenarios.vignette: Following a road accident a young man's right eye sits 'down and out', the lid droops, and the pupil is wide and unreactive to light.
scenarios.q: Which nerve, which muscles unopposed, and why the dilated pupil?
scenarios.a: Complete oculomotor (CN III) palsy. III supplies all extra-ocular muscles except lateral rectus (VI) and superior oblique (IV); these two are unopposed and pull the eye down and out. Loss of levator palpebrae superioris causes ptosis, and loss of the parasympathetic fibres to sphincter pupillae leaves a dilated, unreactive pupil. A 'surgical' III palsy (pupil involved) after trauma suggests compression — an emergency.
pearls: III palsy: down & out, ptosis, dilated pupil
Pupil-involving III palsy = compressive until proven otherwise
Unopposed LR (VI) + SO (IV) cause the eye position

scenarios.title: Diplopia Going Down Stairs
scenarios.vignette: A patient complains of double vision that is worst when looking down and inward — for example descending stairs or reading. The eye is slightly elevated at rest.
scenarios.q: Which muscle and nerve are affected?
scenarios.a: Superior oblique palsy — trochlear nerve (CN IV). The superior oblique depresses the eye when it is adducted, so its weakness gives vertical diplopia worst on looking down and in (stairs, reading). Patients often tilt the head away from the affected side to compensate.
pearls: SO4 — superior oblique = trochlear (IV)
Diplopia worst looking down & in
Compensatory head tilt is characteristic

scenarios.title: The Eye That Can't Turn Out
scenarios.vignette: A patient with raised intracranial pressure develops horizontal double vision. The right eye fails to abduct (turn outward) past the midline and turns inward at rest.
scenarios.q: Which nerve is affected and why is it vulnerable in raised ICP?
scenarios.a: Abducent nerve (CN VI) palsy — the lateral rectus cannot abduct the eye, so it is pulled medially by the unopposed medial rectus. CN VI has the longest intracranial course and bends over the petrous temporal ridge, so it is the first to be stretched when intracranial pressure rises — a 'false localising sign'.
pearls: LR6 — lateral rectus = abducent (VI)
Longest intracranial course → vulnerable to raised ICP
'False localising sign'

quiz.q: How many muscles move each eyeball?
quiz.e: Six: four recti and two obliques.

quiz.q: Which nerve passes through the optic canal?
quiz.e: The optic nerve (II), with the ophthalmic artery, passes through the optic canal.

quiz.q: Tears ultimately drain into the:
quiz.e: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the nose (inferior meatus).

quiz.q: The lateral rectus muscle is supplied by which nerve?
quiz.e: LR6 — the lateral rectus is supplied by the abducent nerve (VI).

quiz.q: The superior oblique muscle is supplied by which nerve?
quiz.e: SO4 — the superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (IV).

quiz.q: The nasolacrimal duct opens into which part of the nose?
quiz.e: It opens into the inferior meatus.

quiz.q: Which muscle raises the upper eyelid?
quiz.e: Levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) raises the upper lid; orbicularis oculi (VII) closes the eye.

quiz.q: Which extra-ocular muscle turns the eye inward (adduction)?
quiz.e: The medial rectus (III) adducts the eye.

quiz.q: The superior orbital fissure transmits all of the following EXCEPT:
quiz.e: The optic nerve (II) uses the optic canal, NOT the superior orbital fissure.

quiz.q: In the pupillary light reflex, the efferent limb travels in which nerve?
quiz.e: The efferent (parasympathetic) limb runs in the oculomotor nerve (III) to the sphincter pupillae.

quiz.q: A complete oculomotor (III) palsy produces a pupil that is:
quiz.e: Loss of parasympathetic supply to the sphincter pupillae leaves the pupil dilated and unreactive.

quiz.q: The superior oblique is clinically tested by asking the patient to look:
quiz.e: Looking down and in isolates the superior oblique; weakness causes trouble going downstairs.

quiz.q: Which smooth muscle's loss contributes to the ptosis of Horner's syndrome?
quiz.e: The sympathetic superior tarsal muscle helps elevate the lid; its loss causes the partial ptosis of Horner's.

flashcards.q: Test the superior oblique by looking?
Ptosis in Horner's is due to which muscle?
Ptosis in CN III palsy is due to which muscle?

flashcards.a: VII → greater petrosal nerve → pterygopalatine ganglion.
Misdirected regrowth of facial parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland.

flashcards.q: Which CN palsy gives a 'false localising sign' in raised ICP?

pearls: III palsy = 'down & out' eye + ptosis + dilated pupil.
Corneal reflex: in by V1, out by VII — localise by testing each cornea and watching both eyes.
Horner's (sympathetic) = miosis + partial ptosis (Müller's) + anhidrosis; the mirror image of a III palsy.
Pupil-involving III palsy after trauma = compression = emergency.
mistakes: Myth: Levator palpebrae superioris is a facial-nerve muscle. Truth: It is supplied by CN III; orbicularis oculi (eye closure) is the facial-nerve muscle.
Myth: A CN III palsy gives a constricted pupil. Truth: It gives a DILATED, unreactive pupil. A constricted pupil with ptosis suggests Horner's.

study.html:
Boundaries of the middle ear (clinically key)

  • Roof (tegmen tympani) → middle cranial fossa / temporal lobe
  • Floor → internal jugular vein
  • Medial wall → inner ear + facial nerve
  • Posterior wall → mastoid antrum & air cells

The two middle-ear muscles

  • Tensor tympani (on the malleus) — supplied by V3
  • Stapedius (on the stapes) — supplied by VII

Parts of the internal ear

  • Cochlea (hearing)
  • Vestibule & semicircular canals (balance)

StructureFunction
Tympanic membraneVibrates with sound and transmits it to the malleus.
Stapes footplateSits in the oval window and pushes the inner-ear fluid to start the hearing signal.
Auditory tubeEqualises pressure across the eardrum (the 'pop' when you swallow or descend in a plane).
StapediusDampens loud sounds by limiting stapes movement (protective).

Tensor tympani vs Stapedius: Tensor tympani is supplied by the trigeminal (V3) and acts on the malleus; stapedius is supplied by the facial nerve (VII) and acts on the stapes.

Conductive hearing loss vs Sensorineural hearing loss: Conductive loss arises in the external/middle ear (e.g. wax, fluid, ossicle problem); sensorineural loss arises in the cochlea or nerve (CN VIII).

1. The stapes sits in the oval window of the inner ear.
  2. The tensor tympani muscle is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).
  3. The stapedius muscle is supplied by the facial nerve (VII).
  4. The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure.
  5. The roof of the middle ear (tegmen tympani) separates it from the middle cranial fossa.

Why sound is amplified across the middle ear

  • Large tympanic membrane focuses onto the small oval window (area ratio)
  • Lever action of the ossicular chain
  • Together they overcome the air-to-fluid impedance mismatch

Routes of spread of middle-ear infection (otitis media)

  • Upward (tegmen) → meningitis / temporal-lobe abscess
  • Backward → mastoid air cells → mastoiditis
  • Medially → facial nerve (palsy) and inner ear (vertigo)

The auditory (Eustachian) tube

  • Connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx
  • Equalises middle-ear pressure with the atmosphere
  • A route for infection to ascend from the throat

StructureFunction
Tensor tympani (V3)Tenses the eardrum to dampen loud, low-frequency sound.
Stapedius (VII)Reflexly dampens loud sound; its loss causes hyperacusis.
Cochlea (organ of Corti)Contains the hair cells that transduce sound vibrations into nerve impulses (CN VIII).
Semicircular canalsDetect rotational (angular) acceleration of the head for balance.

Oval window vs Round window: The stapes footplate drives fluid IN at the oval window; the round window bulges OUT to relieve the pressure wave — both are needed for hearing.

Otitis media spreading up vs Spreading back: Upward spread (through the tegmen tympani) threatens the meninges/temporal lobe; backward spread reaches the mastoid air cells, causing mastoiditis.

1. The middle ear amplifies sound through the area ratio of the eardrum to the oval window and the lever action of the ossicles.
  2. Damage to the facial nerve as it runs in the medial wall of the middle ear can cause facial palsy in chronic ear disease.
  3. Loss of the stapedius (facial-nerve lesion) causes hyperacusis.
  4. Middle-ear infection can spread upward through the tegmen tympani to cause meningitis or a temporal-lobe abscess.
  5. The round window's secondary tympanic membrane bulges outward to dissipate the pressure wave created at the oval window.

study.h: Table · Walls of the Middle Ear & their Dangers
study.html:
WallRelationClinical risk
Roof (tegmen)Middle cranial fossaMeningitis / temporal abscess
FloorInternal jugular veinVascular injury
MedialInner ear + facial nerveFacial palsy, vertigo
PosteriorMastoid antrum & air cellsMastoiditis
AnteriorAuditory tube & carotid canalInfection ascent

scenarios.title: The Discharging Ear with a Facial Droop
scenarios.vignette: A child with months of ear discharge develops a drooping face on the same side and episodes of dizziness.
scenarios.q: Explain how a middle-ear infection caused these new signs.
scenarios.a: Chronic otitis media has spread MEDIALLY, where the middle ear's medial wall is related to the FACIAL NERVE canal (causing the facial palsy) and the INNER EAR (causing the vertigo/labyrinthitis). Other directions of spread include upward through the tegmen tympani (meningitis) and backward into the mastoid (mastoiditis).
pearls: Medial wall = facial nerve + inner ear
Upward (tegmen) = meninges; backward = mastoid
Chronic ear discharge needs prompt attention

quiz.q: How many parts does the ear have?
quiz.e: Three: external, middle and internal ear.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT an ear ossicle?
quiz.e: The three ossicles are malleus, incus and stapes. The vomer is a facial bone.

quiz.q: Which part of the ear is responsible for balance?
quiz.e: The internal ear (vestibule and semicircular canals) handles balance, and the cochlea handles hearing.

quiz.q: The stapes footplate sits in the:
quiz.e: The stapes footplate occupies the oval window, transmitting vibration to the inner-ear fluid.

quiz.q: The tensor tympani muscle is supplied by which nerve?
quiz.e: Tensor tympani is supplied by V3; stapedius is supplied by VII.

quiz.q: The stapedius muscle is supplied by which nerve?
quiz.e: Stapedius is supplied by the facial nerve (VII); its loss causes hyperacusis.

quiz.q: The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects the middle ear to the:
quiz.e: It connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and equalises pressure.

quiz.q: The roof of the middle ear (tegmen tympani) separates it from the:
quiz.e: The tegmen tympani separates the middle ear from the middle cranial fossa (temporal lobe).

quiz.q: Loss of the stapedius muscle causes:
quiz.e: Without stapedius dampening, sounds seem uncomfortably loud (hyperacusis).

quiz.q: Upward spread of middle-ear infection through the tegmen tympani may cause:
quiz.e: Through the thin tegmen tympani, infection can reach the meninges and temporal lobe.

quiz.q: Which window bulges outward to relieve the pressure wave generated at the oval window?
quiz.e: The round window (secondary tympanic membrane) bulges out to dissipate the wave.

quiz.q: A facial nerve palsy in chronic ear disease is explained by the nerve's relation to which middle-ear wall?
quiz.e: The facial nerve runs in the medial wall of the middle ear and can be damaged there.

quiz.q: The middle ear amplifies sound mainly by the eardrum-to-oval-window area ratio plus the:
quiz.e: The lever action of the ossicular chain, plus the area ratio, overcomes the air-to-fluid impedance mismatch.

flashcards.q: Auditory tube connects middle ear to?
Tegmen tympani separates middle ear from?
Medial wall of middle ear relates to?

pearls: Auditory tube → nasopharynx (pressure equaliser & infection route).
Middle-ear spread: up = meninges, back = mastoid, medial = facial nerve + inner ear.
mistakes: Myth: The stapes sits in the round window. Truth: The stapes footplate sits in the OVAL window; the round window bulges out to relieve pressure.
Myth: Middle-ear infection cannot reach the brain. Truth: Upward spread through the thin tegmen tympani can cause meningitis or a temporal-lobe abscess.

study.html:
Movements of the TMJ

  • Depression (open) & elevation (close)
  • Protrusion & retraction
  • Side-to-side grinding (lateral)

Muscles that CLOSE the jaw (elevators)

  • Masseter
  • Temporalis
  • Medial pterygoid
Note: All three are elevators. Temporalis also retracts.

Ligaments of the TMJ

  • Lateral (temporomandibular) ligament — the strong one
  • Sphenomandibular ligament (accessory)
  • Stylomandibular ligament (accessory)

Foramina that carry the inferior alveolar nerve

  • Mandibular foramen (entry, medial ramus)
  • Mental foramen (exit, body, below the premolars)

StructureFunction
MasseterPowerful elevator — the main biting/clenching muscle; easily felt when you clench.
TemporalisElevates the mandible; its posterior fibres retract (pull the jaw back).
Medial pterygoidElevates the mandible; with the lateral pterygoid produces grinding side-to-side movement.
Lateral pterygoidOPENS the jaw and protrudes it by pulling the condyle and disc forward.

Lateral pterygoid vs The other three masticatory muscles: Lateral pterygoid OPENS/protrudes the jaw; masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid CLOSE it. All four are supplied by V3.

Mandibular foramen vs Mental foramen: The inferior alveolar nerve ENTERS at the mandibular foramen (medial ramus) and EXITS as the mental nerve at the mental foramen (below the premolars).

TMJ upper compartment vs TMJ lower compartment: Upper = gliding/translation (forward slide of disc + condyle); lower = hinge/rotation. The disc separates them.

1. All four muscles of mastication are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
  2. The lateral pterygoid is the muscle that opens (protrudes) the jaw.
  3. The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandibular foramen and emerges at the mental foramen.
  4. The masseter is the strongest superficial elevator and is palpable when clenching.
  5. The articular disc divides the TMJ into upper and lower compartments.

Layers / features of the TMJ

  • Articular disc divides it into upper & lower compartments
  • Upper compartment = gliding (translation)
  • Lower compartment = hinge (rotation)
  • Articular surfaces covered by FIBROcartilage, not hyaline

Attachments of lateral pterygoid

  • Upper head → articular disc & capsule
  • Lower head → neck of the mandible (pterygoid fovea)

Branches of V3 relevant to the jaw

  • Inferior alveolar nerve → lower teeth, then mental nerve to chin/lip
  • Lingual nerve → ant. 2/3 tongue sensation
  • Buccal nerve → cheek sensation
  • Auriculotemporal nerve → TMJ + scalp + (carries parotid secretomotor fibres)

StructureFunction
Articular discDivides the joint, absorbs load, and moves forward with the condyle during opening (translation).
Lateral pterygoid (upper head)Controls the disc, easing it back during closing; dysfunction is linked to clicking/derangement.
Sphenomandibular ligamentActs as a swinging hinge ('pivot') for the mandible and is the landmark for inferior alveolar nerve blocks (the lingula lies just in front).
Auriculotemporal nerveSensory to the TMJ and scalp; also conveys parotid secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion.

TMJ articular surface vs Typical synovial joint: The TMJ is covered by FIBROcartilage (not hyaline cartilage) because it forms by intramembranous ossification and bears heavy, repetitive load.

Anterior TMJ dislocation vs Normal opening: In wide opening the condyle + disc translate onto the articular eminence; if they pass too far anteriorly and spasm catches them, the jaw locks open (anterior dislocation).

Inferior alveolar nerve block vs Mental nerve block: The IAN block deposits anaesthetic near the lingula/mandibular foramen (numbs all lower teeth on that side + lip); a mental block numbs only the chin and lower lip.

1. The articular surfaces of the TMJ are covered with fibrocartilage rather than hyaline cartilage.
  2. The upper head of the lateral pterygoid attaches to the articular disc and is implicated in internal derangement (clicking).
  3. The lingula, just anterior to the mandibular foramen, gives attachment to the sphenomandibular ligament and is the key landmark for the inferior alveolar nerve block.
  4. The auriculotemporal nerve (V3) supplies the TMJ and carries parotid secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion.
  5. Reduction of an anterior TMJ dislocation is achieved by pressing downward on the molars while pushing the jaw backward, overcoming the spasm of the elevator muscles.

scenarios.title: The Jaw That Won't Close
scenarios.vignette: After a wide yawn, a young woman's mouth is stuck open. She cannot bring her teeth together and her jaw feels locked forward; there is pain in front of both ears.
scenarios.q: What has happened and how is it corrected?
scenarios.a: Bilateral anterior dislocation of the TMJ: the condyle and disc have translated forward over the articular eminence and the elevator muscles have gone into spasm, trapping them. Reduction is by pressing DOWNWARD on the lower molars (to clear the eminence) while pushing the jaw BACKWARD into the fossa.
pearls: Triggered by wide opening (yawn, dental work)
Reduce: press down on molars + push jaw backward
Lateral pterygoid + elevator spasm maintains the lock

scenarios.title: Numb Lip After a Dental Block
scenarios.vignette: During a lower molar extraction the dentist gives an inferior alveolar nerve block. The patient reports numbness of all the lower teeth on that side and of the lower lip and chin, plus an unexpected numb patch on the side of the tongue.
scenarios.q: Why are the tongue and lip also numb?
scenarios.a: The anaesthetic deposited near the mandibular foramen/lingula also bathes the nearby LINGUAL nerve, numbing the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, while the inferior alveolar nerve itself numbs the lower teeth and (via its mental branch) the lower lip and chin. Both are branches of V3 running close together at that site.
pearls: IAN block targets the lingula/mandibular foramen
Lingual nerve lies just anteromedial and is often co-anaesthetised
Lip/chin numbness is the mental branch of the IAN

scenarios.title: Jaw Locked Open After a Yawn
scenarios.vignette: A woman's mouth is stuck wide open after a big yawn; she cannot close it and there is pain in front of both ears.
scenarios.q: What happened and how do you reduce it?
scenarios.a: Bilateral anterior TMJ dislocation: the condyle + disc translate forward over the articular eminence and the elevator muscles spasm, trapping them. Reduce by pressing DOWN on the lower molars (to clear the eminence) while pushing the jaw BACKWARD into the fossa.
pearls: Condyle slips anterior to the eminence
Reduce: down on molars + push backward
Wrap thumbs to avoid a bite

scenarios.title: Jaw Deviates to the Right on Opening
scenarios.vignette: After a stab wound to the infratemporal fossa a patient's jaw deviates to the RIGHT each time they open the mouth.
scenarios.q: Which muscle/nerve is damaged and why this direction?
scenarios.a: The RIGHT lateral pterygoid (or its nerve from V3). The lateral pterygoid protrudes the jaw and deviates it to the OPPOSITE side; with the right one weak, the intact LEFT lateral pterygoid pushes the jaw across to the weak RIGHT side on opening. So the jaw deviates TOWARD the side of the lesion.
pearls: Lateral pterygoid deviates to the opposite side
Weak muscle → jaw deviates TO that side
All masticatory muscles = V3

scenarios.title: The Clicking Jaw
scenarios.vignette: A young woman has a painful click in front of the ear when she opens, and sometimes the jaw briefly catches before opening fully.
scenarios.q: What structure is at fault and which muscle controls it?
scenarios.a: Internal derangement of the TMJ disc (anterior disc displacement with reduction). The click is the condyle slipping back under a forward-displaced disc. The UPPER HEAD of the lateral pterygoid attaches to the disc/capsule and helps control disc position; its dysfunction is linked to derangement.
pearls: Click = disc displacement with reduction
Upper head of lateral pterygoid attaches to the disc
Disc divides joint into upper (glide) & lower (hinge)

scenarios.title: Cannot Clench — Wasted Cheek
scenarios.vignette: A patient cannot generate a firm bite on the left; the bulge over the angle of the jaw that normally appears on clenching is absent and the area looks wasted.
scenarios.q: Which muscle and nerve?
scenarios.a: The LEFT MASSETER (or its motor supply, the masseteric branch of V3). The masseter is the strongest superficial elevator and is normally palpable as a firm bulge over the ramus/angle on clenching; weakness/wasting abolishes this and weakens the bite.
pearls: Masseter = main clenching muscle
Palpable over the ramus on clenching
Masseteric nerve from V3

scenarios.title: Numb Lower Lip After a Mandibular Fracture
scenarios.vignette: After a blow to the jaw a patient has a fractured mandibular body and numbness of the lower lip and chin on that side.
scenarios.q: Which nerve is injured and where does it run?
scenarios.a: The INFERIOR ALVEOLAR NERVE (a branch of V3) within the mandibular canal. It enters at the mandibular foramen, runs through the body supplying the lower teeth, and exits at the mental foramen as the MENTAL NERVE to the lower lip and chin — hence the numb lip when the canal is disrupted by fracture.
pearls: IAN runs in the mandibular canal
Exits as the mental nerve (lip/chin)
Lip numbness is a sign of canal involvement

scenarios.title: Numb Lip After a Dental Block
scenarios.vignette: After an inferior alveolar nerve block all the lower teeth on that side and the lower lip go numb — and so does the side of the tongue.
scenarios.q: Why is the tongue also numb?
scenarios.a: The block is placed near the mandibular foramen/lingula, where the LINGUAL NERVE (also V3) lies just anteromedial to the inferior alveolar nerve and is bathed by the anaesthetic. The IAN numbs the teeth and (via the mental branch) the lip; the lingual nerve numbs the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
pearls: Lingual nerve lies just anterior to the IAN at the lingula
IAN block often co-anaesthetises the lingual nerve
Lip numbness = mental branch of IAN

scenarios.title: Can't Open Wide — Trismus After a Lower Wisdom Tooth
scenarios.vignette: Days after a difficult lower third-molar extraction a patient cannot open the mouth more than a centimetre and has pain near the angle.
scenarios.q: Which muscle is in spasm and why?
scenarios.a: Trismus from spasm/inflammation of the muscles of mastication — typically the MEDIAL PTERYGOID (and masseter), irritated by the surgery or by infection/haematoma near the pterygomandibular space. The medial pterygoid is a powerful elevator, so its spasm limits opening.
pearls: Trismus = limited mouth opening
Medial pterygoid/masseter spasm common after lower 8s
Consider infection in the pterygomandibular space

scenarios.title: Pain in Front of the Ear When Chewing — No Click
scenarios.vignette: A stressed patient who grinds at night has dull pain over the masseter and temple, tenderness of the chewing muscles, and limited opening — but NO joint click or locking.
scenarios.q: What is the likely diagnosis?
scenarios.a: Myofascial pain dysfunction syndrome (MPDS) / masticatory myalgia — a muscular problem from parafunction (bruxism/clenching), NOT a structural joint derangement. The chewing muscles (masseter, temporalis, pterygoids) are tender and fatigued; treatment is conservative (soft diet, splint, stress reduction).
pearls: Muscle tenderness, no click/lock = MPDS
Driven by bruxism/clenching
Conservative management first

scenarios.title: Jaw Won't Open After Maxillary Surgery
scenarios.vignette: A patient develops progressive inability to open the mouth weeks after surgery/trauma in the region of the coronoid process and temporalis.
scenarios.q: Which muscle's restriction explains this?
scenarios.a: The TEMPORALIS (inserting on the coronoid process) — fibrosis or impingement of the coronoid/temporalis limits the forward-and-down translation needed to open, producing extra-articular trismus. Temporalis also retracts the jaw, so its scarring restricts opening.
pearls: Temporalis inserts on the coronoid process
Coronoid/temporalis fibrosis → extra-articular trismus
Temporalis elevates + retracts

scenarios.title: Side-to-Side Grinding Lost
scenarios.vignette: A patient has lost the ability to make smooth side-to-side (lateral) grinding movements of the jaw, though opening and closing are intact.
scenarios.q: Which muscles produce lateral grinding movements?
scenarios.a: Lateral grinding is produced mainly by the PTERYGOIDS acting alternately: contracting the lateral (and medial) pterygoid of ONE side protrudes that side's condyle and swings the chin to the OPPOSITE side; alternating sides produces the grinding (chewing) cycle. Loss of coordinated pterygoid action abolishes smooth lateral excursion.
pearls: Pterygoids drive lateral/grinding movements
One side's lateral pterygoid → chin to opposite side
Alternating action = chewing cycle

quiz.q: Which is the only movable bone of the skull?
quiz.e: The mandible is the only freely movable bone of the skull, articulating at the TMJ.

quiz.q: How many muscles of mastication are there?
quiz.e: Four: masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid and lateral pterygoid.

quiz.q: Which process of the ramus forms the jaw joint?
quiz.e: The condylar process forms the TMJ; the coronoid process is for temporalis attachment.

quiz.q: The strong biting muscle you can feel when you clench is the:
quiz.e: The masseter bulges and hardens over the ramus when you clench.

quiz.q: Which muscle of mastication OPENS the jaw?
quiz.e: The lateral pterygoid opens and protrudes the jaw; the other three are elevators.

quiz.q: All muscles of mastication are supplied by which nerve?
quiz.e: All four are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).

quiz.q: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandible at the:
quiz.e: It enters at the mandibular foramen and exits at the mental foramen as the mental nerve.

quiz.q: The articular disc divides the TMJ into:
quiz.e: The disc separates the joint into an upper (gliding) and a lower (hinge) compartment.

quiz.q: Which muscle both elevates AND retracts the mandible?
quiz.e: Temporalis elevates the jaw, and its posterior fibres retract it.

quiz.q: The articular surfaces of the TMJ are covered by:
quiz.e: Unusually for a synovial joint, the TMJ surfaces are covered by fibrocartilage.

quiz.q: The upper head of the lateral pterygoid attaches mainly to the:
quiz.e: The upper head attaches to the articular disc/capsule and is implicated in disc derangement (clicking).

quiz.q: The key bony landmark just anterior to the mandibular foramen for an IAN block is the:
quiz.e: The lingula gives attachment to the sphenomandibular ligament and marks the site for the inferior alveolar nerve block.

quiz.q: Anterior TMJ dislocation is reduced by:
o: Pushing the jaw forward and up
Pressing down on the molars and pushing the jaw backward
quiz.e: Press down on the molars to clear the eminence, then push the jaw backward into the fossa.

quiz.q: The auriculotemporal nerve supplies the TMJ and also carries secretomotor fibres to which gland?
quiz.e: It conveys parotid secretomotor fibres from the otic ganglion, in addition to supplying the TMJ and scalp.

quiz.q: During TMJ opening, the forward slide of the condyle and disc onto the eminence is called:
quiz.e: Translation (gliding) occurs in the upper compartment; rotation (hinge) occurs in the lower compartment.

flashcards.q: Auriculotemporal nerve carries fibres to which gland?
Which masticatory muscle opens the jaw?
A weak right lateral pterygoid deviates the jaw to…?
flashcards.a: The RIGHT (toward the weak side) on opening.

flashcards.q: Upper head of lateral pterygoid attaches to…?
flashcards.a: The articular disc & capsule (linked to clicking).

flashcards.q: Trismus after a lower 8 — which muscle commonly spasms?

flashcards.a: The coronoid process of the mandible.
Sling around the angle of the mandible.

pearls: TMJ = fibrocartilage + a disc that splits it into a gliding (upper) and hinge (lower) compartment.
Lateral pterygoid: the ONLY opener; one side deviates the jaw to the OPPOSITE side (weakness → jaw deviates TO the weak side).
Click/lock = disc derangement; muscle tenderness without click = MPDS (bruxism).
All four muscles of mastication = mandibular nerve (V3).
mistakes: Myth: The muscles of mastication are supplied by the facial nerve. Truth: They are supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3). The facial nerve supplies expression muscles.
Myth: The inferior alveolar nerve exits at the mandibular foramen. Truth: It ENTERS at the mandibular foramen and EXITS at the mental foramen.
Myth: A dislocated jaw is reduced by pushing it forward. Truth: It is reduced by pressing down on the molars and pushing the jaw backward.

study.html:
The 5 terminal branches of the facial nerve

  • Temporal
  • Zygomatic
  • Buccal
  • Marginal mandibular
  • Cervical
Note: Mnemonic: 'To Zanzibar By Motor Car' (Temporal, Zygomatic, Buccal, Mandibular, Cervical). They radiate out of the parotid gland.

Trigeminal cutaneous divisions to the face

  • Ophthalmic (V1) — forehead, upper eyelid, dorsum of nose
  • Maxillary (V2) — cheek, lower eyelid, upper lip, side of nose
  • Mandibular (V3) — lower lip, chin, jaw, side of head
Note: The angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2,3), NOT the trigeminal — a classic exception.

Branches of the facial artery (face portion)

  • Inferior labial
  • Superior labial
  • Lateral nasal
  • Angular (terminal)

StructureFunction
Orbicularis oculiCloses the eyelids (palpebral part = gentle blink; orbital part = forced closure).
Orbicularis orisCloses and purses the lips — needed for speech, whistling and eating.
BuccinatorPresses the cheek against the teeth, keeping food on the chewing surface; resists air pressure when blowing.
Levator palpebrae superiorisRaises the upper eyelid — note this is supplied by CN III, not VII.
PlatysmaTenses the skin of the neck and draws the corners of the mouth down.

Buccal branch of VII vs Buccal nerve of V3: VII's buccal branch is MOTOR to buccinator. V3's buccal nerve is SENSORY to the cheek skin and mucosa. Identical name, opposite function — a favourite exam trap.

Facial artery vs Facial vein: The artery is tortuous (to allow facial movement); the vein runs a straighter, more posterior course. Both cross the mandible at the anterior border of masseter.

Angle of jaw sensation vs Rest of the face: The angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2,3); the rest of the face is trigeminal. So jaw-angle numbness is NOT a trigeminal sign.

1. The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen.
  2. The five terminal branches are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical.
  3. The facial artery is a branch of the external carotid artery and can be felt at the lower border of the mandible, just anterior to masseter.
  4. Orbicularis oculi closes the eye; loss of it (facial palsy) prevents eye closure and risks corneal drying.
  5. The buccinator is pierced by the parotid duct opposite the upper second molar.

Intracranial/intratemporal branches of VII (before the face)

  • Greater petrosal nerve — to lacrimal & nasal glands (via pterygopalatine ganglion)
  • Nerve to stapedius
  • Chorda tympani — taste (anterior 2/3 tongue) + secretomotor to submandibular & sublingual glands
Note: These three leave inside the temporal bone, BEFORE the nerve exits the stylomastoid foramen.

Order of structures the facial nerve relates to in the parotid (superficial → deep)

  • Facial nerve & its branches (most superficial)
  • Retromandibular vein
  • External carotid artery (deepest)

The 'danger area' venous connections

  • Facial vein → angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein → cavernous sinus
  • Facial vein → deep facial vein → pterygoid venous plexus → cavernous sinus
Note: The facial vein is valveless, so infection of the upper lip/nose can spread backward to the cavernous sinus.

StructureFunction
Greater petrosal nerve (VII)Parasympathetic secretomotor to the lacrimal gland and the glands of the nose and palate.
Chorda tympani (VII)Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue + secretomotor to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
Nerve to stapedius (VII)Dampens excessive vibration of the stapes; its loss causes hyperacusis.
Buccinator (motor VII / sensory V)Moved by the buccal branch of the facial nerve, but the cheek's sensation is the buccal nerve of V3 — same name, opposite jobs.

Upper motor neuron (UMN) facial palsy vs Lower motor neuron (LMN) facial palsy: UMN (e.g. stroke) SPARES the forehead because the upper face has bilateral cortical input. LMN (e.g. Bell's palsy) paralyses the WHOLE half of the face including the forehead.

Bell's palsy vs Stroke affecting the face: Bell's palsy = LMN, whole half of face, often with hyperacusis/taste loss if the lesion is proximal. Stroke = UMN, lower face only, usually with limb signs.

Parotid (Stensen's) duct vs Facial nerve in the parotid: The duct runs forward to pierce buccinator opposite the upper 2nd molar; the facial nerve runs more superficially and divides the gland into superficial and deep parts.

1. The chorda tympani (a branch of VII) carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and secretomotor fibres to the submandibular and sublingual glands.
  2. The greater petrosal nerve (a branch of VII) is secretomotor to the lacrimal gland via the pterygopalatine ganglion.
  3. A lesion of the facial nerve proximal to the nerve to stapedius produces hyperacusis (uncomfortable sensitivity to loud sound).
  4. The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus through the superior ophthalmic vein and through the pterygoid plexus, making the upper lip and nose a 'danger area' for infection spread.
  5. The marginal mandibular branch of VII supplies the depressors of the lower lip; injury (e.g. in submandibular surgery) causes an asymmetric smile.

study.html:

⭐ Pattern: the maxilla and its gingiva/palate are V2; the mandible, tongue and floor of mouth are V3; taste anteriorly is VII; everything posterior (tongue & oropharynx) is IX.

study.h: Motor vs sensory 'buccal' — and the eye link
study.html:
• Buccal branch of VII = MOTOR to buccinator.
  • Buccal nerve of V3 = SENSORY to cheek skin & mucosa. Same name, opposite job.
  • Orbicularis oculi (eye closure) = facial nerve (VII); levator palpebrae superioris (eye opening) = oculomotor (III) — so a VII palsy leaves the eye OPEN and at risk of drying.

scenarios.title: The Drooping Face
scenarios.vignette: A 52-year-old woman wakes to find the right side of her face has gone slack. The corner of her mouth droops, she cannot close her right eye fully, and she cannot wrinkle the right side of her forehead. There is no weakness of the arm or leg.
scenarios.q: Is this an upper or lower motor neuron lesion, and which nerve is affected?
scenarios.a: A LOWER motor neuron lesion of the right facial nerve (VII) — Bell's palsy. The diagnostic key is that the FOREHEAD is involved: the whole half of the face is paralysed. In an upper motor neuron lesion (stroke) the forehead would be spared because of its bilateral cortical supply.
pearls: Forehead involved → LMN (whole half of face)
Forehead spared → UMN (lower face only)
Failure to close the eye risks corneal exposure — protect it

scenarios.title: The Spreading Lip Infection
scenarios.vignette: A young man squeezes a boil on his upper lip. Days later he develops a high fever, headache, a swollen congested eye and double vision.
scenarios.q: Explain the anatomical route of this dangerous complication.
scenarios.a: Infection has spread from the 'danger area' of the face (upper lip & nose) along the VALVELESS facial vein → angular vein → superior ophthalmic vein → CAVERNOUS SINUS, producing cavernous sinus thrombosis. The eye signs (proptosis, chemosis, ophthalmoplegia) reflect involvement of the structures in and around the sinus (CN III, IV, V1, VI and the internal carotid artery).
pearls: Facial vein is valveless → backward spread is possible
Cavernous sinus contains CN III, IV, V1, V2 in its wall and VI + ICA passing through
Never squeeze upper-lip/nose lesions

scenarios.title: Whole-Face Droop With Dry Eye
scenarios.vignette: A man wakes with the whole right side of his face slack — he cannot wrinkle the forehead, close the eye, or smile on that side — and complains of a dry, sore right eye.
scenarios.q: Upper or lower motor neuron, and why the dry eye?
scenarios.a: Lower motor neuron facial (VII) palsy (Bell's palsy): the WHOLE half of the face including the forehead is paralysed. Orbicularis oculi (VII) cannot close the eye, so the cornea is exposed and dries (risk of exposure keratitis). The eye must be protected (lubricants, taping).
pearls: Forehead involved = LMN (whole half)
Orbicularis oculi failure → dry, exposed cornea
Protect the eye

scenarios.title: Facial Weakness Sparing the Forehead
scenarios.vignette: After a stroke a patient has drooping of the lower right face and cannot smile on the right, but can still wrinkle the forehead symmetrically. The arm is also weak.
scenarios.q: Where is the lesion?
scenarios.a: An UPPER motor neuron lesion of the left motor cortex/corticobulbar tract, causing right lower-face weakness with FOREHEAD SPARING (the upper face has bilateral cortical input). The accompanying limb weakness fits a central (stroke) lesion rather than a peripheral facial-nerve problem.
pearls: Forehead spared = UMN
Upper face = bilateral cortical supply
Look for limb signs in stroke

scenarios.title: Bell's Palsy With Loud-Sound Sensitivity and Taste Loss
scenarios.vignette: A patient with a complete one-sided facial palsy also reports that sounds seem uncomfortably loud and that taste is altered on the front of the tongue.
scenarios.q: What do these extra features tell you about the level of the lesion?
scenarios.a: The lesion is PROXIMAL in the facial nerve, above the branch to stapedius and the chorda tympani. Loss of stapedius → hyperacusis; loss of chorda tympani → reduced taste (anterior 2/3 tongue) and reduced submandibular/sublingual salivation. The more proximal the VII lesion, the more of these features appear.
pearls: Hyperacusis = nerve to stapedius involved
Taste loss = chorda tympani involved
Extra features localise the lesion proximally

quiz.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression?
quiz.e: The facial nerve (VII) supplies all the muscles of facial expression, which develop from the second pharyngeal arch.

quiz.q: Which nerve provides sensation to the skin of the face?
quiz.e: The trigeminal nerve (V) gives general sensation to the face through its three divisions.

quiz.q: Which muscle closes the eyelids?
quiz.e: Orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids; levator palpebrae superioris (CN III) opens them.

quiz.q: The muscles of facial expression develop from which pharyngeal arch?
quiz.e: They develop from the second pharyngeal arch, which is why they are all supplied by the facial nerve.

quiz.q: How many terminal (extracranial) branches does the facial nerve have?
quiz.e: Five: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical — 'To Zanzibar By Motor Car'.

quiz.q: The facial nerve exits the skull through the:
quiz.e: The facial nerve leaves the skull through the stylomastoid foramen, then enters the parotid gland.

quiz.q: The parotid duct pierces which muscle to open opposite the upper 2nd molar?
quiz.e: The parotid (Stensen's) duct pierces buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar.

quiz.q: The angle of the jaw receives its skin sensation from the:
quiz.e: The angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2,3) — the classic trigeminal exception.

quiz.q: The facial artery is a branch of which artery?
quiz.e: The facial artery arises from the external carotid artery and crosses the mandible at the anterior border of masseter.

quiz.q: Which muscle keeps food on the chewing surface of the teeth and is used in blowing?
quiz.e: Buccinator presses the cheek against the teeth and resists air pressure when blowing.

quiz.q: An upper motor neuron lesion of the facial nerve characteristically:
o: Paralyses the whole half of the face
quiz.e: UMN lesions spare the forehead because the upper-face motor neurons receive bilateral cortical input.

quiz.q: Which branch of the facial nerve carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue?
quiz.e: The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and is secretomotor to the submandibular & sublingual glands.

quiz.q: A facial nerve lesion proximal to the nerve to stapedius produces:
quiz.e: Loss of stapedius dampening causes hyperacusis — an uncomfortable sensitivity to loud sounds.

quiz.q: Within the parotid gland, which structure is most superficial?
quiz.e: From superficial to deep: facial nerve → retromandibular vein → external carotid artery.

quiz.q: The 'danger area' of the face drains to the cavernous sinus mainly via the:
quiz.e: The valveless facial vein connects via the angular and superior ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus.

quiz.q: Injury to the marginal mandibular branch of VII during submandibular surgery causes:
o: Drooping of the lower lip / asymmetric smile
quiz.e: It supplies the lower-lip depressors, so injury produces an asymmetric smile with the lower lip.

flashcards.a: Facial nerve → retromandibular vein → external carotid artery

flashcards.q: Why is the upper lip a 'danger area'?
flashcards.a: Valveless facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus

flashcards.q: Why does a VII palsy threaten the cornea?
flashcards.a: Orbicularis oculi can't close the eye → exposure & drying.

pearls: Upper lip + nose = 'danger area' → valveless facial vein → cavernous sinus.
Oral sensation map: maxilla/palate = V2; mandible/tongue/floor = V3; anterior taste = VII; all posterior tongue/oropharynx = IX.
VII closes the eye (orbicularis oculi); III opens it (levator) — a VII palsy leaves the eye open and dry.
Proximal VII lesion adds hyperacusis (stapedius) and taste loss (chorda tympani).
mistakes: Myth: The facial nerve gives sensation to the face. Truth: The facial nerve is mainly motor to the face. Facial skin sensation is from the trigeminal nerve.
Myth: Levator palpebrae superioris is a facial-nerve muscle. Truth: It is supplied by CN III (oculomotor). Orbicularis oculi (eye closure) is the facial-nerve muscle.
Myth: The facial vein has valves that prevent backward spread. Truth: The facial vein is valveless, allowing infection to spread back to the cavernous sinus.

study.html:
Which layers move together

  • Skin + Connective tissue + Aponeurosis move as ONE unit
  • They glide on the loose areolar layer beneath

Arteries of the scalp (all anastomose freely)

  • Supratrochlear & supraorbital (from ophthalmic)
  • Superficial temporal
  • Posterior auricular
  • Occipital

Sensory nerves of the scalp (front to back)

  • Supratrochlear & supraorbital (V1)
  • Zygomaticotemporal (V2)
  • Auriculotemporal (V3)
  • Lesser occipital (C2)
  • Greater occipital (C2)

StructureFunction
Aponeurosis (galea)A tough sheet linking the two bellies of occipitofrontalis; binds the top three layers into one mobile unit.
Connective tissue layerHolds the scalp's many vessels; its fibrous septa keep cut vessels open, causing profuse bleeding.
Loose areolar layerThe 'gliding' plane that lets the scalp move; the surgical plane and the route for spreading collections.

Scalp wound that bleeds heavily vs Why it bleeds so much: Vessels lie in the dense connective tissue layer where fibrous septa hold them open, so they cannot retract and constrict — pressure is needed to stop bleeding.

Gaping scalp wound vs Non-gaping wound: A wound that cuts through the aponeurosis gapes widely (the two bellies of occipitofrontalis pull apart); one that spares the aponeurosis does not gape.

1. The first three layers (skin, connective tissue, aponeurosis) move together as a single unit.
  2. Scalp arteries anastomose freely, so even a large flap usually survives on a narrow pedicle.
  3. Scalp wounds bleed profusely because the vessels are held open by fibrous septa and cannot retract.
  4. A scalp wound gapes only if the epicranial aponeurosis is cut.

Why the 4th layer is the 'dangerous area'

  • Loose areolar tissue lets blood/pus spread widely
  • Emissary veins here connect to intracranial venous sinuses
  • Infection can therefore pass into the cranial cavity

Lymph drainage of the scalp

  • Anterior → preauricular (parotid) & submandibular nodes
  • Posterior → mastoid (retroauricular) & occipital nodes

StructureFunction
Emissary veinsValveless connections between scalp veins and intracranial venous sinuses — a route for infection to spread inward.
PericraniumThe periosteum of the skull; it limits subperiosteal collections to a single bone because it is firmly attached at sutures.

Blood in the loose areolar layer vs Subperiosteal blood (cephalohaematoma): Loose areolar collections spread widely (even causing 'black eyes'); subperiosteal collections are limited to a single bone by suture attachments.

Loose areolar layer infection vs Pericranium infection: Loose-areolar infection can travel via emissary veins into the cranial sinuses (dangerous); pericranial infection stays localised.

1. The loose areolar (fourth) layer is the 'dangerous area' because emissary veins here connect to the intracranial venous sinuses.
  2. Blood or pus in the loose areolar layer can spread anteriorly into the eyelids, producing 'black eyes'.
  3. A subperiosteal collection is limited to one bone because the pericranium is firmly attached at the sutures.
  4. The sensory nerves of the scalp come from all three divisions of the trigeminal anteriorly and from C2/C3 posteriorly.

study.html:
LetterLayerKey point

CConnective tissueVessels & nerves; bleeds profusely
AAponeurosis (galea)Tough sheet; wounds gape if cut
