PPericraniumPeriosteum; limited by sutures

scenarios.title: The Bleeding That Won't Stop
scenarios.vignette: A child falls and sustains a 3 cm cut on the top of the head. Despite its small size it bleeds alarmingly and the edges gape apart.
scenarios.q: Why does it bleed so much and gape, and how do you control it?
scenarios.a: The wound has cut through the connective tissue layer (where vessels are held open by fibrous septa, so they cannot retract) and through the epicranial APONEUROSIS (so the bellies of occipitofrontalis pull the edges apart, making it gape). Firm direct pressure controls the bleeding, and the aponeurosis must be repaired for the wound to heal without gaping.
pearls: Vessels held open by septa → profuse bleeding
Aponeurosis cut → wound gapes
Control with direct pressure; close the galea

quiz.q: What does the 'A' in the SCALP layers stand for?
quiz.e: S-C-A-L-P: Skin, Connective tissue, Aponeurosis, Loose areolar tissue, Pericranium.

quiz.q: How many layers does the scalp have?
quiz.e: Five layers, spelled out by the word SCALP.

quiz.q: The muscle of the scalp is the:
quiz.e: Occipitofrontalis, with frontal and occipital bellies joined by the aponeurosis.

quiz.q: Which three layers of the scalp move together as one unit?
quiz.e: The outer three (skin, connective tissue, aponeurosis) glide together on the loose areolar layer.

quiz.q: Why do scalp wounds bleed profusely?
o: No clotting factors in the scalp
Vessels are held open by fibrous septa and cannot retract
High arterial pressure in the head
quiz.e: In the connective tissue layer, fibrous septa anchor the vessels open so they cannot constrict.

quiz.q: A scalp wound gapes widely only if which layer is cut?
quiz.e: Cutting the aponeurosis lets the two bellies of occipitofrontalis pull the wound apart.

quiz.q: Which scalp layer is the surgical 'gliding' plane?
quiz.e: The loose areolar layer is the natural cleavage/gliding plane and the surgical plane.

quiz.q: Why is the loose areolar layer called the 'dangerous area' of the scalp?
o: Emissary veins connect it to intracranial venous sinuses
quiz.e: Emissary veins here link to the dural venous sinuses, so infection can spread into the cranium.

quiz.q: A subperiosteal collection of blood is limited to one bone because:
o: The pericranium is firmly attached at the sutures
quiz.e: Pericranium (periosteum) is firmly bound at suture lines, confining subperiosteal blood to a single bone.

quiz.q: Blood in the loose areolar layer may track forward to cause:
quiz.e: It can spread into the eyelids since there is no bony barrier anteriorly, producing periorbital bruising.

quiz.q: The posterior scalp is supplied with sensation mainly by which nerves?
quiz.e: The back of the scalp is supplied by the greater and lesser occipital nerves (C2/C3).

quiz.q: Scalp arteries are notable for:
o: Anastomosing freely, allowing flaps to survive on narrow pedicles
Arising from the internal carotid only
quiz.e: Their free anastomoses mean even a large scalp flap can survive on a small pedicle.

flashcards.q: A scalp wound gapes if which layer is cut?

flashcards.a: Loose areolar tissue (emissary veins to sinuses)

flashcards.q: Why is subperiosteal blood limited to one bone?
flashcards.a: Pericranium is firmly attached at the sutures

pearls: Wound gapes only when the aponeurosis is cut.
Subperiosteal blood = one bone; loose-areolar blood = spreads widely.
mistakes: Myth: A subperiosteal haematoma spreads across the whole skull. Truth: It is limited to ONE bone by the suture attachments of the pericranium; it is the loose areolar collection that spreads widely.
Myth: Scalp wounds gape because the skin is tight. Truth: They gape because the APONEUROSIS is cut, letting occipitofrontalis pull the edges apart.

study.html:
Layers of the deep cervical fascia

  • Investing layer (wraps the whole neck, splits for SCM & trapezius)
  • Pretracheal layer (encloses thyroid, trachea, oesophagus)
  • Prevertebral layer (covers the vertebrae & their muscles)
  • Carotid sheath (a condensation of all three)

Subdivisions of the anterior triangle

  • Submental
  • Submandibular (digastric)
  • Carotid
  • Muscular

Contents of the carotid sheath

  • Common/internal carotid artery
  • Internal jugular vein
  • Vagus nerve (X)

StructureFunction
Investing fasciaEncircles the neck and splits to enclose the SCM and trapezius muscles.
Pretracheal fasciaEncloses the thyroid gland and binds it to the larynx, so the thyroid moves on swallowing.
Carotid sheathProtects the great vessels and vagus nerve as they run up the neck.
Accessory nerve (XI)Supplies SCM and trapezius; runs superficially across the posterior triangle where it is vulnerable in lymph-node biopsy.

Investing fascia vs Prevertebral fascia: Investing fascia wraps the whole neck and splits around SCM and trapezius; the prevertebral fascia covers the vertebral column and forms the floor of the posterior triangle.

Carotid sheath vs Pretracheal fascia: The carotid sheath holds the great vessels & vagus; the pretracheal fascia holds the thyroid/trachea and tethers the thyroid to the larynx.

1. There are three layers of deep cervical fascia: investing, pretracheal and prevertebral.
  2. The carotid sheath is a condensation of all three fascial layers.
  3. The pretracheal fascia tethers the thyroid to the larynx, which is why a thyroid swelling rises on swallowing.
  4. The accessory nerve (XI) crosses the posterior triangle to supply the trapezius.

Subdivisions of the posterior triangle

  • Occipital triangle (above the inferior belly of omohyoid)
  • Supraclavicular (subclavian) triangle (below it)

Key fascial spaces (clinical)

  • Retropharyngeal space (can spread to the mediastinum)
  • Submandibular space (Ludwig's angina from teeth)
  • Parapharyngeal space
  • Pretracheal space

Important contents of the posterior triangle

  • Accessory nerve (XI) — crosses it superficially
  • Roots/trunks of the brachial plexus
  • Subclavian artery (third part)
  • External jugular vein

StructureFunction
Prevertebral fasciaForms the floor of the posterior triangle and extends as the axillary sheath around the brachial plexus.
Retropharyngeal spaceA potential space behind the pharynx that allows the pharynx to move on swallowing — and a route for infection to the superior mediastinum.
Submandibular spaceSite of Ludwig's angina; dental infection here can elevate the tongue and obstruct the airway.

Ludwig's angina vs Retropharyngeal abscess: Ludwig's angina is a submandibular-space infection (usually dental) that lifts the tongue and threatens the airway; a retropharyngeal abscess sits behind the pharynx and can track down to the mediastinum.

Accessory nerve in the posterior triangle vs Its surgical risk: The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially (within the investing fascia), so it is easily injured during lymph-node biopsy, causing trapezius weakness and a drooping shoulder.

1. The retropharyngeal space lies between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia and can transmit infection to the superior mediastinum.
  2. Ludwig's angina is a cellulitis of the submandibular space, usually of dental origin, that can obstruct the airway by elevating the tongue.
  3. The inferior belly of omohyoid subdivides the posterior triangle into occipital and supraclavicular triangles.
  4. The prevertebral fascia continues laterally as the axillary sheath around the brachial plexus and subclavian artery.

PretrachealThyroid, trachea, oesophagusThyroid moves on swallowing

SpaceBoundary / contentsClinical danger

PretrachealIn front of trachea, encloses thyroidSpread to the anterior mediastinum
⭐ 'Danger space': between the alar and prevertebral fascia, the retropharyngeal route lets infection descend from the skull base to the diaphragm.

study.h: Triangles of the neck — contents you must know
study.html:
TriangleKey contents

Submandibular (digastric)Submandibular gland, facial artery/vein, hypoglossal & mylohyoid nerves

Supraclavicular (posterior)Third part of subclavian artery, brachial plexus, external jugular vein

scenarios.title: The Dental Infection That Lifts the Tongue
scenarios.vignette: A man with a neglected lower molar infection develops a brawny, tender swelling under the chin and in the floor of the mouth. His tongue is pushed up and he is starting to have difficulty breathing.
scenarios.q: What is this condition and why is it an emergency?
scenarios.a: Ludwig's angina — a spreading cellulitis of the SUBMANDIBULAR space, usually from a lower molar infection. It is an emergency because swelling elevates the tongue and can extend to involve the floor of the mouth and the airway, causing obstruction. Early airway protection is the priority.
pearls: Submandibular space, dental origin
Elevated tongue + airway threat = emergency
Fascial planes determine the direction of spread

scenarios.title: Drooping Shoulder After a Neck Node Biopsy
scenarios.vignette: After excision of a lymph node in the posterior triangle, a patient cannot shrug the shoulder well, the shoulder droops, and arm abduction above the head is weak.
scenarios.q: Which nerve was injured and why is it vulnerable here?
scenarios.a: The ACCESSORY NERVE (CN XI). It crosses the posterior triangle superficially (within the investing fascia) to supply trapezius, so it is easily injured during node biopsy. Trapezius weakness causes a drooping shoulder, weak shrug, and difficulty abducting the arm past 90°.
pearls: Accessory nerve runs superficially in the posterior triangle
Supplies SCM and trapezius
Injury → drooping shoulder, weak shrug

scenarios.title: Brawny Swelling Under the Tongue
scenarios.vignette: A man with a neglected lower molar infection has a tense, tender swelling of the floor of the mouth and under the chin; his tongue is pushed up and he is beginning to drool and struggle to breathe.
scenarios.q: Name the condition and the space involved.
scenarios.a: Ludwig's angina — a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the SUBMANDIBULAR space (sublingual + submylohyoid), usually from a lower molar. Elevation of the tongue and floor of mouth threatens the airway; it is an emergency requiring airway protection and drainage.
pearls: Submandibular space, dental origin
Tongue elevation → airway threat
Emergency: secure the airway

quiz.q: Which muscle divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles?
quiz.e: The sternocleidomastoid (SCM) divides the neck into the anterior and posterior triangles.

quiz.q: The carotid sheath contains all EXCEPT:
quiz.e: The carotid sheath holds the carotid artery, internal jugular vein and vagus nerve; the phrenic nerve lies on scalenus anterior, outside the sheath.

quiz.q: Which gland moves upward on swallowing?
quiz.e: The thyroid is tethered to the larynx by the pretracheal fascia, so it rises on swallowing.

quiz.q: How many layers does the deep cervical fascia have (excluding the carotid sheath)?
quiz.e: Three: investing, pretracheal and prevertebral. The carotid sheath is a condensation of all three.

quiz.q: Which fascial layer splits to enclose the SCM and trapezius?
quiz.e: The investing layer wraps the whole neck and splits around SCM and trapezius.

quiz.q: Which fascia tethers the thyroid to the larynx?
quiz.e: The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid and binds it to the larynx, so it moves on swallowing.

quiz.q: The accessory nerve (XI) is found in which triangle?
quiz.e: The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially, supplying SCM and trapezius.

quiz.q: Which subdivision is NOT part of the anterior triangle?
quiz.e: The occipital triangle is a subdivision of the POSTERIOR triangle.

quiz.q: The prevertebral fascia forms the floor of which triangle and continues as the:
quiz.e: It forms the floor of the posterior triangle and extends as the axillary sheath around the brachial plexus.

quiz.q: Ludwig's angina is an infection of which space?
quiz.e: Ludwig's angina is a submandibular-space cellulitis, usually of dental origin, threatening the airway.

quiz.q: A retropharyngeal abscess is dangerous mainly because it can spread to the:
quiz.e: The retropharyngeal space communicates inferiorly with the superior mediastinum.

quiz.q: Injury to the accessory nerve during a posterior-triangle node biopsy causes:
quiz.e: Loss of trapezius function produces a drooping shoulder and difficulty shrugging/abducting the arm fully.

quiz.q: The inferior belly of omohyoid subdivides the posterior triangle into:
quiz.e: Omohyoid's inferior belly separates the occipital (upper) from the supraclavicular (lower) triangle.

flashcards.q: Which space infection can reach the superior mediastinum?
Accessory nerve (XI) lies in which triangle?

flashcards.a: Carotid bifurcation, IJV, vagus, hypoglossal, ansa cervicalis.

flashcards.q: Third part of the subclavian artery lies in which triangle?

pearls: Pretracheal fascia tethers the thyroid → it rises on swallowing.
Accessory nerve runs superficially in the posterior triangle — easy to injure.
Retropharyngeal/'danger' space connects the skull base to the mediastinum — infections can descend fast.
Accessory nerve is superficial in the posterior triangle — protect it in node biopsy.
mistakes: Myth: The accessory nerve is deep and well protected in the neck. Truth: It runs superficially across the posterior triangle and is easily injured in node biopsy.
Myth: Ludwig's angina is an infection of the retropharyngeal space. Truth: It is a SUBMANDIBULAR space infection (usually dental).

study.html:
The 8 branches of the external carotid artery

  • Superior thyroid
  • Ascending pharyngeal
  • Lingual
  • Facial
  • Occipital
  • Posterior auricular
  • Superficial temporal (terminal)
  • Maxillary (terminal)
Note: Mnemonic: 'Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students'.

Branches of the internal carotid in the neck

  • NONE — the internal carotid gives no branches in the neck

The four arteries feeding the circle of Willis

  • Two internal carotid arteries
  • Two vertebral arteries (which join to form the basilar artery)

StructureFunction
Facial arteryMain supply to the face; tortuous to allow facial movement.
Superficial temporal arterySupplies the side of the scalp; its pulse is felt in front of the ear (and is biopsied in temporal arteritis).
Lingual arteryMain blood supply to the tongue.
Superior thyroid arterySupplies the thyroid; runs with the external laryngeal nerve.

Internal carotid in the neck vs External carotid in the neck: Internal = no neck branches; external = eight branches. Both begin at the carotid bifurcation (upper border of thyroid cartilage).

Carotid sinus vs Carotid body: Sinus = baroreceptor (pressure); body = chemoreceptor (oxygen/CO₂). Both are innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).

1. The common carotid artery divides at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.
  2. The external carotid artery has eight branches.
  3. The internal carotid artery gives no branches in the neck.
  4. The superficial temporal artery pulse is felt just in front of the ear.
  5. The facial artery crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anterior border of masseter.

Clinically key branches of the maxillary artery

  • Middle meningeal artery (enters foramen spinosum)
  • Inferior alveolar artery (to the lower teeth)
  • Sphenopalatine artery (the main artery of epistaxis)

Carotid sinus & body (at the bifurcation)

  • Carotid sinus — a baroreceptor (senses blood pressure)
  • Carotid body — a chemoreceptor (senses O₂/CO₂)
  • Both are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)

Subclavian artery — the three parts (by scalenus anterior)

  • First part (medial) — vertebral, internal thoracic, thyrocervical trunk
  • Second part (behind) — costocervical trunk
  • Third part (lateral) — usually no branches

StructureFunction
Middle meningeal arterySupplies the dura; injured at the pterion → extradural haemorrhage.
Sphenopalatine arteryThe 'artery of epistaxis' — main supply to the nasal cavity.
Carotid sinusBaroreceptor that reflexly slows the heart and lowers blood pressure when stretched (IX).
Circle of WillisAn arterial ring at the base of the brain providing collateral flow if one feeding vessel is blocked.

Right common carotid vs Left common carotid: The right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk; the left arises directly from the arch of the aorta.

Middle meningeal artery vs Sphenopalatine artery: Both are branches of the maxillary artery: the middle meningeal supplies the dura (extradural bleed), the sphenopalatine supplies the nose (epistaxis).

1. The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the maxillary artery and enters the skull through the foramen spinosum.
  2. The sphenopalatine artery (a branch of the maxillary) is the principal artery supplying the nasal cavity and a major source of posterior epistaxis.
  3. The carotid sinus is a baroreceptor and the carotid body a chemoreceptor, both supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).
  4. The circle of Willis is formed by the two internal carotid and two vertebral (basilar) arteries, joined by communicating arteries.
  5. The right common carotid arises from the brachiocephalic trunk, whereas the left arises directly from the aortic arch.

scenarios.title: The Severe Nosebleed
scenarios.vignette: An elderly hypertensive man has a torrential nosebleed from deep in the nose that is not controlled by pinching the nostrils. The bleeding appears to come from far back in the nasal cavity.
scenarios.q: Which artery is the likely source, and from what is it derived?
scenarios.a: A posterior epistaxis from the SPHENOPALATINE ARTERY, the principal artery of the nasal cavity and a branch of the MAXILLARY artery (itself a terminal branch of the external carotid). Posterior bleeds are harder to control than anterior (Little's area) bleeds and may require packing or arterial ligation/embolisation.
pearls: Sphenopalatine = 'artery of epistaxis'
Branch of the maxillary artery (external carotid system)
Posterior bleeds are deep and harder to control

quiz.q: The common carotid artery divides into the:
quiz.e: It divides into the external (face/neck) and internal (brain/eye) carotid arteries.

quiz.q: Which artery supplies the brain?
quiz.e: The internal carotid artery supplies the brain (and the eye via the ophthalmic artery).

quiz.q: Where can you feel the superficial temporal artery pulse?
o: Just in front of the ear
In the midline of the neck
quiz.e: Its pulse is felt just anterior to the ear, over the temple.

quiz.q: How many branches does the external carotid artery have?
quiz.e: Eight branches — 'Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students'.

quiz.q: How many branches does the internal carotid artery give in the neck?
quiz.e: The internal carotid artery gives no branches in the neck.

quiz.q: The common carotid divides at the level of the:
o: Upper border of the thyroid cartilage
quiz.e: The bifurcation is at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (about C3–C4).

quiz.q: Which artery is the main supply to the tongue?
quiz.e: The lingual artery is the main blood supply to the tongue.

quiz.q: The facial artery crosses the mandible at the anterior border of which muscle?
quiz.e: The facial artery crosses the lower border of the mandible at the anterior edge of masseter, where its pulse can be felt.

quiz.q: The middle meningeal artery is a branch of the:
quiz.e: It is a branch of the maxillary artery and enters the skull via the foramen spinosum.

quiz.q: The principal artery involved in severe posterior epistaxis is the:
quiz.e: The sphenopalatine artery (a maxillary branch) is the main artery of the nasal cavity.

quiz.q: The carotid sinus functions as a:
quiz.e: The carotid sinus is a baroreceptor (senses blood pressure); the carotid body is the chemoreceptor.

quiz.q: Both the carotid sinus and carotid body are innervated by the:
quiz.e: Both receive their afferent supply from the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).

quiz.q: The left common carotid artery arises directly from the:
quiz.e: The left common carotid arises directly from the aortic arch; the right arises from the brachiocephalic trunk.

quiz.q: The circle of Willis is fed by the internal carotid arteries and the:
quiz.e: Two internal carotids plus two vertebral arteries (forming the basilar) feed the circle of Willis.

flashcards.a: Some Anatomists Like Freaking Out Poor Medical Students

flashcards.q: Middle meningeal artery is a branch of?

pearls: Carotid SINUS = pressure (baro); carotid BODY = oxygen (chemo); both IX.
Middle meningeal & sphenopalatine are both maxillary-artery branches.
mistakes: Myth: The middle meningeal artery comes from the internal carotid. Truth: It is a branch of the MAXILLARY artery (external carotid system).
Myth: Both common carotids arise from the brachiocephalic trunk. Truth: Only the RIGHT does; the LEFT arises directly from the aortic arch.

study.html:
Tributaries forming the retromandibular vein

  • Superficial temporal vein
  • Maxillary vein
Note: It then splits: an anterior division joins the facial vein, a posterior division helps form the external jugular vein.

The 'collar' of superficial lymph nodes

  • Occipital
  • Mastoid (retroauricular)
  • Parotid (preauricular)
  • Buccal (facial)
  • Submandibular
  • Submental

Key deep cervical nodes

  • Jugulodigastric node (tonsil & tongue)
  • Jugulo-omohyoid node (tongue)

StructureFunction
External jugular veinDrains the superficial scalp and face; visible on the side of the neck and used as a guide to central venous pressure.
Deep cervical nodesThe final common pathway for ALL head-and-neck lymph; they lie along the internal jugular vein.
Jugulodigastric nodeThe 'tonsillar node' — enlarges in tonsillitis and tongue/oropharyngeal cancer.

Submental nodes vs Submandibular nodes: Submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue, the central lower lip and the chin; submandibular nodes drain most of the face and the rest of the anterior tongue.

Jugulodigastric node vs Jugulo-omohyoid node: Jugulodigastric (high, near the jaw angle) = tonsil/tongue; jugulo-omohyoid (lower) = the 'node of the tongue'.

1. The deep cervical lymph nodes lie along the internal jugular vein and receive all head-and-neck lymph.
  2. The retromandibular vein forms from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins within the parotid gland.
  3. The jugulodigastric node enlarges in tonsillitis.
  4. The tip of the tongue drains to the submental lymph nodes.

Dangerous venous connections of the facial vein

  • Facial → superior ophthalmic → cavernous sinus
  • Facial → deep facial → pterygoid plexus → cavernous sinus
Note: Valveless, so infection can flow backward into the skull.

Specific node drainage you must know

  • Tongue tip → submental nodes
  • Most of the tongue → submandibular & jugulo-omohyoid nodes
  • Lower lip (central) → submental nodes
  • Tonsil → jugulodigastric node

StructureFunction
Facial veinDrains the face; its valveless link to the cavernous sinus makes the upper lip and nose a 'danger area'.
Jugulo-omohyoid nodeThe 'lymph node of the tongue' — important in staging tongue cancer.
Thoracic duct / right lymphatic ductReturn all head-and-neck lymph (left/​right respectively) to the great veins at the root of the neck.

Facial vein vs Retromandibular vein: The facial vein (with its valveless cavernous-sinus link) drains the front of the face; the retromandibular vein forms within the parotid from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.

Tongue tip drainage vs Tongue body drainage: The tip drains to the SUBMENTAL nodes (and can cross the midline — important in cancer), while the body drains to submandibular and jugulo-omohyoid nodes.

1. The facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and via the pterygoid plexus, and is valveless.
  2. The jugulo-omohyoid node is known as the lymph node of the tongue.
  3. Lymph from the tongue tip may cross the midline to nodes on both sides, which is important when staging tongue cancer.
  4. Head-and-neck lymph drains via the jugular lymph trunks into the thoracic duct (left) or the right lymphatic duct (right) at the root of the neck.

Node groupDrains
SubmentalTongue tip, central lower lip, chin
SubmandibularMost of the face, anterior tongue, gums
Parotid (preauricular)Scalp side, eyelid, external ear
OccipitalBack of the scalp
JugulodigastricTonsil, tongue (the 'tonsillar node')
Jugulo-omohyoidTongue ('node of the tongue')
Deep cervicalEverything (final common pathway)

scenarios.title: The Lump Behind the Jaw with a Sore Throat
scenarios.vignette: A teenager with a severe sore throat and swollen tonsils has a tender, enlarged lymph node just below and behind the angle of the mandible.
scenarios.q: Which node is this and why is it enlarged?
scenarios.a: The JUGULODIGASTRIC node (the 'tonsillar node'), a member of the deep cervical chain lying just below and behind the angle of the jaw. It enlarges because it drains the palatine tonsil, which is inflamed in tonsillitis. Persistent enlargement without infection should raise concern about tongue or oropharyngeal cancer.
pearls: Jugulodigastric = the tonsillar node
Drains tonsil and tongue
Persistent node → think malignancy

quiz.q: What is the main vein draining the head and neck?
quiz.e: The internal jugular vein is the principal (deep) drainage of the head and neck.

quiz.q: All lymph of the head and neck ultimately drains to the:
quiz.e: The deep cervical chain (along the internal jugular vein) is the final common pathway.

quiz.q: The external jugular vein is found:
o: Superficially on the side of the neck
In the floor of the mouth
quiz.e: It runs superficially across the sternocleidomastoid.

quiz.q: The retromandibular vein is formed by the superficial temporal vein and the:
quiz.e: It forms within the parotid from the superficial temporal and maxillary veins.

quiz.q: The tip of the tongue drains to which lymph nodes?
quiz.e: The tongue tip drains to the submental nodes (and may cross the midline).

quiz.q: Which node is the 'tonsillar node'?
quiz.e: The jugulodigastric node, near the angle of the jaw, drains the tonsil and tongue.

quiz.q: The deep cervical nodes lie along which structure?
quiz.e: The deep cervical chain runs along the internal jugular vein.

quiz.q: The facial vein is dangerous because it connects to the cavernous sinus and is:
quiz.e: Being valveless, it permits backward (retrograde) spread of infection to the cavernous sinus.

quiz.q: The jugulo-omohyoid node is best known as the node of the:
quiz.e: It is the 'lymph node of the tongue' and is important in staging tongue cancer.

quiz.q: Why is tongue-tip cancer staged carefully on BOTH sides of the neck?
o: Tongue-tip lymph may cross the midline to both submental sides
It drains only to the thoracic duct
quiz.e: Tongue-tip lymphatics can cross the midline, so disease may involve nodes bilaterally.

quiz.q: Head-and-neck lymph from the LEFT side returns to the venous system via the:
quiz.e: The left side drains via the thoracic duct; the right via the right lymphatic duct.

quiz.q: The facial vein connects to the cavernous sinus via the:
quiz.e: Via the angular and superior ophthalmic veins (and the pterygoid plexus).

flashcards.q: Why is the facial vein dangerous?

pearls: Jugulodigastric = tonsillar node; jugulo-omohyoid = node of the tongue.
Facial vein is valveless → cavernous-sinus danger.
mistakes: Myth: The tongue tip drains to the submandibular nodes. Truth: The tongue TIP drains to the SUBMENTAL nodes (and may cross the midline).
Myth: Each side of the neck drains via the thoracic duct. Truth: Only the LEFT side drains via the thoracic duct; the right uses the right lymphatic duct.

study.html:
The three conchae (turbinates) of the lateral wall

  • Superior concha
  • Middle concha
  • Inferior concha
Note: Each overhangs a 'meatus' into which sinuses or ducts drain.

What drains into each meatus

  • Inferior meatus → nasolacrimal duct (tears)
  • Middle meatus → frontal, maxillary & anterior ethmoidal sinuses
  • Superior meatus → posterior ethmoidal sinuses
  • Sphenoethmoidal recess → sphenoid sinus

Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus)

  • A meeting of several arteries on the anterior nasal septum
  • The commonest site of (anterior) nosebleeds

StructureFunction
Olfactory mucosa (roof)Contains the receptors of smell; their nerves (CN I) pass through the cribriform plate.
Maxillary sinusThe largest sinus; its high opening makes it prone to retained infection (sinusitis).
Little's areaA vascular watershed on the anterior septum — the usual source of childhood nosebleeds.

Inferior meatus vs Middle meatus: The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct (tears); the middle meatus receives the frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoidal sinuses.

Anterior epistaxis vs Posterior epistaxis: Anterior bleeds come from Little's area on the septum (common, easy to control); posterior bleeds come from the sphenopalatine artery (heavier, harder to control).

1. The maxillary sinus is the largest of the paranasal sinuses.
  2. The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus.
  3. The frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle meatus.
  4. Little's area on the anterior septum is the commonest site of nosebleeds.

Arteries supplying the nasal cavity

  • Sphenopalatine artery (maxillary) — the main one
  • Anterior & posterior ethmoidal arteries (ophthalmic / internal carotid)
  • Greater palatine, superior labial, septal branches
Note: Little's area is where the internal and external carotid supplies meet.

Why the maxillary sinus drains poorly

  • Its ostium (opening) is HIGH on its medial wall
  • So it must drain against gravity
  • → predisposes to sinusitis

StructureFunction
Sphenopalatine arteryThe principal artery of the nasal cavity and the main source of severe posterior epistaxis.
Cribriform plate relationFracture here tears the meninges, causing CSF rhinorrhoea and a route for meningitis.
Maxillary sinus floorClosely related to the upper molar roots — dental infection or extraction can involve the sinus.

Maxillary sinus drainage vs Other sinuses: The maxillary sinus drains through a HIGH opening, so it must work against gravity and is the most prone to infection; the others drain more favourably.

Sphenopalatine artery vs Ethmoidal arteries: The sphenopalatine (external carotid system) supplies most of the cavity; the ethmoidal arteries (internal carotid system, via ophthalmic) supply the roof — they meet at Little's area.

1. The sphenopalatine artery is the principal artery of the nasal cavity and the main source of severe posterior epistaxis.
  2. The maxillary sinus opening lies high on its medial wall, so it drains poorly and is prone to sinusitis.
  3. The floor of the maxillary sinus is related to the roots of the upper molar teeth, linking dental and sinus disease.
  4. Olfactory nerve filaments pass through the cribriform plate; a fracture there causes CSF rhinorrhoea and anosmia.
  5. Little's area is a watershed where branches of both the internal and external carotid systems anastomose.

SiteWhat drains there
Inferior meatusNasolacrimal duct (tears)
Middle meatusFrontal, maxillary, anterior ethmoidal sinuses
Superior meatusPosterior ethmoidal sinuses
Sphenoethmoidal recessSphenoid sinus

scenarios.title: The Toothache That Was Really Sinusitis
scenarios.vignette: A patient complains of aching upper back teeth and facial pressure that worsens on bending forward, following a cold. The teeth themselves look healthy on dental examination.
scenarios.q: What is the link between the teeth and the sinus here?
scenarios.a: Maxillary sinusitis. The FLOOR of the maxillary sinus is closely related to the roots of the upper molar and premolar teeth, so sinus inflammation can be felt as toothache. The pain worsens on bending because the sinus drains through a HIGH opening and pressure rises when the head is lowered. (Conversely, a dental infection can spread into the sinus.)
pearls: Maxillary sinus floor ≈ upper molar roots
High ostium → poor drainage → pain worse bending forward
Dental and sinus disease can masquerade as each other

scenarios.title: Unilateral Cheek Pain and a Bad Taste
scenarios.vignette: A patient has aching in one cheek and upper teeth, nasal blockage and a foul taste after a recent upper molar root-canal. Tapping the upper molars reproduces the pain.
scenarios.q: What is the diagnosis and the anatomical link?
scenarios.a: Odontogenic maxillary sinusitis. The floor of the maxillary sinus overlies the roots of the upper molars/premolars, so a periapical infection (or an oroantral communication after extraction) can seed the sinus. The high sinus ostium drains poorly, so pus collects, giving facial pain worse on bending and a foul taste/discharge.
pearls: Maxillary sinus floor ≈ upper molar roots
High ostium → poor drainage → stasis
Dental source must be treated too

quiz.q: How many pairs of paranasal sinuses are there?
quiz.e: Four pairs: frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal and sphenoidal.

quiz.q: Which is the largest paranasal sinus?
quiz.e: The maxillary sinus is the largest.

quiz.q: The conchae (turbinates) function to:
o: Increase surface area to condition air
quiz.e: They increase surface area and create turbulence to warm, moisten and filter air.

quiz.q: The nasolacrimal duct drains into which meatus?
quiz.e: Tears drain via the nasolacrimal duct into the inferior meatus.

quiz.q: The frontal and maxillary sinuses drain into which meatus?
quiz.e: They drain into the middle meatus, along with the anterior ethmoidal sinuses.

quiz.q: The commonest site of nosebleeds is:
o: Little's area on the anterior septum
quiz.e: Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the anterior septum is the usual source of nosebleeds.

quiz.q: Olfactory nerve filaments reach the brain by passing through the:
quiz.e: They pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

quiz.q: The principal artery of the nasal cavity is the:
quiz.e: The sphenopalatine artery (a maxillary branch) is the main artery and the source of posterior epistaxis.

quiz.q: Why is the maxillary sinus prone to retained infection?
o: Its opening is high on the medial wall (drains against gravity)
quiz.e: Its ostium is high, so it must drain against gravity, favouring stasis and sinusitis.

quiz.q: The floor of the maxillary sinus is closely related to the:
o: Roots of the upper molar teeth
quiz.e: It overlies the upper molar/premolar roots, linking dental and sinus disease.

quiz.q: A fracture of the cribriform plate can cause:
quiz.e: It tears the meninges and shears olfactory filaments, causing CSF leak from the nose and loss of smell.

quiz.q: The sphenoid sinus drains into the:
quiz.e: The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha.

flashcards.q: Main artery of the nasal cavity?
Why does the maxillary sinus drain poorly?

flashcards.a: Roots of the upper molar teeth

flashcards.q: Why does odontogenic infection reach the maxillary sinus?
flashcards.a: The sinus floor overlies the upper molar/premolar roots.

pearls: Maxillary sinus drains through a HIGH opening → prone to sinusitis; floor sits on the upper molar roots.
Cribriform plate fracture → CSF rhinorrhoea + anosmia.
mistakes: Myth: Most nosebleeds come from the sphenopalatine artery. Truth: Most (anterior) bleeds come from Little's area; the sphenopalatine causes the heavier POSTERIOR bleeds.
Myth: Upper molar roots are unrelated to the sinuses. Truth: The maxillary sinus floor overlies the upper molar roots, so dental and sinus disease can mimic each other.

study.html:
Nerve supply of the ANTERIOR 2/3 of the tongue

  • General sensation → lingual nerve (V3)
  • Taste → chorda tympani (VII)
Note: Two different nerves for the front of the tongue.

Nerve supply of the POSTERIOR 1/3 of the tongue

  • Both general sensation AND taste → glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)
Note: One nerve does both at the back.

The intrinsic vs extrinsic idea

  • Intrinsic muscles change the tongue's shape
  • Extrinsic muscles (genioglossus, hyoglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus) change its position

StructureFunction
GenioglossusProtrudes (sticks out) the tongue; the safety muscle that keeps the airway open.
Lingual nerve (V3)General sensation (touch, pain, temperature) of the front of the tongue.
Chorda tympani (VII)Taste from the front of the tongue (and saliva control).
Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)Both taste and general sensation of the back of the tongue, including the gag reflex afferent.

Anterior 2/3 of tongue vs Posterior 1/3 of tongue: Front: TWO nerves — lingual (V3) for sensation, chorda tympani (VII) for taste. Back: ONE nerve — glossopharyngeal (IX) for both.

Lingual nerve vs Chorda tympani: The lingual nerve (V3) carries general sensation; the chorda tympani (VII) hitches a ride with it but carries TASTE.

1. General sensation of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is by the lingual nerve (V3).
  2. Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is by the chorda tympani (VII).
  3. Both sensation and taste of the posterior third of the tongue are by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).
  4. Genioglossus protrudes the tongue.
  5. The hard palate is supplied with sensation by the greater palatine and nasopalatine nerves (V2).

Motor supply of the tongue muscles

  • ALL tongue muscles → hypoglossal nerve (XII)
  • EXCEPT palatoglossus → pharyngeal plexus (vagus, X)

Muscles of the soft palate & their nerves

  • Tensor veli palatini → mandibular nerve (V3) — the exception
  • Levator veli palatini → pharyngeal plexus
  • Palatoglossus → pharyngeal plexus
  • Palatopharyngeus → pharyngeal plexus
  • Musculus uvulae → pharyngeal plexus

Sensory supply of the palate

  • Hard palate → greater palatine & nasopalatine nerves (V2)
  • Soft palate → lesser palatine nerves (V2) + some IX

StructureFunction
Hypoglossal nerve (XII)Motor to all tongue muscles except palatoglossus.
PalatoglossusA tongue muscle in name, but a palate muscle in supply — pharyngeal plexus (vagus), not XII.
Tensor veli palatiniTenses the soft palate AND opens the auditory tube; supplied by V3 (the soft-palate exception).
Levator veli palatiniRaises the soft palate to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing (pharyngeal plexus).

All tongue muscles (XII) vs Palatoglossus (vagus): Every tongue muscle is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve EXCEPT palatoglossus, which is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus).

Tensor veli palatini (V3) vs Other soft-palate muscles (vagus): Tensor veli palatini is the soft-palate exception (supplied by V3); all the others are pharyngeal plexus (vagus).

1. All muscles of the tongue are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (XII) except palatoglossus, which is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus).
  2. All muscles of the soft palate are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus except tensor veli palatini, which is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).
  3. Tensor veli palatini also opens the auditory tube, which is why swallowing 'pops' the ears.
  4. In a hypoglossal nerve lesion the protruded tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion (the weak genioglossus).
  5. The lingual nerve lies close to the third lower molar, where it is at risk during extraction.

Posterior 1/3Glossopharyngeal (IX)Glossopharyngeal (IX)

scenarios.title: The Tongue That Points to the Lesion
scenarios.vignette: After a penetrating neck injury a man is asked to stick out his tongue. It deviates to the right, and over time the right half looks wasted and wrinkled.
scenarios.q: Which nerve is damaged and why this direction of deviation?
scenarios.a: The right HYPOGLOSSAL nerve (XII). The genioglossus protrudes the tongue by pushing it forward; with the right one paralysed, the intact left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak side, so the protruded tongue deviates TOWARD the lesion. Chronic denervation causes wasting and wrinkling on that side.
pearls: Tongue deviates TOWARD the side of an XII lesion
Genioglossus is the protrusor
Wasting/fasciculation suggests a lower motor neuron lesion

quiz.q: The palate is divided into which two parts?
quiz.e: A hard (bony, anterior) palate and a soft (muscular, posterior) palate.

quiz.q: Which muscle sticks the tongue out?
The soft palate rises during swallowing to close off the:
quiz.e: It seals the nasopharynx so food does not enter the nose.

quiz.q: General sensation of the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is carried by the:
quiz.e: The lingual nerve (V3) carries general sensation; taste is by the chorda tympani.

quiz.q: Taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue is carried by the:
quiz.e: The chorda tympani (a branch of VII) carries taste from the front of the tongue.

quiz.q: Both taste and sensation of the posterior 1/3 of the tongue are by the:
quiz.e: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) supplies both modalities at the back of the tongue.

quiz.q: The hard palate receives sensation mainly from which division of the trigeminal?
quiz.e: The greater palatine and nasopalatine nerves (branches of V2) supply the hard palate.

quiz.q: Which tongue muscle is NOT supplied by the hypoglossal nerve?
quiz.e: Palatoglossus is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus); the rest are hypoglossal.

quiz.q: Which soft-palate muscle is NOT supplied by the pharyngeal plexus?
quiz.e: Tensor veli palatini is supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3) — the exception.

quiz.q: In a hypoglossal nerve lesion the protruded tongue deviates:
o: Toward the side of the lesion
quiz.e: It deviates toward the lesion because the intact genioglossus pushes the tongue to the weak side.

quiz.q: Besides tensing the soft palate, tensor veli palatini also:
quiz.e: It opens the auditory tube, which is why swallowing equalises ear pressure.

quiz.q: The lingual nerve is at particular risk during extraction of which tooth?
quiz.e: The lingual nerve runs close to the lower third molar and can be injured during its extraction.

quiz.q: The chorda tympani joins which nerve to reach the tongue?
quiz.e: The chorda tympani (VII) joins the lingual nerve (V3) to be distributed to the anterior tongue.

flashcards.a: Toward the side of the lesion

flashcards.q: Tensor veli palatini also does what?

pearls: All soft-palate muscles = vagus EXCEPT tensor veli palatini (V3).
XII lesion → tongue points TOWARD the lesion.
mistakes: Myth: All soft-palate muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. Truth: All EXCEPT tensor veli palatini, which is V3.
Myth: In an XII lesion the tongue deviates away from the lesion. Truth: It deviates TOWARD the lesion side.

study.html:
Where each duct opens

  • Parotid duct → opposite the upper 2nd molar
  • Submandibular duct → floor of mouth, beside the frenulum
  • Sublingual ducts → along the floor of the mouth

The structure running THROUGH the parotid

  • Facial nerve (VII) — divides it into superficial & deep parts
  • Retromandibular vein
  • External carotid artery

StructureFunction
Parotid duct (Stensen's)Carries saliva forward, piercing buccinator to open opposite the upper 2nd molar.
Submandibular duct (Wharton's)Runs forward and UPWARD to open beside the frenulum — a course that favours stones.
Facial nerve in the parotidPasses through the gland (dividing it) but does not supply it — a vital surgical relationship.

Parotid duct opening vs Submandibular duct opening: The parotid duct opens high, opposite the upper 2nd molar; the submandibular duct opens low, in the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum.

Facial nerve & the parotid vs Facial nerve & the submandibular gland: The facial nerve runs THROUGH the parotid (key in parotid surgery) but only relates to the submandibular gland via its marginal mandibular branch nearby.

1. The parotid duct opens opposite the upper second molar.
  2. The submandibular duct opens in the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum.
  3. The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland, dividing it into superficial and deep parts.
  4. The submandibular gland produces most of the resting saliva.

Parasympathetic (secretomotor) supply

  • Parotid → glossopharyngeal (IX) via the OTIC ganglion
  • Submandibular & sublingual → facial (VII) via the SUBMANDIBULAR ganglion (chorda tympani)
Note: Two glands, two pathways — the classic exam point.

Why the submandibular gland forms stones easily

  • Its duct runs upward (against gravity)
  • Its saliva is thicker (more mucous)
  • → stasis favours stone formation

StructureFunction
Otic ganglionThe parasympathetic relay for the PAROTID; fibres come from IX and reach the gland via the auriculotemporal nerve.
Submandibular ganglionThe parasympathetic relay for the SUBMANDIBULAR & SUBLINGUAL glands; fibres come from VII via the chorda tympani.
Auriculotemporal nerveCarries the parotid's secretomotor fibres; injury and misdirected regeneration cause Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating).

Parotid parasympathetic (IX, otic) vs Submandibular parasympathetic (VII, submandibular ganglion): Parotid is driven by glossopharyngeal fibres relayed in the otic ganglion; the submandibular & sublingual are driven by facial fibres (chorda tympani) relayed in the submandibular ganglion.

Submandibular stone vs Parotid stone: Stones are far more common in the submandibular gland because its duct runs uphill and its saliva is more mucous; parotid stones are uncommon.

1. Parasympathetic secretomotor supply to the parotid is from the glossopharyngeal nerve, relayed in the otic ganglion and carried by the auriculotemporal nerve.
  2. Parasympathetic supply to the submandibular and sublingual glands is from the facial nerve via the chorda tympani, relayed in the submandibular ganglion.
  3. Salivary stones are most common in the submandibular gland because its duct runs upward and its secretion is mucous.
  4. Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating) results from misdirected regeneration of parotid parasympathetic fibres into sweat glands after injury or surgery.
  5. A swelling that enlarges before and during meals suggests duct obstruction by a stone.

GlandDuct opensParasympathetic pathway

scenarios.title: The Swelling That Comes with Meals
scenarios.vignette: A man notices a painful swelling under his jaw that appears just before and during eating and then slowly settles. No saliva can be milked from the duct opening in the floor of his mouth.
scenarios.q: What is the diagnosis and why this gland?
scenarios.a: A SUBMANDIBULAR salivary stone (sialolithiasis) obstructing the duct. The submandibular gland is the commonest site because its duct (Wharton's) runs UPWARD against gravity and its saliva is thicker (mucous), favouring stasis and stone formation. Stimulating saliva at mealtimes raises pressure behind the blockage, producing the painful 'mealtime swelling'.
pearls: Mealtime swelling = obstructive sialadenitis
Submandibular = the classic stone gland (uphill, mucous duct)
Stone may be palpable in the floor of the mouth

quiz.q: How many pairs of MAJOR salivary glands are there?
Which is the largest salivary gland?
quiz.e: The parotid gland is the largest.

quiz.q: Which gland produces most of the resting (unstimulated) saliva?
quiz.e: The submandibular gland contributes most of the resting saliva.

quiz.q: The parotid duct opens opposite the:
quiz.e: The parotid (Stensen's) duct opens opposite the upper second molar.

quiz.q: The submandibular duct opens:
o: In the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum
quiz.e: Wharton's duct opens in the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum.

quiz.q: Which structure runs through the parotid gland, dividing it?
quiz.e: The facial nerve runs through the parotid, dividing it into superficial and deep parts.

quiz.q: Salivary stones are most common in which gland?
quiz.e: The submandibular gland, because its duct runs uphill and its saliva is mucous.

quiz.q: The parasympathetic supply to the PAROTID is relayed in which ganglion?
quiz.e: Parotid secretomotor fibres (from IX) relay in the otic ganglion.

quiz.q: The parasympathetic supply to the SUBMANDIBULAR gland comes from which nerve?
quiz.e: From the facial nerve via the chorda tympani, relayed in the submandibular ganglion.

quiz.q: The parotid's secretomotor fibres reach the gland on which nerve?
quiz.e: They travel from the otic ganglion on the auriculotemporal nerve.

quiz.q: Frey's syndrome (sweating while eating) after parotid surgery is due to:
o: Misdirected parasympathetic fibres regrowing into skin sweat glands
quiz.e: Regenerating parotid parasympathetic fibres reconnect to sweat glands, so eating triggers facial sweating.

quiz.q: A malignant parotid tumour may present with facial weakness because:
o: It invades the facial nerve passing through the gland
quiz.e: The facial nerve runs through the parotid and can be invaded by malignant tumours, unlike benign ones.

flashcards.a: Facial nerve (divides it), retromandibular vein, external carotid
Gustatory sweating after parotid injury (misdirected fibres)

pearls: Submandibular = the stone gland (uphill duct + mucous saliva).
Parotid duct opens opposite the upper 2nd molar.
mistakes: Myth: The submandibular duct opens opposite the upper 2nd molar. Truth: That is the PAROTID duct. The submandibular duct opens in the floor of the mouth.
Myth: The facial nerve supplies secretion to the parotid. Truth: It passes THROUGH the parotid but supplies the submandibular & sublingual glands instead.

study.html:
The three constrictor muscles

  • Superior constrictor
  • Middle constrictor
  • Inferior constrictor
Note: They contract in sequence to push the food bolus downward (peristalsis).

The three 'longitudinal' (elevator) muscles

  • Stylopharyngeus
  • Palatopharyngeus
  • Salpingopharyngeus

Lymphoid ring guarding the entrance (Waldeyer's ring)

  • Pharyngeal tonsil (adenoid)
  • Tubal tonsils
  • Palatine tonsils
  • Lingual tonsil

StructureFunction
Superior constrictorBegins the squeeze at the top of the pharynx during swallowing.
StylopharyngeusElevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing; the only muscle supplied by IX.
Pharyngeal plexusThe shared nerve network (mainly vagus) that drives almost all pharyngeal muscles.
Palatine tonsilLies in the oropharynx between the two arches; commonly inflamed (tonsillitis).

Constrictor muscles vs Longitudinal muscles: Constrictors squeeze the bolus downward (circular); longitudinal muscles (stylo-, palato-, salpingo-pharyngeus) shorten and widen the pharynx to receive it.

Gag reflex afferent (IX) vs Gag reflex efferent (X): Touching the oropharynx is sensed by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX, afferent); the muscular response is via the vagus (X, efferent).

1. The three constrictor muscles contract in sequence to push the food bolus into the oesophagus.
  2. Most pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus).
  3. The palatine tonsils lie in the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
  4. The auditory tube opens into the nasopharynx.

Motor supply of the pharynx

  • All constrictors + palatopharyngeus + salpingopharyngeus → pharyngeal plexus (vagus, X)
  • Stylopharyngeus → glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) — the exception

Sensory supply (lining)

  • Nasopharynx → maxillary nerve (V2)
  • Oropharynx → glossopharyngeal (IX)
  • Laryngopharynx → vagus (X)

Killian's dehiscence

  • A weak gap between the two parts of the inferior constrictor (thyropharyngeus & cricopharyngeus)
  • Site of a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum)

StructureFunction
Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)Motor to stylopharyngeus and sensory to the oropharynx; carries the afferent limb of the gag reflex.
Vagus nerve (X)Motor to all other pharyngeal muscles (via the plexus) and the efferent limb of the gag reflex.
Inferior constrictor (cricopharyngeus part)Acts as the upper oesophageal sphincter; failure to relax contributes to a pharyngeal pouch.

Stylopharyngeus (IX) vs All other pharyngeal muscles (X): Stylopharyngeus is the ONLY pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve; everything else is the pharyngeal plexus (vagus).

Killian's dehiscence vs The rest of the pharyngeal wall: Killian's dehiscence is a weak gap in the inferior constrictor where mucosa can herniate to form a pharyngeal pouch; the rest of the wall is fully muscular.

1. Stylopharyngeus is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX); all others are supplied by the vagus via the pharyngeal plexus.
  2. The afferent limb of the gag reflex is the glossopharyngeal nerve and the efferent limb is the vagus.
  3. Killian's dehiscence is a weak area between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor, the site of a pharyngeal pouch.
  4. Sensation of the nasopharynx is by V2, the oropharynx by IX, and the laryngopharynx by the vagus.
  5. The palatine tonsil is supplied by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery and drains to the jugulodigastric node.

scenarios.title: The Regurgitated Food and Neck Lump
scenarios.vignette: An older man complains of food coming back up undigested hours after eating, bad breath, and a gurgling swelling in the lower neck that he can sometimes empty by pressing on it.
scenarios.q: What is the lesion and where anatomically does it arise?
scenarios.a: A pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum): mucosa has herniated through KILLIAN'S DEHISCENCE, the weak gap between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor. Failure of cricopharyngeus to relax raises pressure and pushes the lining out, forming a pouch that collects food and regurgitates it later.
pearls: Killian's dehiscence = between thyropharyngeus & cricopharyngeus
Regurgitation of undigested food + halitosis
Cricopharyngeus dysfunction is the driver

quiz.q: How many parts does the pharynx have?
How many constrictor muscles does the pharynx have?
quiz.e: Three: superior, middle and inferior constrictors.

quiz.q: The palatine tonsils are located in the:
quiz.e: The palatine tonsils lie in the oropharynx between the two arches.

quiz.q: The auditory (Eustachian) tube opens into which part of the pharynx?
quiz.e: The auditory tube opens into the nasopharynx.

quiz.q: Most pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the:
quiz.e: The pharyngeal plexus (mainly vagus) supplies almost all pharyngeal muscles.

quiz.q: The constrictor muscles function to:
o: Push the food bolus down in sequence
quiz.e: They contract sequentially to propel the bolus into the oesophagus.

quiz.q: Which lymphoid structure is the 'adenoid'?
quiz.e: The pharyngeal tonsil (in the nasopharynx roof) is called the adenoid when enlarged.

quiz.q: Which pharyngeal muscle is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)?
quiz.e: Stylopharyngeus is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by IX; the rest are vagus.

quiz.q: The afferent limb of the gag reflex is carried by the:
quiz.e: Sensation (afferent) is via IX; the motor response (efferent) is via the vagus (X).

quiz.q: A pharyngeal pouch herniates through which weak area?
quiz.e: Killian's dehiscence lies between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor.

quiz.q: Sensation of the nasopharynx lining is mainly by which nerve?
quiz.e: The nasopharynx is supplied by the maxillary nerve (V2).

quiz.q: The palatine tonsil typically drains to which lymph node?
quiz.e: The palatine tonsil drains to the jugulodigastric ('tonsillar') node.

pearls: Gag reflex: in by IX, out by X.
Pharyngeal pouch = Killian's dehiscence (between thyro- and cricopharyngeus).
mistakes: Myth: The palatine tonsils are in the nasopharynx. Truth: They are in the OROPHARYNX, between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.
Myth: A pharyngeal pouch comes through the piriform fossa. Truth: It herniates through KILLIAN'S DEHISCENCE in the inferior constrictor.

study.html:
The cartilages of the larynx

  • Thyroid (1)
  • Cricoid (1) — the only complete ring
  • Epiglottis (1)
  • Arytenoid (2 — paired)
  • Corniculate (2)
  • Cuneiform (2)

The two nerves of the larynx (both from the vagus)

  • Superior laryngeal nerve (external + internal branches)
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve

What each laryngeal nerve does

  • Internal laryngeal → SENSATION above the vocal cords
  • External laryngeal → MOTOR to cricothyroid
  • Recurrent laryngeal → MOTOR to all other muscles + SENSATION below the cords

StructureFunction
Cricoid cartilageThe only complete ring of cartilage in the airway; landmark for the cricothyroid membrane (emergency airway).
Posterior cricoarytenoidThe only muscle that ABDUCTS (opens) the vocal cords — vital for breathing.
CricothyroidTenses the vocal cords to raise pitch; supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
Internal laryngeal nerveSensation above the cords; its loss abolishes the cough reflex (aspiration risk).

Superior laryngeal nerve vs Recurrent laryngeal nerve: The superior laryngeal supplies sensation above the cords (internal) and cricothyroid (external); the recurrent supplies all other muscles and sensation below the cords.

Above the vocal cords vs Below the vocal cords: Sensation above the cords = internal laryngeal nerve; sensation below the cords = recurrent laryngeal nerve. The cords are the dividing line.

1. The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway.
  2. Both laryngeal nerves are branches of the vagus.
  3. The internal laryngeal nerve supplies sensation above the vocal cords.
  4. The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.

Actions on the vocal cords

  • Posterior cricoarytenoid → the ONLY abductor (opens the cords)
  • Lateral cricoarytenoid & others → adduct (close the cords)
  • Cricothyroid (external laryngeal) → tenses/lengthens the cords (pitch)
  • Vocalis/thyroarytenoid → relax & fine-tune

Why the recurrent laryngeal nerves take different paths

  • Right → hooks under the right subclavian artery
  • Left → hooks under the arch of the aorta (so it is longer & more vulnerable)

StructureFunction
Recurrent laryngeal nerveMotor to all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid, and sensation below the cords.
External laryngeal nerveMotor to cricothyroid; runs with the superior thyroid artery (at risk in thyroid surgery → loss of pitch).
Cricothyroid membraneThe site for an emergency surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy).

Posterior cricoarytenoid vs All other intrinsic muscles: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only ABductor (opens the cords); all the others ADduct (close) or tense them. Bilateral loss is life-threatening.

Right recurrent laryngeal nerve vs Left recurrent laryngeal nerve: The right hooks under the subclavian artery; the left hooks under the aortic arch and is longer, so it is more often injured (e.g. by lung/aortic disease).

1. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal cords.
  2. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid.
  3. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch of the aorta, while the right hooks under the right subclavian artery.
  4. The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery and may be injured in thyroid surgery, weakening the voice (loss of pitch).
  5. Sensation below the vocal cords is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

scenarios.title: The Hoarse Voice After Thyroid Surgery
scenarios.vignette: A patient is hoarse after a thyroidectomy. On examination one vocal cord lies motionless near the midline.
scenarios.q: Which nerve was injured, and what does it normally do?
scenarios.a: The RECURRENT LARYNGEAL NERVE on that side. It supplies all the intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid, including the only abductor (posterior cricoarytenoid). Unilateral injury leaves the cord paralysed near the midline, causing hoarseness. The nerve is at risk near the inferior thyroid artery during thyroid surgery.
pearls: Recurrent laryngeal nerve = all muscles except cricothyroid
Near the inferior thyroid artery in surgery
Bilateral injury can obstruct the airway — an emergency

quiz.q: Which cartilage forms the Adam's apple?
quiz.e: The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple).

quiz.q: What structure covers the airway during swallowing?
quiz.e: The epiglottis folds back over the laryngeal inlet during swallowing.

quiz.q: The two jobs of the larynx are airway protection and:
quiz.e: The larynx protects the airway and produces the voice.

quiz.q: Which laryngeal cartilage is the only COMPLETE ring?
quiz.e: The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the airway.

quiz.q: Both nerves of the larynx are branches of which cranial nerve?
quiz.e: Both the superior and recurrent laryngeal nerves arise from the vagus (X).

quiz.q: The internal laryngeal nerve supplies sensation:
quiz.e: The internal laryngeal nerve supplies sensation above the vocal cords.

quiz.q: The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the:
quiz.e: Cricothyroid is the only intrinsic muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.

quiz.q: Which is the ONLY muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal cords?
quiz.e: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor; bilateral loss endangers the airway.

quiz.q: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles EXCEPT:
quiz.e: Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve; all others are recurrent laryngeal.

quiz.q: The LEFT recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the:
quiz.e: The left hooks under the aortic arch (the right hooks under the right subclavian artery).

quiz.q: The external laryngeal nerve runs with which artery and is at risk in thyroid surgery?
quiz.e: It runs with the superior thyroid artery; injury weakens the voice (loss of pitch via cricothyroid).

quiz.q: An emergency surgical airway (cricothyroidotomy) is made through the:
quiz.e: The cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, is the site for an emergency airway.

quiz.q: Sensation BELOW the vocal cords is supplied by the:
quiz.e: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below the cords (the internal laryngeal supplies above).

flashcards.q: Only abductor of the vocal cords?
Recurrent laryngeal supplies all muscles except?

pearls: Sensation: above cords = internal laryngeal; below = recurrent laryngeal.
Left recurrent laryngeal loops under the aortic arch (longer, more vulnerable).
mistakes: Myth: Both recurrent laryngeal nerves loop under the aortic arch. Truth: Only the LEFT does; the right loops under the right subclavian artery.
Myth: The thyroid cartilage is a complete ring. Truth: The CRICOID is the only complete ring; the thyroid is incomplete posteriorly.
